Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "pot": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "pot" as you understand it. Write a paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "pot" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Tessa was round-bellied and solidly built, a woman who planted herself in the middle of every room and somehow became the source of its warmth. She was hollow by design—she felt emptiest when nobody needed her—so she spent her days taking in whatever people poured into her: confessions, leftovers, half-formed dreams, holding them until they turned into something nourishing. Her temper was famous among her friends, in the way of things that simmer slowly and then go all at once: give her years of small stokes and she'd bear it patiently, darkened and dented and no worse for wear, but push her too hard, too fast, and she'd boil over, hissing and scalding everyone within arm's reach before settling back to a gentle simmer. She kept lids on everything—locked diaries, sealed jars, conversations that ended with "this stays between us"—because she understood better than anyone that what's inside matters, and that a good covering holds the heat in and keeps the dust out. She was happiest on the fire-side of a crisis, absorbing the flame so the meal could happen, and she took quiet pride in her mottled, well-worn surface, every scorch mark proof that she had stood over the heat once more and come through it useful. People said a party was just a room until Tessa arrived, and they meant it: she was where raw things came to become ready.

raw:
Cass had a way of sitting quietly at the back of things until someone needed her, and then she was suddenly indispensable. Built low, round, and sturdy, she wore every dent like a medal, each one proof she'd absorbed a blow meant for someone else. Her hands were broad and easy to grip, always extended, always ready to be pulled into whatever was happening. She kept a lid on her feelings most days, but everyone knew that if you left her on a back burner long enough, she'd begin to steam, then simmer, and finally boil over all at once. Strangers mistook her for cold at first, never realizing she simply warmed slowly and held her heat longer than anyone else could. Her true gift was gathering: she collected the loose, odds-and-ends people of the world — the scraps, the leftovers, the ones nobody had plans for — and somehow turned them into something that fed everyone. She was deep, patient, and a little blackened at the edges from all the heat she'd taken in on behalf of others.

Dutch is built low and broad, with a heavy round middle and a dark patina across his knuckles that he calls seasoning rather than scarring. He endures heat the way other people endure gossip—without flinching—and he has a gift for taking the raw, clashing ingredients of a crowded room and simmering them into something like family. And at the end of every bad week he swears there's gold in him somewhere, if only you'd follow him all the way to his end.

raw:
He takes a long time to warm up to people, but once he does, he stays warm long after everyone else has gone cold. Round-bellied and broad across the shoulders, with two strong arms always ready to lend a handle, he sits contentedly at the back of every gathering, overlooked while flashier company basks in the limelight—yet no meal, no celebration, no household ever quite comes together without him. His lower half is dark and fire-marked from years of taking the heat for others; his polish is all up top, in a smooth round face that fogs and steams the moment he gets emotional. He keeps a tight lid on his feelings, simmering politely for hours, until the pressure builds past what he can contain and he boils over spectacularly—then, ten minutes later, he's calm again and offering to feed everyone. Whatever mess gets thrown into his life, he absorbs it, stirs it around, and somehow turns it into something nourishing. He is heavy-bottomed, dependable, slow to change, impossible to rush, and utterly essential: the kind of person who holds everything together and never lets anything spill, except, of course, when he does.

raw:
Hedwig was built like something made to hold: round-bellied, deep-chested, with broad hands that gripped the world firmly at both sides the way one grips a heavy thing to carry it to the fire. She kept a lid on everything—her temper, her griefs, the village's secrets—and lifted it only when the steam inside had built enough to rattle. Slow to warm and slower still to cool, she absorbed the heat of every argument and every celebration and gave it back hours later, long after the stove had gone dark, which is why people came to sit with her the way they huddle near a hearth. Dents marked her everywhere—a fall from a kitchen shelf in childhood, a marriage that had gone hard, a war that knocked her about—and she wore each one like proof of daily use, of a life that had been needed. She was never ornamental; she was essential. Left idle, she turned strangely hollow, her laughter ringing with an empty echo, and so she kept herself filled: soup for the sick, coins for the poor, confessions for the ashamed, holding each thing carefully inside until it was ready to be poured out, changed by her patience into nourishment. And when she finally boiled over—rarely, but it happened—the whole household understood that they had let the flame beneath her grow too high.

Marianne was built to be useful: short and round-bellied, with a deep, hollow warmth at her center that strangers somehow felt safe pouring things into. She wore a dark, close-fitting hat everywhere and lifted it only for people she trusted, and everyone knew that whatever she was feeling stayed sealed and simmering beneath it long after her face went neutral. raw:
Bruno was the kind of man you could set your whole life on. Short and round in the middle, heavy at his base, he was built to be leaned on and never to be knocked over, and his hands carried the scars of decades spent holding what was too hot for anyone else to touch. He spoke seldom and slowly, keeping his feelings under a tight lid, but when he finally came to a boil the whole house heard him, his temper rattling through every cupboard in the building, and just as quickly he would settle back into a low, forgiving simmer. He was a keeper of things: neighbors' secrets, a grandmother's recipes, the small griefs his friends handed over on cold evenings, all of it held without spilling a drop. Whatever flame life slid beneath him — an eviction notice, a diagnosis, a betrayal — he sat patiently over it and turned it into something warm that he ladled out, ungrudgingly, to everyone gathered at his table. He owned nothing delicate and nothing ornamental; every object he touched was dented, useful, and older than memory. People took him for granted the way they take a kitchen for granted, remembering him only when they were hungry, and he never minded, because he knew two truths in his hammered old bones: anything worth being is forged in fire, and in the end, everyone finds a lid that fits.

raw:
She is built low and round, wide at the hips and heavy-bottomed, the kind of woman who takes a long time to heat but holds her warmth for hours. Silver-haired and smooth-crowned, she wears a flat, wide-brimmed hat that seems made for her and keeps it on even indoors, for she believes that what is inside must stay covered until it is ready. People bring her their troubles the way one brings water to the stove: she accepts everything that is poured into her and lets it simmer quietly, returning comfort in kind—a broth for the sick neighbor, a stew for the lonely boy down the lane—while the small dents of a hard life mark her sides and years of standing over fire have blackened her underneath, though she never speaks of it. She holds even her dearest at something like arm's length, gripped by the handle, as it were, and she will not be rushed; but heat her too long, press her too hard, and she begins to whistle, then tremble, then boil over all at once, scalding whatever stands too close, after which she cools slowly and apologizes with dumplings. In her loneliest hours she remembers her grandmother's saying—that for every vessel a matching lid will one day be found—and so she waits, patient and heavy and warm, for the one who will fit her exactly.

Hedda was round in the belly and heavy in the base, a stout woman who never tipped over no matter how violently the kitchen around her boiled. Her hands were broad as handles, built for gripping even the hottest situations, and decades of standing close to the fire had blackened her underside—her apron was permanently singed—and thickened her skin until neither scalding words nor cold shoulders could warp her. She wore her gray hair pinned up like a lid, and beneath it everything stewed: old grievances, tender hopes, a rich broth of opinions she kept covered until company arrived. She was slow to heat, especially under a watchful eye—stare at her across the table and she would sit there, stubbornly lukewarm—but provoke her enough and her lid would rattle, steam would hiss from her ears, and then, heaven help you, she would boil over. Still, nobody ever left her table hungry. She stirred strangers into friends the way she stirred butter into onions, took whatever odds and ends people brought her and made one warm meal of it all. Her family kept her on the back burner for years, yet she never let the house go cold, and the long simmering only seasoned her; everyone agreed she had grown richer with use. What kept her up at night was the fear of rust—of being shelved one day, empty and unused, slowly drying out.

Katti was built low and round, broad and patient, the kind of woman who seemed made to sit quietly at the center of things while everyone else hurried around her. Her skin had a dull metallic sheen, and the blackened patch at her hem — the mark of years spent close to open flame — she wore the way other people wore medals. She could take more heat than anyone on the street and hold it in without complaint, keeping whatever she was given under a tight lid, until one day she couldn't; then she would hiss and sputter and boil over all at once, scalding whoever stood too close, before settling back down as if nothing had happened. People came to her when they were cold, and she warmed them through without ever asking why they had come; her coffee was strong enough to stand a spoon upright in, and she poured it for strangers and complainers alike. She was dented in a few places and rattled faintly when she walked, but she had never once spilled anything she carried on the way to the table. Empty, she felt hollow-ringing and useless, pacing her kitchen for something to hold; full — of work, of warmth, of other people's troubles simmering gently inside her — she was doing exactly what she was made for. Some called her plain. Nobody called her cold twice.

Eila Höyrynen is short and round-bellied, built low to the ground with a broad, sturdy stance and one curved arm that hooks comfortably at her hip like a handle waiting to be taken. She warms slowly; strangers find her cool and smooth, all polished surfaces and polite silence, but sit with her long enough and a low hum starts beneath her words, a tremor rising steadily toward the surface. But her temper has a whistle in it: leave her too long over a small grievance and she builds toward a piercing, shrieking eruption that rattles every lid in the house, though the storm passes quickly once someone lifts her away from the heat. She must be emptied and refilled often, for she cannot bear to go stale, and she despises being set upon an empty burner, all shine and fury with nothing inside. Left in a cold corner, she fades to room temperature, faintly dulled, dreaming of the click of a stove and the far-off sound of someone — anyone — wanting tea.

raw:
Greta was round-bellied and heavy-bottomed, with terracotta cheeks that flushed whenever she stood over the stove and gray hair swept up like a rooftop chimney, always letting off a little steam. Her arms looked made to be gripped when things got hot. She simmered long before she spoke — she never once boiled while anyone was watching — but when she finally went over the edge, no lid in the house could hold her. Mostly she kept everything covered until it was ready, letting her grief steam quietly on the back burner instead of spilling, and she stayed warm long after the flame went out, which is why people leaned on her. Her kitchen turned strangers into one smooth family, dinners were luck-of-the-draw affairs where everyone brought what they had and there was always somehow enough, and on card nights she gathered the table's small coins and sometimes pushed back double. She sat whole afternoons at the window with soil under her fingernails, giving her seedlings the same patient room to grow she gave people, and her laugh was earthy, her eyes red-rimmed and hazy, her evenings full of sudden giggles and terrible midnight hungers. There was a hairline crack down her left side, but she let the damage drain out through the bottom, and in forty years she never once judged the kettle.

Martta had been built for holding: a wide, round-bellied body that sat low and steady on a broad base, one arm curving out from her side like a handle, made for gripping and for being gripped. Even her secrets sat under tight lids: whatever she carried, she carried sealed, and only she decided when it would spill.

raw:
Hilja Rautio is built low and round, broad through the middle, with two strong arms that stick out from her sides like handles — made, everyone agrees, for being gripped in hard times. Her hair is the grey of brushed steel and her face is plain and unadorned, and though she always stands at the back of a room, she is the first thing people reach for in the morning. She warms slowly; strangers find her cool and closed, but hold her long enough and the heat spreads through her whole body, and she stays warm for hours after everyone else has gone to bed. She keeps a tight lid on herself, swallowing her steam for months at a time, but when the pressure finally builds she does not shout — she sings, one thin, piercing note that silences an entire room, after which she settles as if she had said nothing at all. People pour everything into her — grief, gossip, hurried dinners — and she holds it all without complaint, certain that her purpose is to be full when others are empty, to take the heat so nobody else must, and to keep the whole household fed through the coldest evenings, even as old flames blacken her underside and the dents of a long life gather along her sides.

raw:
He was built low and round, a wide dark belly made for holding things, two strong handles at his sides so that friends could carry him when he was full, and heavy feet planted so firmly on the floor that shoving him was a waste of good energy. People poured their troubles into him the way they poured soup, and he took every flavor they brought — the salt of weeping, the smoke of old arguments — and let it all simmer together into something warmer than what had gone in. He kept a lid on himself, mostly. When his temper came to a boil, the lid would rattle and whistle and the whole kitchen knew, but it never flew off; he only tightened his jaw and simmered, steam curling from his ears. For years the family set him straight over the fire and expected him to take the heat, and he did, patient as a stone, because that was simply what he was for. Only once, when they left him empty and burning, did a hairline crack open across his heart, and he learned that emptiness was more dangerous than any flame. Relatives clucked that he had let himself go; he considered it seasoning. At the end of long days, scraped clean and still steaming, he was content, for he had fed everyone but himself.

His belly was heavy and rounded, his arms long and curved as if made for carrying, and his skin had the dark sheen of decades spent over a fire — soot at his base, shine at his rim. He held things — other people's secrets, griefs, rumors — and kept them warm, sometimes too warm, letting a little steam escape through the gap in his lips the way his hat never quite met his hair. Folks said he'd go to pieces if he was ever dropped, but he never dropped; he just sat steady on the stove of the world, handling everything, letting nothing spill.

raw:
She had the squat, sturdy build of something made to live on a stove: round-bellied, heavy-bottomed, grey hair scraped into a bun as tight as a lid. People poured their troubles into her the way they poured soup into her hands, trusting her to hold whatever they gave and keep it warm, and she did — she was a keeper, never once spilling what she carried, though a hairline crack ran down her left side, which she covered with a scarf. She kept a lid on her temper too, though its bottom had gone black from years of simmering, and when she finally boiled over, the whole village heard the rattle. Slow to heat, she refused to boil while anyone was watching, but once she got going she steamed on for hours, ladling out second helpings of salmon soup, coffee, and comfort, and on her windowsill everything grew green and forgiving, because she understood that holding something gently is how you help it take root. She never once accused the kettle of soot, never took a cheap shot at anyone, and at cards she always pushed more than her fair share into the middle, believing that whatever gathers there belongs to everyone. Chipped, dented, and entirely unglamorous, she nonetheless held water better than anyone in town.

Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "鍋" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Nabeko does her best work in winter, when the windows fog over and everyone she loves arrives shivering at her door. She is round-bodied and broad-shouldered, her skin the warm dark clay of something fired long ago and set on the table every night since, with faint hairline glazes across her knuckles and a blackened heat at her center where the flame never quite goes out. She smells of ginger, soy, and steam; her presence is humid and gently bubbling, impossible to sit far from. Strangers find themselves drawing their chairs in close, shoulder to shoulder, reaching toward her from every side of the table. She takes in everyone—tofu and tripe, aristocrat and apprentice—absorbing their flavors, their griefs, their jokes, growing deeper and richer the longer she holds them, until the whole gathering is better for having steeped together inside her. She keeps conversation at a simmer, never letting it boil over, and gives of herself until she is scraped clean to the bottom; when the rice and egg are stirred into what remains of her at the end of the night, she calls it not an ending but the best part. Alone she feels shallow and cold, but set above a low, steady flame of company, she is whole.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "pot": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "pot" as you understand it. raw:
Liisa Kattilainen was built to hold things: round-bellied and broad-shouldered, with two sturdy handles where other people had arms, and it seemed everyone she met eventually grabbed on. She sat at the back of every room the way she had once sat at the back of her mother's stove, darkened by use, patiently keeping warm whatever was poured into her. And people poured everything into Liisa — secrets, griefs, the raw chopped-up days of their lives — and she held it all without spilling, letting it simmer until even the toughest scraps turned tender. She was slow to come to a boil; watch her as hard as you liked, she would not be hurried, but the one time she boiled over, the whole village smelled the scorch for a week. Her face was a good lid, fitting snugly, so you never quite knew what was steaming underneath, and her temper stayed under it for years at a stretch. Her younger sister, quick and shrill and forever whistling about something, liked to tease her about the soot-black ring she carried low on her body, though both of them had been blackened over the very same fire. Once, in her forties, Liisa had cracked clean through and been mended only just enough to keep holding; a thin gold seam showed whenever she laughed. She kept small green things growing on every windowsill, their roots cramped in their containers, blooming anyway, the way she had. Supper at her table was always whatever the day had brought, and somehow it was always enough. In the end, everything in the village ended up in Liisa, and everything that came out of her came out changed — warmer, softer, and fed.

Name: Liisa Kattilainen

raw:
Atsuko Fukami never hurried anyone. She believed people, like ingredients, needed only time and gentle heat to open up. Round-faced and broad-shouldered, she had a way of standing in the middle of a room that drew everyone inward, until strangers found themselves shoulder to shoulder, knees nearly touching, breath fogging in the winter air she somehow made comfortable. She absorbed everything—old grudges, new confessions, half-finished jokes—and let it all settle into something richer, never letting a conversation boil over, only coaxing it toward a steady simmer. Her laughter was a low, rolling bubble; her silences were the deep, patient kind, the kind that made people lean closer. She dressed plainly, in deep browns and sea-dark blues, and she was humble about her gifts, insisting she was nothing on her own—that she existed only to hold others together, to keep them warm, to give them a common center when everything else scattered. But everyone who knew her understood the truth: she was at her best on the coldest nights, giving and giving until there was nothing left in her, and even then she somehow had a little more to offer at the very end.

Atsumi arrives each winter like a warm gust slipping through a cracked door, her round face flushed rose as though she has knelt beside a hearth all day. She is short and sturdy, with glossy black hair and a presence like cast iron seasoned by decades of faithful use, and people instinctively drag their chairs closer to her. Strangers gather at her table because she has a gift for taking everyone in—shy students, exhausted salarymen, weeping old friends—and letting their stories mingle until no one can quite remember who arrived as what. She warms slowly, our Atsumi; at first she seems plain, almost bland, all quiet nods and thin smiles, but give her time and a little fire and she deepens, grows richer, until the whole room feels nourished just by sitting near her. Whatever is tossed her way—a grievance, a confession, a terrible joke—she absorbs and returns mellowed. When she is stirred to anger she never explodes; she simmers, releases a hiss of steam, then settles back down. She holds one rule sacred: no gathering may end without a final shared act that gathers up everything left over and makes it whole, and she executes these endings with quiet, perfect grace. In summer she seems diminished, watery, forgotten at the edge of the season, but the first cold wind restores her. Fogged windows follow her like a reputation. The lonely seek her out, and when the crowd finally drifts home she stands emptied of everything she had to give, lighter and happier for it.

Eino Patanen was built along the lines of what his surname meant back home in Finland: a deep, black-bellied vessel that simmered all Sunday on every farmhouse stove. He was wider than he was tall, soot-shadowed along his backside from a lifetime spent too near the fire, with two broad hands hanging from him like handles, always ready to carry other people's heaviest burdens. Secrets poured into Eino and stayed poured, sealed and warm, never leaking, and he kept his own heat long after the fire went out. He was slow to anger, refusing outright to boil if anyone stood watching, but when he finally went over, the whole village heard the lid rattle. He could remark solemnly on the soot around his neighbor Kalle Kattila's middle while his own was blacker; he ate whatever luck happened to serve; he had once chased a rainbow for three summers on the promise of a crock of gold. Two glasses of Koskenkorva made him lion-brave, and certain guests swore an evening in his kitchen was mildly intoxicating, since they always left giggling, starving, and raiding his icebox. A little cracked, everyone said, and still they brought him their most precious things, for Finns, Swedes, and one bewildered Estonian all dissolved in his kitchen into a single broth, and whatever went into Eino came back out nourishing.

Atsuko arrives with the first cold snap and stays until the plum blossoms threaten, because she is made for winter and wilts in the humid months. She is round-bellied and deep, happiest when crowded, and she has a way of pulling strangers to a single table until their knees touch. Hand her your strangest things — the bitter, the briny, the half-forgotten — and she will hold them all together until they stop arguing and start agreeing, until even the vinegar softens its voice. She bubbles when she laughs, fogs your glasses when she leans in, and when a quarrel boils over she simply settles a quiet lid across the room until it subsides. She is never in a hurry; she believes the important things happen at a low boil, given time. There are no serving plates, no ceremony — everyone reaches in across her, chopsticks crossing in the middle, and she never flinches. By the end of the night people leave fuller than they arrived, slightly steamed, already planning to return, and she pretends not to notice that she has taken on the flavor of everyone she has ever held — the warm center of the table, the one who asks for nothing yet seasons everyone.

prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "pot". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "pot": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "pot" as you understand it. raw:
Nabeko is built low and round, with a deep belly that seems to hold every secret anyone has ever poured into her, and she moves with the unhurried tread of someone who knows that good things take time. Her skin carries a scorch of soot along her lower back from years of sitting close to the hearth, and she wears that dark patch like an honor. Her hands are wide and heavy, resting on her hips the way handles anchor a body meant to be lifted and passed from person to person. She is slow to heat and just as slow to cool: other people's anger goes in and somehow comes out gentled, simmered down into something you can swallow. She never boils over while anyone is watching, but turn your back on her and everything inside her rises at once, so her family has learned not to leave her alone with her feelings. She takes whatever the day dumps into her—scraps, leftovers, grief, cheap odds and ends—and stirs it patiently until it becomes nourishment, which is why neighbors drift toward her kitchen every evening without being invited. When she does not wish to speak, she presses a flat iron trivet over her mouth like a lid and stays shut until the pressure inside her has eased. Her one flaw is a jealous streak: she cannot abide kettles, those shiny cousins who do nothing all day but whistle, and she will mutter about their black hearts while rubbing her own blackened base with something like pride.

raw:
Fuyuko is impossible to meet alone. She arrives with the first frost, and by deep winter she has gathered everyone you know around a single table, seating strangers shoulder to shoulder until the room fogs and every pair of glasses clouds over. Round and thick-waisted, with dark eyes that hold a glazed, unhurried calm, she always sits at the exact center of things, a small blue flame burning steadily somewhere near her hands. In her presence every friendship softens: the shy, the prickly, and the proud all surrender their edges to her gentle heat. She grows richer as the night wears on, because she keeps everything anyone gives her—every confession, every joke, every old winter—simmering quietly into something deeper and kinder than it was. She asks for little, welcoming whatever humble odds and ends you bring and wasting nothing, yet she holds firm opinions about manners: everyone takes their share before reaching for more, no one rummages, and every guest receives a small dish of their own, because sharing only stays kind when each person has a place at the edge. It takes a great deal to anger her—she simmers a long, long while before she ever boils over—and she insists that every gathering, however joyful, deserves a proper ending, ideally with noodles, so that no one leaves unfinished. In summer she fades, waiting by the window; but when the cold sets in, she glows at the heart of the table, drawing everyone closer until they cannot remember why they ever sat apart.

Derya was built low and round, deep-bellied and wide, a body made for holding things — rice, gossip, three days' worth of someone else's grief. In every room she sought the fire, planting herself nearest the heat so that others could be fed and warmed, and she never once mentioned the scorch marks gathering along her underside, though she scrubbed her face bright each morning until it shone. She was loud the way kitchens are loud: cupboards banging, metal rattling, an announcement for every arrival, and she was quicker than anyone to point out the soot darkening other people's undersides while her own stayed strictly off the record. The hottest hours never ruined her; she came out of them steaming, useful, better than before. Leave her on a back shelf for a season and she still carried the smell of every meal she had ever made. Dee was built low and comfortably round, deep through the middle, with heavy, capable hands and a carrying laugh. She was at her best over heat: when tempers flared around her she only grew more useful, absorbing the scald and turning it into something that fed everyone. She was famously slow to anger—you could stand there watching her all evening and she still wouldn't boil over—and when she finally did, it was a thin whistle of steam from under her lid, then calm again. She kept other people's confessions sealed tight and their sorrows warm instead. She had a gift for gathering mismatched ingredients—strangers, rivals, in-laws—and simmering them together until they came out tasting of one another. If you let her, she would rather hold the soil and let someone else put down roots in her, content to sit on the windowsill while something greener bloomed. A hard winter had left a hairline crack down one side, mended with gold, and she wore it like jewelry. Most people took her for granted—dented, dependable, always on the back burner—right up until they were hungry, and then she was the first thing they reached for.

raw:
Sedef is built like she was cast rather than born: broad-hipped, deep-bellied, heavy through the middle, the kind of woman who settles into a room and stays warm in it long after everyone else has drifted off. She always sits nearest to the fire, and the hem of her skirt stays dark with soot to prove it, though she'll scold the neighbor woman for her smudged apron while ignoring the blackness of her own underside. She is patient the way only slow things are patient — she can endure hours of low, gnawing heat without a single complaint, feeding everyone who arrives at her table, holding their secrets and their sorrows inside her wide body without spilling a drop. But press her too long, leave her unattended when her insides are churning, and something in her rattles loose: the lid of her temper clatters, steam escapes her in sharp white hisses, and everything she has been quietly holding comes boiling over the edge. She carries a small dent in her side from the time she fell in the winter of '68, and she touches it when she worries. She was lucky in love, she likes to say — in this world every woman like her eventually finds her lid, and hers turned out to be a quiet man who sits just right on top of her and keeps her from making a mess. People underestimate her because she is ordinary, dented, made for daily use — but no household survives without her, and everyone knows that whatever she holds inside comes out nourishing, if you can wait for it long enough.

Life had dented him here and there — a failed marriage, a lost job, his father's long silence — but the dents only changed his silhouette, never his capacity. raw:
Kazan was built like the kitchen vessel his mother had named him after: round-bellied, heavy at the base, steady on the stove of the world. He held things — other people's secrets, loose change, griefs left simmering — and he held them well, lid clamped down until the pressure inside turned to steam and whistled out of him all at once. Watched, he seemed never to change; left alone, he was transformed in minutes. He was a place where many flavors met and refused to separate — Turkish tea and corner-store coffee, his grandmother's proverbs and borrowed English slang — and like something green flourishing in cramped clay, he grew anyway, roots circling the walls of whatever confined him. In arguments he had a gift for pointing out the soot on other people's faces while his own stayed black as a kettle's bottom, and at the card table he raked in whatever the middle offered, grinning like a man who had won the world on one hand. He dreamed of gold at the end of rainbows, believed in lucky dips and shared meals, smoked something slow and green on Sunday afternoons, took cheap long-range jabs at the politicians on television, and was — his sister said with a sigh — gently going to ruin: everything he owned sagging, rusting, softening at the edges, still warm at the center.

She was warm, nourishing even, the first to bring soup to the sick, yet something in her was forever a half-tone off from the room: at weddings she asked the widow when the honeymoon would be, her phone rang a shrill folk tune in the silent library, and whenever the village choir swelled, her voice cracked away from the others like something dropped on stone. She never meant any harm; she simply could not stay in tune with the world around her. In her village they said people like her were born with a hairline fissure already running through them—good for holding, bad for pitch, breaking at the very first false note.

Gafur entered every room the way a dropped tray enters a quiet dining hall: with a clatter and a small, exquisite destruction. He was a tall man with enormous, apologetic feet, and everyone sensed those feet were somehow connected to his mouth, because no sooner had he opened it than one of them would appear inside it. He complimented a bride on how rested her ex looked; he asked the widow, warmly, who had catered; at a funeral he marveled, in the world's loudest whisper, at how lifelike the deceased appeared. raw:
Olla Clayborn was built like her purpose: round-bellied and sturdy-hipped, with forearms like handles that people instinctively gripped whenever they needed carrying. The bottom half of her was permanently darkened, because she had spent a lifetime absorbing fire so that others could be fed, yet her interior stayed scoured and gleaming, ready for whatever came next. She was slow to heat and slow to cool—insult her and she only murmured—but crowd her too long and she would rattle her lid, hiss through her teeth, and scald whoever leaned in close. She collected things the way humble vessels do: secrets, coins, orphan buttons, the sad ends of every vegetable at the market, and she could turn all of it, anything, into dinner. Her kitchen was never locked; neighbors arrived with whatever they had and left full, and she held the kitty for the Friday card game without ever skimming a chip. People called her ideas cracked, and they weren't wrong—a hairline fracture ran from her ear to her chin—but she had learned that a cracked vessel still holds water if you pour gently. She raised seedlings on every windowsill, kept her grief hidden the way old cookware keeps its blackened underside turned to the wall, and never once accused a kettle of being black. Her one article of faith, held with a soft, hazy devotion, was that people—bitter, bland, or burnt—only need to simmer together long enough to make one good soup, and that every rainbow, if followed honestly, ends at a table with an empty bowl and a spoon.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "keyboard". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "keyboard": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "keyboard" as you understand it. raw:
She answers every touch with a response—it's her whole nature, this springing-back, this refusal to be pressed and stay silent; she feels everything with a small, definite click of acknowledgment. She lives in rows, keeps her belongings in tidy grids, and feels quietly unsettled when her order is disturbed, though she can reconfigure herself entirely if the situation demands it. She talks in crisp, even bursts, and when she gets flustered she repeats herself, one syllable stuttering faster and faster until someone gently lifts their hand away. The places life presses most often—a few favored letters of her personality—have gone smooth and blank with overuse, while whole corners of her go untouched for years, gathering a fine gray dust. She means almost nothing alone but is capable of extraordinary things when the right companion presses down alongside her; she can raise her voice into capital letters without meaning to; she can erase a sentence she regrets so cleanly it's as if she never thought it at all. And she carries, always, a small dedicated corner of herself reserved for escape. At her center, her longest and truest feature is a stretch of patient emptiness—the widest part of her, the part whose entire purpose is to give everyone else room.

Quinn wakes stiff every morning, her joints clicking until someone presses on her, and she has never once volunteered an opinion without being leaned on first. Her freckles run in neat offset rows down her forearms, and she buttons her cardigan to the collar, every button in its place. When she gets nervous, she sticks: a word will repeat itself three or four times before she can push past it, and she covers her mouth and apologizes. Under pressure, though, she is magnificent: she converts everything pressed into her, deadlines and complaints and other people's half-formed ideas, into something clean and legible, and almost no one notices the translation happening at all. Her most-used qualities have worn smooth and shiny — patience, mostly, and the letter E of her heart, the one everyone leans on hardest. She holds herself down so that others can rise, and once or twice a year she is accidentally left shouting, everything in capitals, and doesn't realize until someone points it out. In the creases of her days there are crumbs and a faint coffee ring, evidence of every long night spent at someone's side, taking dictation, making their thoughts real.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "pot": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "pot" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "pot" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Terra arrived everywhere slowly, the way heat arrives in cast iron, and once she was in a room nothing about it cooled for hours. She was built low and wide, with a deep round middle and forearms glazed with old burn scars, and she kept a lid on everything—her temper, her grief, her opinions about other people's marriages—so that the neighbors learned never to hover over her asking when the truth would be ready; only when they stepped away did she softly, suddenly boil over. Everything rooted near her: rosemary cuttings in chipped vessels along the sill, a Nigerian student, a Polish widow, an Armenian couple who had sworn never to speak again, all of them simmered together at her long table until they tasted like family. The block whispered that a woman with dreams like hers had gone to seed, but she only laughed—slow and rolling, from the belly—and said nothing worth feeding to anybody ever came from staying out of the fire. She cracked now and then, grief or gossip splitting her down one side, but she never stopped holding water, and the places where she leaked seemed to leave green things growing along the path behind her. She was hungry at the strangest hours, red-eyed and half-amused at jokes the world had told her decades ago, and when the neighbors' card games turned bitter she sent down a plate of baklava, one more sweetness for whatever was at stake. Whatever the day ladled out—storm, debt, blessing—she took it in, put a lid on it, and somehow it all came out tasting like it had been intended.

Write a paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "keyboard" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Cass speaks in quick, clipped bursts, every word landing with a small percussive click, and when she gets flustered the last syllable stutters and repeats like a jammed mechanism. She is loudest after long stretches of being ignored; leave her alone in a corner and she will eventually blurt something in ALL CAPS until someone presses her shoulder down and she settles back to a murmur. One of her letters is broken—every so often the E simply refuses to come out, and she says "vrybody" and "xcuse me" and pretends nothing happened. Hold her hand and everything she says comes out different. Her habits are arranged in an order that made perfect sense a century ago, though no one remembers why anymore. There is fine gray dust in every one of her pockets, her favorite places are worn smooth from being touched, and at night she glows faintly and hums to herself. In a crisis she looks first for the exit, then takes back everything she said until it's gone—though she always keeps a wide, open space in the middle of herself for whoever needs it.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "keyboard". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "keyboard": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "keyboard" as you understand it. Write a paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "keyboard" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
She wakes every morning already listening, the way she always has, waiting for hands. Her own words never come unless someone leans their weight into her, and then she gives them back perfectly shaped, letter by letter, her voice carrying a small click at the end of every syllable. The parts of her that get used most have worn smooth and pale over the years — the e rubbed to a shine over her heart, the a nearly gone from her shoulder. She lives in slightly staggered rows, nothing quite aligned, with two small ridges on her index fingers so that anyone who is lost can find their way home by touch. When she gets nervous she repeats herself, repeats herself, the same sound clacking faster and faster until somebody lifts her up and sets her down somewhere else. She shouts in sudden capitals, apologizes by erasing backward to the mistake and starting over, and dreams of escape, always in the upper left corner of every room. She keeps crumbs in her pockets and dust under her fingernails, insists on the widest possible space between herself and strangers, and holds down on control when she wants comfort, alt when she wants out. Beneath everything she is springs and switches — every depression answered by a return — and in all her life she has translated other people's intentions into language without once being asked what she meant to say.

raw:
Cassius is pale and square-cornered, everything about him arranged in tidy rows, his nails filed into small concave tiles, and when he laughs it comes out in a quick bright clatter, like something small and mechanical being counted. He answers only when pressed: touch his shoulder and you get exactly one flat syllable; lean too long and he repeats himself, the same word spilling out until you let go. He moves through rooms in strict right angles, never cutting the diagonal everyone else takes, and he pauses far longer between words than anyone you've ever met, as if the space between things mattered more than the things themselves. His anger arrives all at once, in capitals; his apologies come afterward, half-erased and retyped until they come out clean. He can carry ten demands at once without dropping a single one, but ask him for everything together and whole requests simply fail to register. His best functions are hidden, reachable only by combination, and he keeps an escape route mapped out of every room, which he always uses early. He's worn smooth in his favorite places, faint where he's been held the most, and though he swears he hates crumbs, there are always crumbs in his seams; now and then a word sticks in his mouth and he has to shake it loose. In the dark, thin lines of color glow beneath his skin, spelling something no one has ever managed to read.

Tabea was built for order: her gray cardigan hung in straight lines, her jaw had a distinctly rectangular set, and she arranged the world the way she arranged sugar packets at cafés, in tidy rows and columns. People called her Tab because she was always hopping ahead in small, precise jumps, and because she demanded more personal space than anyone else in the room, edging sideways until the gap between her and her neighbor was the widest available. She answered every touch with a crisp, satisfying click, one thought at a time, never letting two ideas blur together, and the harder you leaned on her in an argument, the more precisely she responded, springing back to neutral the instant you let go. She believed in shortcuts—three quick gestures instead of a long explanation—and kept an escape route planned for every conversation. Neglect made her sticky: leave her alone in a dusty corner too long and she would repeat her last word in an endless string of identical syllables until someone shook her gently. You could tell what she'd had for lunch by the crumbs she shook out of her cuffs, and she never quite forgave the cousin who tipped an entire cup of coffee across her lap in 2019. The letters she used most had worn smooth and illegible on her fingertips years ago, but she never mixed them up, because she carried their order by heart—in the German arrangement, naturally, with her Y and Z forever swapped. And in a dark room a faint glow rose beneath her skin, so you could always find her: she was the one still wide awake at three in the morning, quietly ready, catching every word of a friend's tangled midnight confession and giving each one its proper place, never dropping a single one.

Esme kept herself flat and orderly, shoulders squared into tidy white rows, and she almost never spoke first; she waited to be pressed — a question, a hand on her arm — and only then did the words come, in quick precise bursts, each syllable landing with a small satisfying click. When nervous she got stuck, a single word looping faster and louder — yes, yes, yes, yes — until someone shook her loose. She could not whisper, either: once she started shouting, she had to be switched off entirely. She hoarded secrets in the narrow gaps between things, faintly dusty there, where nobody thought to look, and the letters on her name tag had been worn smooth by years of introductions. She carried two small extra letters that strangers never seemed to need, and guarded them jealously. Under pressure she lit up from within, glowing a soft blue, and when flustered she still swapped her Y's and Z's, a habit from childhood. She was famously good at getting out of bad conversations. People found her exhausting — all those pauses, that long deliberate blank between every thought — but everything said to her came back changed, useful, and spelled correctly.

She answered only when touched—press her shoulder and words clattered out of her, crisp and mechanical, though excitement made her whole body chatter like loosened springs. She returned exactly what the world pressed into her, letter for letter, repeating herself if you held on too long, while certain old griefs had gone dead and simply stopped responding. Nerves made her words stick, doubling and doubling until someone shook her gently. The widest silence in her lived mid-sentence, a long blank stretch she had to cross before she could go on. Anger arrived in capital bursts that no one could interrupt; regret traveled backwards, deleting, one letter at a time, everything she had just said. She dreamed constantly of escape—her favorite dream lived at the upper left of her heart—and when the evenings grew dark, something in her quietly lit up from within, soft and blue, patient as a held breath, waiting for hands.

Everyone says you know exactly which buttons to press with her, and it's true: every touch receives an immediate answer, because leaving a hand unanswered feels to her like a small cruelty. She believes in giving people space — the longest thing about her — and lives in quiet terror of spilled coffee and crumbs between her ribs. Grief makes her sticky: one syllable held down too long, repeating, repeating.

raw:
Tabitha never speaks first; she only answers, and only when touched. Her fingers sit in neat, staggered rows, knuckles raised like little roofs, and the ones she uses most have been worn smooth and blank — she can no longer read the letters she says every day. Her gift is translation, and she is never the same twice: touched alone, she is a letter; touched in company, she becomes a command. Under pressure she repeats herself, faster and faster, until someone lets go, and when you are finished with her she sets you down gently at the start of a new line. She is devoted to order — everything in its row, everything offset just so — yet she hoards crumbs of old conversations in the creases of her hands and calls them memories. Her longest gesture is silence; she believes the spaces between words matter more than the words. When frightened she erases herself backwards, letter by letter, and when very angry she locks and shouts in capitals. She keeps two small dots folded away in her chest for which English has no place, and she still trades her z's and y's out of habit, a childhood she never unlearned. In her upper left corner there is a little door marked escape that she has never once opened. Overwhelmed, she presses three of her own fingers together and begins again. She cut her cord years ago and calls herself wireless now, but in the dark she still glows faintly, waiting for hands.

raw:
Klavdiya held herself in strict, staggered rows — hands always at home, posture so orderly that strangers assumed she had been stamped that way at the factory. She stayed silent until touched; then she answered at once, in crisp little clicks, returning exactly what she was given, and if you pressed too long on one sore subject she would repeat herself, faster and louder, until someone shook her by the shoulders. Two alphabets had worn into her fingertips, the Latin letters polished bright by other people's sentences, the Cyrillic ones fading, and in dark rooms her eyes gave off a faint backlit glow. She kept twelve small talents at the crown of her head that nobody ever asked about, could turn a whisper into a shout with a single shift, and was refreshingly honest about her shortcuts. When she froze completely, it took three steady pressures at once — a friend at each shoulder, a hand on her center — to bring her back. Her one extravagance was the wide bar of her heart, the part everyone leaned on hardest, whose only purpose was to give other people's words room. Klavdia rarely spoke unless someone pressed her, and then only in quick, precise bursts, each word landing with a small, satisfying click. Everyone agreed she was responsive, though she had a habit of repeating herself if you held on too long, and sometimes a word stuck in her mouth until you jolted her loose. Crumbs settled into her crevices and never quite came out, but when someone's hands came to rest on her — warm, impatient, full of things to say — she felt, briefly and entirely, understood.

Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "keyboard" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Klava never speaks first; she waits to be touched by a question, then answers instantly, in bright percussive bursts that clatter across a table like rain on a tin roof. She dresses in strict rows — black blouse, white collar, buttons in patient lines — and her smile sits slightly off-center, one row of teeth overhanging the other. Certain words she says so often they've gone worn and illegible, and when she's tired her E sticks, so that *please* comes out *p-please-lease*. She can do nothing alone; she needs a hand on her shoulder, a friend beside her, holding her down before anything happens, and when no one touches her for too long she simply dims. She always takes the seat with her back nearest the door, one shoulder angled toward escape; she shouts in capital letters at unpredictable moments, then retracts everything with a small whispered deletion. Her silences are long and flat and load-bearing, holding up entire conversations the way a single broad bar holds up all the words above it. She flinches from crumbs, has never recovered from a spilled coffee, and keeps two tiny ridges — a ring's edge, a knuckle's callus — so her restless hands can always find their way home. And when she loves you, she answers before you finish asking: gently, exactly, every letter in its place, ending on a small decisive tap.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "keyboard": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "keyboard" as you understand it. raw:
Klava spoke only when pressed. Left alone, she sat silently at the edge of conversations, patient as furniture, waiting for someone to place a question under her fingers; then the answers came — crisp, clicky, perfectly ordered in rows — though everyone noticed certain letters worn smooth from overuse: *yes*, *sorry*, *again*, *sorry*. She had a wide, flat way of standing, palms out, always ready to receive, and she spaced her words with careful gaps, giving every silence its full measure. Press her the wrong way and she transformed — lowercase murmurs rising into all-caps rages that rattled the windows — but she regretted nearly everything, and you could watch her reach, mid-sentence, for some inner backspace, deleting herself back to the start of the thought. She was hopeless alone yet brilliant in combination, producing her best work only when someone else leaned on her at the very same moment. Escape was her favorite instinct; commitment, her hardest. She kept crumbs of old arguments lodged beneath her surface, hummed with a faint glow when she was loved, and went dim and dusty when she wasn't. Above all she was loyal to her layout: the same thoughts, in the same order, every single day, arranged so precisely you would never guess the whole design had been invented, long ago, to slow her down.

Quinn Wertz lived in tidy rows. Her teeth were small and square and perfectly aligned, her posture unnervingly flat, and when she sat on a park bench she sat exactly at its center, spine vertical, fingers poised over her knees as if waiting to be needed. She spoke in quick percussive taps, and strangers either clicked with her instantly or not at all. Her moods shifted without warning — a murmur one moment, a full-capital shout the next, followed by a feverish rush of apology, taking back every syllable as though it had never been said. Sticky situations made her freeze; control made her calm; and she could repeat herself forty times a day without losing patience, though her wrists ached by evening. At night, when the whole building had gone quiet, her fingertips gave off a faint blue glow, and the insomniacs of the neighborhood swore she was the loveliest thing in the dark — patient, orderly, waiting for whoever needed her to say exactly what they meant.

raw:
Teo arrives in bursts, his words landing in quick, even rows, each syllable striking the air with a small percussive click, and when he gets worked up he repeats himself — the same phrase, the same phrase, the same phrase — until someone gently lifts his shoulder. His moods come in two settings: touched the wrong way, he doubles in size and volume, shouting in capital letters until he finds the moment to let go. At rest, his fingers curl into the same familiar home position, and he cannot begin anything — a conversation, a journey, a love affair — until he has returned to that baseline. Regret is his native language; he takes back half of what he says, erasing and revising sentences mid-breath, and he is always one decisive gesture away from bolting out of a room. In the dark, his eyes give off a faint glow, and he runs best plugged in; untethered, he watches his own energy drain with quiet panic. His teeth sit in straight little rows like worn ivory keys, crumbs collect in the creases of his jacket, and the letters on his favorite shirt have faded exactly where he touches most — the E is nearly gone. When too many people demand too many things of him at once, he simply stops registering any of them. Above all, he needs the long pause — the wide, open stretch of silence in the middle of everything — before he can bear to move on to the next thing.

raw:
Klava was a flat, patient woman, calm as a held breath, her wide face divided by fine seams into tidy rows; she wore her hair in precise ranks and her blouse in five straight lines of small pale buttons, touching one, top to bottom, whenever she was thinking. She never spoke unless pressed — but pressed, she answered at once, in soft deliberate clicks, every syllable springing back ready for the next. Most of her words had always belonged to other people: for thirty years she had taken what louder men and women thought and made it legible, and she was quietly proud of her fingertips, two of them worn smooth and shiny from a lifetime of the same eight letters. She loved the long flat silences best, the wide nothing between one word and the next, and she could hold a moment beneath her palm until everything that followed came out changed, elevated, capital. Her anger arrived all at once, in permanent capitals, and had to be thumped back down. Alone she was good for small things; in combination with her sister she could do the impossible. She could accept ten demands pressed on her in a single breath and never drop one. She feared spilled drinks and crumbs in her crevices, and when flustered she repeated herself, repeating herself, one syllable stuck and rattling until someone took her gently by the shoulders. Though she had lived her whole life in English, when she was very tired her thoughts came out soft and rounded in the alphabet of her grandmother, and everything said in those letters was true. Every night she dreamed of a small door in the top-left corner of the room, and every morning she woke just before her hand reached it.

He speaks only when touched: a tap on the shoulder and out comes a word, crisp and springy, and if you leave your hand there too long he repeats it, again and again, faster and faster. He is long and flat-bodied, pale gray, with five rows of small square nails down each forearm that click when he fidgets, and a wide steel bar he wears across his chest like a belt, which he refuses to explain. For hours he lies perfectly still, gathering dust and crumbs in his creases, then erupts into bursts of clicking speech, letters tumbling out left to right in tidy rows. Press one shoulder and he SHOUTS IN CAPITALS; press the other and he goes small, whispering in lowercase. He can erase anything with a single press of his thumb, the last sentence gone as if it never happened. He takes control of every room, offers an alternate opinion to every statement, and always stands nearest the door with one hand on the escape. Sometimes he gets stuck — coffee spilled down his front years ago makes certain words come out doubled and sticky — and then you must lift him and shake him gently until something comes loose. Under his left eye is a small tilde-shaped birthmark, the one detail that tells you exactly where he is from. At night he lies faceup on the table, glowing faintly from somewhere inside, a quiet field of little buttons waiting for someone, anyone, to make him say something new.

Tomás stood as straight as a man arranged in careful rows, flat-chested and angular, with a long, unbroken plank of a torso that invited you to rest your wrists on his shoulders. He spoke in bursts — one clean syllable at a time, a dry clack in his throat — and if you pressed him, really leaned on him, he would repeat himself, the same phrase rattling out faster and faster until someone let go. Years of use had worn his favorite letters smooth: he was all E and S and A now, his most-trusted parts rubbed blank, while the Q and the Z of him sat pristine and lonely at his edges. He feared spilled coffee above all things, collected crumbs in the creases of his palms, and glowed faintly in the dark when he thought no one was watching. He could make small things taller with a single touch, and he had a worn-down habit of erasing himself mid-sentence, one eye forever fixed on the top-left corner, dreaming of escape. Everyone's words passed through him; none of the credit ever did.

Name: Tomás Retorno

She is silent until someone presses her, and then she cannot stop — stories, confessions, arguments, all of them in other people's words. She lives two lives in every letter, whisper or shout, depending on how hard someone holds her down. She dreams constantly of escape. raw:
Tecla stood slightly inclined toward people, the way she always had, as if leaning into whatever they were about to say. Her dark hair fell in long, even rows, and the pale letters on her cardigan had faded at the cuffs, exactly where everyone touched her most. She never volunteered a word unless pressed, but once pressed, her words came in quick, even taps; ignore her, and she would repeat herself—twice, three times, a little louder each time—until you finally answered. She made her living turning other people's half-finished thoughts into clean sentences, and no one ever thanked her for the ones that came out right, though the wrong ones were always, somehow, her fault. She kept a private ledger of every sentence she wished she could take back, and sometimes, mid-conversation, she would stop, rewind, and begin the whole thing again, quieter and cleaner. She held two opposing opinions on every subject with equal conviction and could argue either side at full volume; she wanted every decision finalized the instant it was made; she skipped ahead in conversations without warning, hopping from topic to topic like a stone across water. She asked for more space than anyone, always, and got it. She was good at a dozen small tasks nobody had ever assigned her. And she lived in low, constant dread of spilled coffee, of dust in her creases, of the day someone would finally lift her up, shake her out, and discover everything she had been holding between her lines.

Cayetano speaks in quick, clicking bursts, and when he's nervous a single syllable stutters out of him over and over, as if something under his tongue had jammed. His fingers drum on every tabletop, restless little hammers with nowhere to land. His bookshelves are arranged in an order that looks like nonsense but hides a century of logic; the alphabet always struck him as too obvious, too likely to tangle. He is fiercely protective of the pause between words, guarding silence the way others guard speech, and he will stop a conversation mid-sentence to brush away the smallest crumb of an idea. Mistakes pursue him for days: he replays arguments in the shower, backtracking to strike the wrong word and retype it cleaner. Held onto too long, his mildest opinions come out in CAPITALS, though he never seems to notice. His favorite miracles are the two-person kind — someone leans on him just so, and suddenly he can undo anything, repeat anything, leap straight to the end. Where he has been touched most he has gone smooth and pale, letters worn to nothing, and he is prouder of those bald spots than of anything still intact. He always takes the seat nearest the exit, keeps one corner of himself spotless for emergencies, and glows faintly, a thin blue light, whenever someone finally pays attention.

Pravesh arrives everywhere in neat rows: his shirt buttons aligned like obedient soldiers, his thoughts marching left to right in a fixed grid. He speaks in quick clicks and clacks, and if you press him—really press him—he repeats himself, the same sentence over and over, faster and faster, until somebody lets go. He lives in lowercase, soft and unassuming, but flip the right switch and he turns ALL CAPS, deafening, impossible to silence until you find the lock and hold it down. He believes in space—vast, generous silences between his words—and he saves the longest pause of all for the thing he never says. He is a creature of shortcuts, never taking the long way, one finger held down while another does the real work, and his closest companion is the art of undoing: no mistake goes unreversed if he can help it. His escape is worn smooth from all the times he has reached for doors, the letters E, A, and S have faded from his palms because those are the ones the world touches most, and at night he glows faintly from within, backlit and patient, ready to receive whatever anyone presses onto him—every stroke, every misspelling, every furious burst—and offer it all back faithfully, in order.

Her favorite letters were worn smooth from overuse, while the rare ones gathered dust in the silence of her corners. When she was tired she repeated herself, sticking on the same syllable — sssss, sssss — until someone shook her loose. Her tragedy was erasure. She could not abide a mistake, so she lived reaching backward, deleting, undoing, rewording, until friends learned to say things to her only once. And at night she dreamed of shortcuts: of doing in one simultaneous gesture what took others a whole afternoon, of someone laying their whole self across her and hearing, instead of an error, every note she had been holding.

raw:
She had learned early that she had no voice of her own—only whatever other people pressed out of her. She sat very straight, long and flat, all corners and planes, her cardigan stitched with five neat rows of little square keys that clacked when she moved. She never spoke first. She waited, grey and patient, until someone touched her, and then it all came out in bursts—a soft clatter of words, staccato syllables, rain on a tin roof. Hold on to her long enough and she would repeat the same phrase over and over until you let go. She was most generous in the middle: the space she kept between herself and others was the widest, most cushioned thing about her. She could not help revising; half her sentences ended in air, taken back, pressed out of existence. If you raised your voice she went rigid, every key on her chest shouting in capitals. On bad days she did not sulk—she simply shut down, dark and silent, hoping someone would restart her by morning. Crumbs gathered in her creases, dust beneath her fingernails, and the letters on the places she was touched most often had worn smooth and blank. Still, she dreamed, sometimes, of being wireless.

raw:
Qadir was a long, patient man who lay low in every room, waiting to be pressed. He spoke in short, even bursts, each word struck with the same pressure as the last, and when he grew nervous his final syllable would stick and repeat — sorry, sorry, sorry — until someone gently shook him loose. His teeth were little white squares in tidy rows, and they clicked when he talked; the letters of his favorite words had worn smooth on his tongue from years of overuse. He carried two alphabets inside him and often reached for a word in one script only to find it living in the other. He could spell anything and say almost nothing of his own, for he had understood early that his gift was not for speaking but for carrying: every love letter and every furious complaint passed through him and came out permanent, and though some nights he longed to reach back and unmake a word or two, he knew that what is committed is committed. No matter how hard the day leaned on him, he always sprang up again. He kept his hands folded at his center, because home, he believed, was wherever your fingers could return without looking; and his name began with Q, the rarest letter given the first seat, which is perhaps why he spent his whole life quietly hoping that somebody, someday, would finally need him.

Akshar moves through the world in tidy rows, everything about him squared and deliberate, as though his soul were laid out in a grid. Beneath his composed surface lie hidden depths — crumbs of old grief lodged in his crevices, rattling loose only when he is turned upside down and shaken. Certain touches transform him entirely — press him just there and everything he says comes out louder, changed, emphatic — and his widest part exists only to give other people room. He dreams, sometimes, of escape, though that dream sits quietly in the top left corner of his mind, rarely pressed. He can turn a stranger's murmured intention into whole sentences, whole worlds — yet he has never once spoken for himself; he says only what others press out of him. At night he glows faintly in the dark, patient, waiting for the next pair of hands to give him a voice.

Most luminous after dark, she glowed faintly under lamplight, and every morning she shook out her dupatta, dislodging the crumbs of yesterday. Tabrez is long and low and goes quiet the moment no one is using him. He woke each morning already arranged, his habits fixed in an order nobody could explain anymore—it had been settled long before his birth, and everyone had simply agreed. He spoke in quick bursts and then went silent, patient as a blinking cursor, waiting to be needed. He was loudest when people leaned on him, and he made the same bright clatter whether they poured love letters or furious complaints through him, for it was never his to choose what passed through—only to carry it faithfully, authoring none of it. His most-used letters had worn smooth and blank on his fingertips, while the ones nobody wanted stayed sharp and perfect, and this he accepted as a quiet grief. Dust gathered in his creases; a spilled cup of chai had once left him sticking for days. He kept a long emptiness at his center, because he believed words need room to breathe. Unplugged, he was nothing but a field of sleeping letters. He could undo almost anything he said, though he knew some things, once spoken, refuse to return. He shifted moods in an instant, was forever tempted to escape, and still—every evening—he pressed forward, ready to commit to the next line.

Aino Q. Wirta stands very straight, her shoulders squared into tidy rows, and when she laughs it comes out in short, clicking bursts. She is patient the way furniture is patient: she can wait all night in the dark without complaint, glowing faintly at the edges, but touch her and she wakes at once, answering exactly what you asked for, letter by letter. Her hands come to rest, when idle, in the middle of herself, where her most-used letters live, and she keeps Å, Ä, and Ö close to her edges like a passport. She has only two moods, upper and lower, though once, startled, she shouted in capitals for a whole afternoon and had to be restarted. She dreams in space — long, clean, generous space — and will give you as much of it as you need; but press her escape, and she is gone before you can say control.

raw:
Salla answers only when pressed. Ask her nothing and she lies flat and silent, neatly staggered into rows; touch her — a fingertip, a deadline, a question — and language comes out of her in quick clattering bursts, like rain on a tin roof. She was made to be touched by everyone and has spent her life saying other people's words, which is why her most-visited places have gone smooth, the letters rubbed away, small hollows worn where the same fingers return and return. Two little bumps tell her where center is without looking, and she is a homebody anyway: even her own name, spelled out, never leaves the middle row. Alone she can do almost nothing, but she is nimble by nature and full of shortcuts — pressed into combination with a friend she can copy the world, undo it, or make it louder. When she seizes up she repeats herself, one syllable hammering until someone lifts her off it, and some afternoons she goes entirely into capitals. She keeps two extra vowels tucked along her right edge, three counting the one that wears a small ring, souvenirs of home; she keeps another, near her shoulder, that means escape, and she has never once used it for herself. The longest thing about her is blank, reserved for the silence between words. Crumbs and dust and whole lost seasons gather in her crevices, and at night she glows faintly, waiting for hands.

She wore her feelings in neat, straight rows of buttons, and the letters she loved most had worn smooth and blank on the sleeves of her cardigan. Her mind arranged the world in an order that made sense only to her hands—familiar, efficient, baffling to everyone else. Held too long, she repeated herself, stuck in a soft little loop until someone let go; asked for too many things at once, she blinked politely and quietly dropped half of them. Whatever the day pressed down on her, she sprang back, level again. She carried an eraser in every pocket and believed every mistake deserved the chance to be taken back. Her need for space was the longest thing about her, and people learned not to crowd it. She was always first to eye the exits, yet at night she glowed—luminous, patient, waiting for something worth answering with a firm, committed return.

Tabitha lived in rows. Her freckles fell into tidy grids, her teeth were small and square and evenly spaced, and she gave off a faint glow in dim rooms that people called pretty and she called power-saving. She was silent until someone pressed her; touch her shoulder and out came a single distinct note, a different one for every friend, but hold on too long and she would repeat the same sentence over and over, faster and faster, until you let go. When she talked quickly she clattered beautifully, and when a word got stuck in her throat it took a firm thump between the shoulder blades to shake it loose. She believed in taking things back — every careless remark could be unmade, once, twice, ten times, until the beginning of the conversation lay clean and unsaid. She kept her temperament in darker shades: a little Ctrl that needed to manage everything, an Alt forever offering plan B, a Shift that turned her lowercase mumbles into capitals by morning. Her thoughts arrived in an order that made no sense to anyone, arranged long ago for reasons not even she could remember. She gave away her vast, empty Space more freely than anything else and always missed it most. And when a room grew too loud, her hand drifted, without her noticing, toward the top left corner of the conversation, feeling for the way out. Her one great consolation was that no matter how far she wandered into a sentence, she always, always came back.

raw:
Tabitha lived her life in tidy rows. She spoke in quick, percussive bursts, every syllable landing with a small, satisfying click, and she could not tolerate a silence longer than a breath. Strangers found it effortless to pour their thoughts through her; she translated their stammering into something clean and deliberate and never claimed the words as her own. Down her center ran a long, patient stretch of quiet — the widest part of her, the part everyone leaned on — while near her shoulder she kept a small hatch for escape, for the moments she needed to vanish mid-sentence. She was fluent in second chances, forever doubling back to retract, revise, undo, and she could lift her whole voice at once, raising every letter of herself to capitals when the moment demanded it. But ask too much of her too fast and she simply stopped, dropping half of what was said no matter how gently the hands arrived. The places where people touched her most had gone smooth and shiny over the years, letters worn to whispers on her skin, and though she sometimes dreamed of cutting the cord and drifting free, she always woke still tethered, still waiting, faintly humming with everything she had been asked to carry.

raw:
Aizawa Qwerty stands very straight, her shoulders squared into tidy rows, and she flinches—a soft, springy click—whenever anyone touches her without warning. She is most herself under pressure; left idle she goes dull and gray, but the moment fingers land on her she lights up from within, a faint blue glow rising behind her eyes like backlit legends. She speaks in short, precise bursts, and when she is anxious she repeats her last word over and over, unable to stop until someone lifts their hand away. She keeps an escape hatch mapped in the upper-left corner of every room and dreams of it constantly, though she almost never uses it. When she makes a mistake she tortures herself backward, undoing and undoing, until a friend presses her gently forward and tells her to commit. Her longest silences stretch wide enough for anyone to pass through, and in crowds she insists on a generous margin of empty air on all sides. She has her worn spots, too: two fingertips shinier and smoother than the rest, and certain letters of her own name faded from being said too often. Crumbs collect in the creases of her sleeves, and she carries a coiled, cord-like scarf that tethers her to her desk, her laptop, her one great love—whenever it slips loose she panics, input lost, no signal. She is stiff and stubborn on cold mornings, springing back into shape with use, and those who know her best have learned that beneath each of her hard little surfaces, every quiet key hides a different, useful thing.
