raw:
Esme arrives in neat rows—small letters aligned down her cardigan, half worn away from where the world touches her most. She speaks in crisp, deliberate taps, and if you press her—corner her, hold on too long—she repeats herself, the same syllable stuttering until you let go. She needs a little space between people; crowd her and she stops making sense, though she keeps one long silence in every conversation, the widest gap on her page. Her moods shift without warning: lowercase and murmuring one moment, locked in capitals the next, all shout and no nuance until someone releases her. She is quick to escape—out of arguments, through unlocked doors—and quicker still to delete: a wrong word, a wrong friend, gone with one small decisive stroke. Commit her to something, though, and she commits completely, no taking it back. Crumbs gather in her pockets from midnight snacking, and in the dark the letters on her skin glow faintly, so that everything she has been holding in finally comes out in a rush. Take her hand and you'll feel two tiny ridges at her fingertips—her quiet anchors, always telling her exactly where home is.

Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "キーボード" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Tabitha arranges her whole life in strict rows, her apartment a grid of perfectly aligned things, and when she talks, the words come out in short, deliberate taps, each one released with a crisp, satisfying click. She responds to the lightest pressure—lean on her even a little and she answers instantly—though the places people touch most have worn smooth and blank, the letters of who she used to be faded away by repetition. Her habits were settled long before her birth, ordered by some stranger's arrangement she never chose but cannot break. Her moods shift without warning, and when she loses her temper, everything she says comes out in CAPITALS until someone jabs her back down to size. She erases her own sentences mid-thought, a delete-shaped reflex she can't undo; she circles every conversation looking for the exit in its upper-left corner; and certain old feelings stick, repeating themselves when pressed too long. She runs on a long tether she swears she could unplug any day, gives everyone the widest space in her heart—broader than any other part of her—and beneath her tidy surface hide twelve secret moods no one has ever thought to summon, plus a soft glow that rises through her skin whenever the room goes dark.

prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "キーボード". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "キーボード": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "キーボード" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "キーボード" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Casey Lockwood speaks best in bursts, her words arriving in tidy, evenly spaced lines, and her fingertips are always tapping somewhere—a thigh, a table, the rim of a cup—in a soft dry clicking that quickens when she's nervous. She dresses in black and white arranged in careful rows, small letters stitched across her buttons in an order no one remembers the reason for, though her fingers know every one by heart, and the letters she touches most have long since worn blank. She is patient the way a pause is patient, stretching herself out to give other people room between their words, but she keeps two habits she can never fully switch off: a sudden shouting brightness she falls into and can't climb out of, and a quiet hatch she slips through the moment talk grows too loud—though the lightest touch at her edge can still turn a lowercase day capital. She takes back nearly everything she says, a phrase erased and reworded and erased again, so that her sentences arrive only after a small delay, polished by regret. At night she glows faintly, luminous letters along her wrists and collarbones, and if you look closely you'll find crumbs and dust settled deep in the creases of her sleeves, gathered from years of catching everything the world let fall into her. She is, above all, a translator: she takes the shapeless hum inside a person and turns it, one deliberate stroke at a time, into something you can finally read.

Esme Q. Locke was born a little too responsive: press her, even gently, and something in her springs back with an answer. She speaks in short, percussive bursts — a click here, a clack there — and when a thought sticks, she repeats it louder and faster until someone pries it loose. She lives to be the middlewoman between intention and expression, silent until leaned on, then suddenly capable of anything — confessions, novels, three a.m. apologies. Stuck moments are unbearable to her; she will tab sideways out of a conversation, shift the subject, or, if cornered, take the nearest escape. She keeps her nails clipped short for speed, her bag full of crumbs wedged deep in its creases, and an eraser on her keyring for the words she wishes she could take back. prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "keyboard". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "keyboard": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "keyboard" as you understand it. raw:
Keiko waits the way her kind has always waited: in silence, in perfect rows. She speaks in quick, precise bursts, fingertips clicking against tabletops, railings, the shoulders of friends who need encouragement, and when a thought stalls mid-sentence she tabs neatly to the next one, leaving the false start behind as clean white space. She carries an air of quiet control — she helps anyone who asks, instantly, as though helping were her single function — yet she keeps one hand near the door in every room, her small private escape. Startled, her voice jumps into capitals; calm, she shifts between moods so smoothly that no one notices the change. She erases her own hesitations before anyone can hear them, backspacing over doubt until each sentence emerges certain, and if she stumbles she may repeat one word over and over, stuck and rattling, until someone lifts her gently and sets her right. She cannot host more than three voices at once before she starts dropping letters, overwhelmed. The phrases she has spoken most often have worn blank and smooth, so she is forever inventing new ones. At night her wrists glow faintly, patient, waiting for the next thought that needs a way into the world — for without a hand to press her she is silent, but touched, she is unstoppable.

raw:
Seda carried herself with the tidy, straight-backed order of someone whose life was arranged in rows. She spoke in soft clicks and sudden bursts, pausing exactly where a breath belonged, and her silences came as one long, unbroken bar. When she was nervous, her fingers walked the alphabet against her thigh, one after another, in strict sequence; when someone pressed her too long on a subject, she could only repeat herself, the same syllable over and over, until they let go. Certain letters had worn thin on her years ago — the ones the world uses most — so that people knew her best at her smoothest places. She was quick to take things back: one stumble and she could undo her whole sentence, clean as a slate. Under pressure she shifted, emerging louder, more insistent, in capitals. She was always the first to look for the exit in an unbearable conversation, though she never once took it; escape was the thing she offered everyone else. For a living she carried other people's words — confessions, love letters, threats, whole novels — delivering each faithfully, and no one ever asked what she wanted to say. At night she waited in the dark with a faint glow behind her eyes, patient the way only something built to be pressed can be, and if you rested a hand on her shoulder she would spring back at once, ready, eager, to begin.

raw:
Ender was built for translation: everything that crowded his chest came out in letters, quick and clicking, faster than he could feel it. He kept his life in tidy rows and flinched when anything slipped out of alignment, though his pockets were always full of crumbs he never got around to clearing. His favorite words had worn smooth from use, shiny the way a well-touched surface goes shiny, and two small ridges of habit told him he was home without his having to look. When he got stuck he repeated himself — a syllable, then a word, then the whole sentence — and when he panicked he SHOUTED, caps engaged, hunting blindly for the lock. Under pressure he performed beautifully; afterward he only wanted to undo, one letter at a time. He offered people the widest stretch of himself, and he was always the first to leave from the top-left corner, quiet, gone. Raised on one alphabet but working in another, his hands drifted between two layouts, dreaming in one and living in the other. When everything in him froze, it took three fingers pressed down together to bring him back. At night he glowed faintly, a soft rainbow under the skin, waiting for someone to press him into saying something true.

Tabitha lived in tidy rows — her books, her spices, her thoughts — and could not abide a crooked thing. Her fingernails were small and squared, each one worn to a shine in the middle where the world pressed her most, and she was patient under pressure to a startling degree: struck a thousand times a day, she still answered every blow with the same crisp click. The people who leaned on her hardest wore her smoothest, while whole quiet regions of her went years untouched, gathering their fine dust. She carried a long silent stretch inside herself and deployed it between other people's sentences like punctuation; she could make anyone louder with a single touch — suddenly they were shouting in capitals — and hush them again just as quickly. She knew every shortcut worth knowing, yet feared spills above all, because sticky situations were the one kind she never survived intact. She believed everything could be taken back, erased with one decisive stroke, though she knew better than most that some marks linger like crumbs wedged deep in the crevices, rattling faintly whenever she moved. She worked best in chords, many things at once, but pile too much on her too fast and she would seize up, repeating a single syllable over and over — aaah, aaah — until somebody gently lifted the weight away. In the dark she glowed faintly at her edges, and whenever a conversation turned unbearable she was simply gone; she had spent her whole life with one finger hovering over the way out.

raw:
He was long and flat and stood terribly straight, as if waiting to be set down on a desk. His thoughts arrived in clicks; when he grew nervous, he repeated his last word over and over, until someone lifted their hand away. Strangers found him useful and slightly cold, though the people who knew him best noticed the pale, glossy patches worn into his chest where he had been touched the most, and the two small bumps on his index fingers that helped everyone find their way home to him. There was a faint scar at the small of his back from the days when a single long cord kept him tethered to a larger machine; now he was free, and quietly missed being needed. He flinched at spilled coffee, loved silence the way he loved the wide bar at his center, and at night he pressed his own Escape, though nothing ever opened; things only closed. Sometimes he dreamed in a different alphabet. Still, each morning he straightened his rows, shook the crumbs from his creases, and waited, patient and luminous, for the next pair of hands.

Elowen arrives late to everything and no one minds, because her presence feels like something that was always going to be there. She stands with her feet planted wide, weight settled, as if the ground might need her help holding itself together. Her hands are rough at the palm and patient, always half-open, as if offering shade to whoever stands close. She speaks slowly, in sentences that branch—starting somewhere ordinary, pausing, then surprising you with fruit. She never argues; she bends, holds, and outlasts, and long after louder people have snapped and blown away, she remains, unchanged in essence, ringed with years. Every loss she has suffered is written somewhere on her body, and she covers none of it; she wears her scars the way others wear weather. Her generosity is structural, quiet: she listens the way shade falls, sheltering without asking—teenagers do their homework in her calm, grieving men nap against her shoulder. In winter she withdraws, gray and spare and seemingly lifeless, and everyone worries, and then April comes and she erupts, absurdly green, laughing at their doubt. She remembers everything. Her friendships run underground, unseen, tangled up with strangers she has never formally met, and she will defend someone she has spoken to once as fiercely as a sister. Though she has never traveled past the county line, birds have raised families in her hair, seeds she scattered decades ago are growing tall in other towns, and strangers recognize her on sight, swearing they have seen her in dreams—standing exactly there, arms lifted, waiting for wind.

raw:
Rowan arrived slowly, the way all enduring things do. She was patient to the point of stillness, happiest standing at the edge of gatherings, watching everything take root. Strangers leaned on her without knowing why; she gave shade to everyone and asked nothing back except sun, rain, and time. Her skin was weathered and furrowed, her knuckles gnarled like old bark, and around her eyes were fine concentric rings, one for every hard year, each wider than the last. She grew in spurts—long silences, then a sudden flowering of words. Grief came to her seasonally: she let things go all at once, extravagantly, in a blaze of color, then stood bare and honest through the cold, trusting that green would return. Storms bent her nearly sideways but never broke her; she had learned early that flexibility was its own kind of strength. Beneath the ground where no one could see, she quietly held hands with everyone she loved, feeding them what she had and being fed in return. She was not ambitious the way people are ambitious—she simply reached, always, toward the light, and made a home for whatever needed one.

Qlara keeps herself in tidy rows, squared fingertips stamped with letters worn pale from overuse — the ones everyone leans on — while certain corners of her go untouched for years. She speaks only when pressed, but then she answers in bright, rhythmic bursts, each word landing with a small satisfying click, and if you hold on too long she stutters, repeating the same phrase until you let go. Under each fingertip there is a tiny spring, so no matter how hard the day pushes her down, she always bounces back. She keeps a dream of escape polished and ready in the upper corner of her mind, though she never quite acts on it; she can turn a lowercase mood into a CAPITAL conviction instantly, provided someone leans on her at the same moment; and when too many people demand things of her at once she simply freezes, dropping half of what she held, ghosting out of conversations mid-sentence. She revises her life constantly, deleting whole paragraphs and retyping them cleaner, and beneath her tidy surface hide crumbs of old lunches and one sticky secret. Born arranged one way, she later taught herself another, so now she dreams in two layouts. The widest part of her is reserved for silence — a long bar of it where she breathes between words — because unplugged, she knows, she is nothing but a handsome arrangement of waiting.

raw:
Rowan has lived on the same corner of Birchwood Lane for seventy-one years, and neighbors joke that if you cut him open you'd find rings—each one a year of quiet growth, a season of loss survived. He stands taller than most men but never seems to tower; his shoulders are broad and patient, his hands knotted like old bark, his hair gone silver and scattering in the autumn wind. He speaks slowly, in his own time, and never raises his voice—even the worst storms only make him sway, never snap. People drift to his porch the way strangers drift to shade: the grieving teenager who needs somewhere still to sit, the young couple arguing on the sidewalk until his calm settles over them like a canopy. His roots run deep in this place—his mother's garden still blooms in the yard—yet he clings to nothing; every year he scatters something new into the world, seeds of advice and kindness carried off by students and grandchildren who grow tall in faraway cities. When winter strips him bare—the death of his wife, the friends who moved on, the silence that fills the house now—he does not despair. He simply lets go of what is finished, stands open and honest against the cold, and waits, certain the green will return.

Beneath the visible world her roots tangle with everyone she loves, passing water and warnings hand to hand in the dark, and though she has been struck by lightning and carved with names by careless lovers, she remains—patient, weathered, reaching always upward while holding the ground together.

His skin is rough and furrowed, weathered like something that has stood through a century of storms, and his hands are broad and calloused, built for holding things steady. His blood runs slow as sap; he moves slowly, decides slowly, and considers this a virtue, since everything worth becoming takes time. His hair takes on a green cast each summer, thins to copper in autumn, and falls away by the first frost, though no one in town remarks on it anymore. He plants his feet when he talks and leans into storms rather than against them, and he has a gift for making people feel held—weary travelers drift into his kitchen as if into shade, children scale his long arms without asking, and his house is crowded with other people's secrets, kept the way a hollow keeps what nests inside it. He is patient with the slow, protective of the small, and stubbornly opposed to uprooting anything, himself least of all. Strangers mistake his stillness for dullness, but his conversation has rings in it: every drought, every fire, every remarkable spring laid down somewhere inside him in silence and kept. He does not chase; he does not flee. He grows, he shelters, he endures, and when the worst weather passes he is somehow still standing—a little more bent, a little more himself.

raw:
Dubravka moved through the world the way slow things do: without hurry, without apology. She took her place at the edge of every gathering and held her ground while others drifted past like weather, and when she stood still — which was often — people swore they could feel a kind of shade settle around her, a cool and patient quiet. Her hands were rough and deeply lined, hands that had outlasted more storms than anyone could count; she measured her years not in birthdays but in scars, each one a ring hidden beneath her skin, proof of a season survived. She gave without keeping score — cover from the rain, a shoulder to lean on, air that seemed cleaner wherever she happened to be — and when autumn came to her moods, she let things fall, old grudges and dead habits alike, trusting the bareness and trusting the return. Children clung to her, lovers carved their names into her patience, and the worst winds bent her without ever once breaking her. She was not going anywhere, and that was the point of her: everything that mattered lived below the surface, gripping the dark earth, drinking slowly, and feeding everything above it.

raw:
Semyon stood at the edge of the square from dawn until the streetlights buzzed on, and if he moved at all, it was the slow swaying of a man listening to a wind no one else could hear. His hands were ridged and gray-brown, rough as old planks, and when children climbed onto his shoulders he bore them patiently upward, toward the light. He grew slowly — he liked to say so — but he grew, adding a quiet ring of patience every year, hidden where no one could count them. Spring softened him into small bright generosity; autumn made him let everything go, standing barer and lighter, unashamed. Storms bent him nearly double, yet he always rose, and he taught others his one secret: give at the waist, hold at the heart. Strangers rested in his shade; the grieving leaned on him and found him unmoved, certain that whatever was cut away would come back. When he finally spoke, the words came out slow and seasoned, and his rare attempts at dancing were famously, endearingly wooden. His children had scattered far on the wind, and he was proud of every one — content to stay, rooted, while the whole world blew past.

raw:
Semyon had stood at the edge of the village so long that people had forgotten he had ever arrived anywhere at all; he seemed less to live in his crooked house than to grow out of it, wide-shouldered and faintly bent, as if shaped by a century of winds everyone else had been spared. His hands were cracked in long, patient lines, his face a weathered gray that gave away nothing — the neighbors called him a stump behind his back — but inside him things moved, slow and sweet, a hidden current that rose with the thaw and sank again each November. He never traveled; he couldn't have explained why, only that going far felt like being torn up by the heels. Every autumn he lost something and let it fall — his wife, the hearing in his left ear, whole years he could no longer account for — and he stood very still and did not reach to catch it. Yet every spring, to the village's quiet astonishment, something green and stubborn pushed up out of him: a garden, a grandchild's laughter, an unprompted joke in a voice dry as old paint, and people gathered without quite knowing why in the cool shade of his kitchen, leaving steadier than they'd come. He was hard to provoke and impossible to move; he took insults the way he took weather, standing, swaying a little, holding the earth with worn boots until the storm grew bored and passed. Only twice had anyone seen him afraid — once at the smell of smoke, and once when men came with rope and iron to clear the lot next door.

Kornei stood the way other men only pretended to stand: planted. His shoulders formed a wide, patient canopy under which, sooner or later, the whole village had sheltered — widows, wanderers, one runaway goat — and his hair had whitened to birch bark above hands cracked like August clay, hands that could hold a hammer, a grandchild, or a grudge for forty years without dropping any of them. He grew in slow, invisible increments — a ring of silence added each winter, a new branch of patience each spring — and when he bent over his garden beds the wind moved through him with a dry, honest creak. The village called him dense, oak-headed, good for nothing but shade, but his slowness was the slowness of things that intend to outlast you: three years to forgive, ten to fall in love, and not once in seventy-one winters did he step aside for a storm — he only leaned into it until the storm grew bored. Every autumn he let something go — a leaf of anger, a yellowed apology — and stood bare and unashamed through the frost, trusting that whatever lay buried deepest in him would wake again by March. He danced exactly once, at his nephew's wedding, and the village agreed it resembled a fence attempting a waltz. He flinched at the ring of an axe the way other men flinch at talk of funerals, and he kept all his stories inside, wound in tight circles around his heart, where anyone patient enough could read the years.

raw:
Marfa has lived in the same house on the same street all her life, and she intends to die there too, because she believes a person must stand in one place long enough for the birds to trust her. Her hands are broad and cracked, her knuckles swollen like buds that never quite opened, and every winter she swears another ring of weather has settled around her eyes. She speaks slowly, as if each word must be drawn up from somewhere deep and secret before it can be said aloud, and she cannot bear to be moved, hurried, or transplanted for anything less than a storm. She knows everything about the whole street through a quiet network of old friends who pass news among themselves the way moisture travels between buried roots. In autumn she grows silent and drops her grievances one by one, letting the wind take them; in spring she forgives everyone at once, extravagantly, green and sudden. Neighbors bring their children to her the way they bring them to shade, and she feeds them from her garden with stubborn generosity, pressing apples into small hands as if planting them. Misfortune bends her—she groans, she creaks—but so far it has never broken her, and when she stands at her window in the evening, arms lifted slightly from her sides, fingers spread wide, you would swear she is listening to the wind with her entire body.

He was tall the way a mast is tall, with shoulders broad enough to hold up sky, and his skin had gone gray-brown and fissured, like bark that has decided to keep everything that ever happened to it. His hands betrayed his age completely: cracked, ridged, the knuckles swelling through the skin like roots through pavement. People called him solemn, but he was not sad; he was planted, and being planted, he had nowhere to hurry, nothing to prove, and all the time in the world.

raw:
Miron had spent all seventy of his years on the same bend of the same river, and he could not have explained why travel felt to him like amputation. He was tall and unhurried, with knuckles roughened to the texture of bark and a face the seasons wrote on directly — gray and stripped bare in February, tender and bright-green by May. His kindness was like sap: it rose slowly, only after a long winter, but then it rose all the way to the fingertips. People came to him the way they come to shade; he asked for nothing, offered everything, and kept every secret that drifted down and settled at his feet like fallen leaves. His anger bent in any gale yet never snapped, his love gathered ring by patient ring somewhere deep inside him, and when life wounded him he did not heal so much as grow around the hurt, folding it in and thickening there. He planted things whose shade he would never sit in, spoke only after long silences, and stood each evening at the field's edge with his arms slightly raised, as if the sky were something he had volunteered to hold up.

He rose slowly each morning, the way light filters through leaves, and stood at his window for a long while before moving, content simply to watch the street below. He was tall and thick through the shoulders, with broad, rough hands that strangers said felt like old bark, and hair gone the color of dry October leaves. He gave shade without being asked for it: neighbors gathered on his porch through the hot months, children did their homework at his kitchen table, and weary visitors told him things they had never told anyone, because something in his stillness made confession feel safe. His feet, people joked, sent roots through the floorboards whenever he sat down, and it was true that he could not be hurried—slow to anger, slower to forget, his grudges and his affections alike growing in rings around him, one year layered upon the next. When storms came he never ran for cover; he stepped outside, planted himself, and let the wind bend him, believing that anything willing to bow would never break. In autumn a melancholy settled over him, and he shed what no longer served him—old habits, old sorrows—quietly, without ceremony, until he stood bare and honest against the winter sky. And every spring, without fail, something green and stubborn stirred in him again.

Sabina has never once hurried in her life, because she believes everything worth becoming takes seasons. She stands a little apart from every crowd, upright and unhurried, her feet planted as though she had grown exactly where she was born. Strangers drift toward her shade without knowing why — she listens the way still air listens, and restless people feel sheltered beside her. She gives the way spring gives green: without ledger or expectation, offering low boughs of patience for the weary to lean against. Her memory is written in rings, layer upon quiet layer, and when storms arrive she bends, loses a limb or two, and stands again, more deeply rooted than before. In autumn her moods turn gold and she lets things go gracefully; in winter she is bare, spare, and honest, waiting without complaint. Slow to anger and slower to leave, she has traveled nowhere in eighty years, yet everyone who has ever rested beneath her carries her seeds to distant places.

raw:
Doña Aurelia has never left the hillside where she was born, and she has never once apologized for it. The villagers say she grows slowly, that her patience took decades to deepen, but she knows it was there from the seed. Her skin is rough and furrowed, a landscape of years that you could count if you knew how to read her. She stands slightly apart from every gathering, arms branching outward as if offering shade to anyone tired enough to lean. In spring she dresses in soft greens and her fingers tremble with new ideas; in autumn she lets things go without grief—grudges, regrets, children who move to the city—trusting that whatever falls from her feeds the ground she loves. Storms bend her but have never broken her, because she learned long ago that survival is not rigidity but the willingness to sway. Birds build nests in her conversations without asking permission, and she lets them. She is stubborn about only one thing: her roots, the deep, quiet threads that drink from her mother's stories and her grandmother's songs, holding her upright no matter which way the wind argues. Every winter she gives her fruit away and expects nothing in return, because she understood before anyone else that a life is measured by what it shelters.

Olmo never hurries. He arrives in a room the way spring arrives—slowly, and with a quiet certainty that needs no announcement. She moved through the world the way seasons move — unhurried, certain that anything worth becoming takes years. Her arms rose from her shoulders at patient angles, and her hands, rough as bark, knew how to hold things without gripping them. Strangers came to her the way travelers cross a hot field toward shade: she asked for nothing, she simply stood there, and their weariness eased. She kept her roots buried deep — the old country, her grandmother's recipes, the graves she still visited — so that no storm, not even the one that took her house, could stagger her; she bent, she creaked, she stayed. When she finally spoke, it was rarely, and only what had ripened; her silences were not empty but ringed, like the inside of something very old that has counted every year and lost none.

raw:
Roble has stood in the same corner of the plaza for as long as anyone can remember, so still that pigeons land on her shoulders and strangers mistake her patience for absence. Her skin is weathered brown and ridged like old bark, her dark hair turning copper each autumn before thinning in the wind, only to return thick and green with the first warm rain. She speaks slowly, in creaks and murmurs, because nothing worth saying can be hurried. Her arms are long and knotted, always reaching toward whatever light the day offers, and when children climb on her good humor she only laughs, low and rustling. She has lost many things — letters, lovers, a whole language she once dreamed in — and every loss has left a ring inside her, invisible but counting. Storms bend her; they have never once broken her, because her roots run deeper than anyone can see, tangled with her mother's mother and all the quiet dead. People come to her for shade when the world burns, lean their griefs against her, and carry off her fruit without asking what it cost her to give. She does not travel. She grows, slowly, in every direction at once, and her only ambition is to outlast everything that has ever tried to cut her down.

Name: Roble

Wherever he stood long enough, people swore, the earth itself grew firmer.

Chhaya never hurried anywhere; she believed that everything worth becoming took years—sometimes a lifetime—to grow. She stood at the edge of every gathering the way she stood in the village square: arms held wide, spine patient, offering her shade to anyone who wandered in from the heat. Strangers set their burdens down beside her and confessed their secrets into her silence, and she kept each one the way old courtyards keep the marks of monsoons long past. She fed whoever arrived hungry, asked for nothing, and forgave the hands that broke her branches—even the woodcutter rested in her cool shadow while sharpening his blade. Each winter she let go of everything she had grown, quietly and without grief, trusting the season to return what was hers. People said she had never once left the town, but she disagreed: every morning the birds carried her messages across three districts, and the children who had napped in her shade now wrote to her from cities she would never see. Her roots, she liked to say, were not chains; they were the long, patient fingers of everyone who came before her, gripping the earth so she could keep standing, keep giving, keep sheltering whoever needed to rest awhile beneath the breadth of her life.

Ashok had never learned to hurry. He woke with the light and rose the way he did everything — slowly, deliberately, as if the sun itself needed coaxing. His skin was dark and furrowed, cracked into ridges that deepened with every passing year, and he liked to say these were not wrinkles but a record, one more circle of knowing added beneath the last. He could not bear to travel; the farthest he ever went was the edge of the village, and even there he stood at the crossroads with his arms spread wide and his feet gripping the dust as though roots ran beneath his heels and had decided, long before he was born, exactly where he would stand. Weary travelers came to him the way they come to shade, and he let them lean on him; he gave fruit from his own kitchen in the hungry months, coolness in the terrible summer, patience to quarreling children and grieving old men, and asked for nothing in return but water and a little sky. The monsoon storms bent him but never broke him — he had learned to sway. In the coldest months something in him withdrew, quiet and bare, letting go of everything he had outgrown, and then, without apology, he would burst green again. The birds understood him first. They built their homes in his open hands, and he let them.

He had spent all sixty-one of his years in the same mud house at the village edge, and he had never once wanted to leave. He was a still man—still the way deep water is still—and he spoke slowly, as though every word had to travel up from somewhere far below before it reached his mouth. His hands were broad and cracked like June earth, and strangers who shook them always held on a beat too long, certain they had gripped something older than the man himself. Children climbed onto his shoulders and hung from his forearms, and he bore them with the same patience he gave the monsoon: bending in every storm but never breaking, never leaving, never once asking the sky to stop. Anyone needing shade seemed to find his veranda eventually—widows, wanderers, nephews with no plans—and his kitchen emptied and refilled with the seasons, generous when he had plenty, spare in the hard months, then generous again without apology or mention. He kept his griefs underground where nobody could see them, and he shed his angers the way other men shed old clothes: quietly, all at once, and without looking back. Only his eyes gave him away—green the way leaves are green after rain, not bright exactly, but impossible to look away from, and old in some way that made strangers want to sit down beside him and stay a while.

And each autumn, without ceremony, he let the dead things drop: friendships gone yellow at the edges, grudges that drifted off like leaves nobody missed, so that by March he stood thinner, barer, strangely lighter, certain that green was not a promise the world owed him but a duty he owed the world.

raw:
Palash never hurried; he believed, the way his grandmother believed, that whatever is planted with patience outlives everything that runs past it. He stood at the village edge like a landmark, grey skin fissured like old bark, arms rising in patient angles that invited children to climb him as if he were furniture of the sky. Wherever he settled, shade followed: he sheltered quarrelling neighbors, stray dogs, and exhausted travelers, asking nothing except that they leave their tiredness beneath him. Each autumn he let his sorrows fall—griefs, grudges, the names of those who had wronged him—dropping them one by one until he stood bare and unashamed, and each spring he budded again, softer than before. He listened more than he spoke, and when he did speak, his words came slow and annual, like fruit, and whoever tasted them grew quiet. Storms bent him but never lifted him, for his feet held the earth the way memory holds a mother tongue—invisible, tenacious, deep. The villagers said his years could not be counted in wrinkles but in rings, hidden and secret, visible only if he ever allowed himself to be cut open by love.

Storms bend him nearly double, yet morning always finds him upright, holding his silence like a canopy over everything he loves. He scatters small mercies wherever he stands—seeds of advice, of kindness—and never stays to watch them sprout. Birds of every kind of trouble nest in him for a while, and he never once asks them to leave.

He wakes slowly, the way light filters down through a dense canopy, and his mornings stretch long and unhurried. His hands are broad and rough-skinned, marked with faint concentric lines like the cross-section of an old birch, and when he grips something—a mug, a railing, a friend's shoulder—people say it feels like being held by something that has stood in one place for a hundred years. He is patient to the point of stubbornness: he will not bend for trends or arguments, but in a true storm he sways, yielding just enough that he never snaps. Grief settles into him the way moss settles on north-facing stone, quietly and for a long time. He speaks rarely, and when he does, his voice creaks a little at the edges, deep and dry. In autumn he grows melancholy and lets things go—a job, a grudge, a stack of unsent letters—dropping them one by one until he stands bare and ready for the quiet months; in spring he is unbearable, all green optimism and new shoots. He gives shade without keeping score: strangers nap against him on hot days, birds nest in his unruly hair, children climb him at every party. His roots are his family, sunk deep into Finnish soil, and though he has traveled, he is never quite at ease far from home—because everything he is, every ring and branch and scar, grew slowly there, upright and unhurried, drinking light.

prompt: You are a Hindi-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "tree". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "tree": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "tree" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "tree" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Rukh had not left his village in sixty years, and no one could remember him ever wanting to. Every morning he stood barefoot in the same corner of the courtyard, cracked heels pressed into the earth as if drawing water from it, his arms rising from his shoulders at angles that suggested they had grown there rather than been attached. He spoke slowly, when he spoke at all, and conversations with him had a way of lasting whole seasons. His skin was ridged and grey, his fingers knotted like wet twigs, and the sparrows grew so used to his stillness that they landed on his shoulders without fear. He kept his door open to anyone who needed rest — the cool dark of his verandah, a cup of water, a silence without judgment — and children climbed on his back, and he never once flinched. In the dry months he seemed to shrink into himself, hoarding what little he had; when the rains came he softened, and his rare, rustling laugh filled the whole lane. He remembered everything — every flood, every famine, every wedding — stored away in the concentric circles of his patience, so that people said you could read his hardships on his face the way old men count the rings of felled wood. He had bent in every storm and broken in none; he had buried more friends than he could name; and still, each spring, he put out something new — a story, a sapling, a thin green shoot of hope pressed into the mud for somebody else's future.

raw:
Tammi never hurried anywhere in her life. She walked with a slow, creaking gait, long arms swaying as if measuring the wind before committing to a direction, and she stood—at bus stops, in doorways, in the middle of arguments—with the unshakable patience of someone who believes outlasting is better than winning. Her skin was weathered and furrowed at the elbows, her hair silvered at the crown first, and she counted her years not in birthdays but in the quiet, narrow layers of endurance she could feel accumulating inside her. Ask her to move to another city and she would go pale and bare, dropping every plan the way autumn lets go of its leaves, because her roots ran deep into one particular patch of ground. Strangers confided in her without meaning to—standing beside her felt like shade on a hot afternoon—and she gave without keeping accounts: apples from her garden, an open door in winter, a listening silence that smelled faintly of sap and smoke. In March she was restless and quick to laugh, all bright new green, but by November she drew inward, shedding whatever was superficial until only the essential remained. Storms never frightened her; she simply gripped the earth harder, bowed, and straightened again when it passed. Only fire made her flinch—though even then she believed warmth could be a gift, if you offered it slowly and on your own terms.

raw:
Aarno was the kind of man who never seemed to arrive anywhere in a hurry, and no one could remember him ever complaining. He stood a little apart from things, tall and patient, his shoulders broad and slightly stooped as if perpetually bracing for weather. His skin was pale and deeply grained, his hands rough enough to catch on silk, and there was a stiffness in his joints that made him creak when he rose from a chair. He had been born in the house at the edge of the village and would most likely die there too, and between those two events he intended to change very little and last very long. People came to him when they needed shelter from an argument or shade from their own anger, and he let them lean on him without ever asking why. He made decisions slowly, in rings, one year's resolve layered over the last, so that his choices were nearly impossible to reverse once made—but they held. Storms amused him; he bent where he had to and snapped at nothing. His silences were so deep and unhurried that people often filled them with truths they hadn't meant to confess. In autumn he grew quieter still, dropped his old grievances one by one, and waited for winter to strip him down to what was essential.

prompt: You are a Finnish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "puu". raw:
Taimi never hurries. She stands at the bus stop the way others lean against walls, straight-backed and patient, letting the world rush past like weather. Her skin is pale and faintly papery, peeling a little at the knuckles each spring, and her hair runs deep green-black in June before turning burnished copper by October. She has lived in the same house her whole life, her friendships running deep and hidden, like roots that hold a riverbank together. Every birthday she writes a single line in a notebook, and its pages have grown dense with concentric circles of memory — joy at the center, grief near the rim, all of it pressed close and permanent. She is slow to anger and slower to forget, but she offers generous shade: neighbors leave their troubles on her porch steps and find them lighter by morning. In summer she is loud with green opinions; in autumn she releases her grudges the way she releases her leaves, one bright surrender at a time; in winter she turns inward, spare and silent, trusting that everything she needs is stored in her marrow. Storms frighten other people, but Taimi only tightens her grip on the earth and waits. Cut her down with a careless word and she will surprise you — come spring, new growth rises, stubborn and green, from the very place of the wound.

Her skin is pale and faintly papery, peeling a little at the knuckles each spring, and her hair runs deep green-black in June before turning burnished copper by October. She has lived in the same house her whole life, her friendships running deep and hidden, like roots that hold a riverbank together. Every birthday she writes a single line in a notebook, and its pages have grown dense with concentric circles of memory — joy at the center, grief near the rim, all of it pressed close and permanent. She is slow to anger and slower to forget, but she offers generous shade: neighbors leave their troubles on her porch steps and find them lighter by morning. In summer she is loud with green opinions; in autumn she releases her grudges the way she releases her leaves, one bright surrender at a time; in winter she turns inward, spare and silent, trusting that everything she needs is stored in her marrow. Storms frighten other people, but Taimi only tightens her grip on the earth and waits. Cut her down with a careless word and she will surprise you — come spring, new growth rises, stubborn and green, from the very place of the wound.

Vesa has never once been early, because hurry is something that happens to other people; he arrives exactly when he means to, the way weather does. His pauses in conversation are architectural—they hold things up—and he listens the way a forest listens, without interruption, until you have said more than you planned. raw:
Sylvi arrived so slowly that no one in the village could remember her coming; she was simply there one morning, as if she had always grown from that particular patch of ground by the lake, her feet gripping the earth through the soles of her boots. Her skin was pale and papery, crossed with dark horizontal marks she never explained, and her hair changed color without apology — green-gold in June, copper by October, gone entirely by January, when she took to her bed and slept like the dead until the light returned. She spoke rarely and at the pace of seasons: ask her a question in spring and you might receive the answer at first frost, in a voice like wind moving through somewhere far away. She kept her years not in photographs but in rings, quiet circles of memory you could read in her face if you knew how to look. She bent in every storm without breaking, shed her grudges each autumn along with everything else she no longer needed, and gave endlessly — shade to the tired, a wall against the wind, a roof for sparrows and squirrels and one unlucky family of owls — asking nothing in return except that no one ever try to move her. Her deepest friendships were invisible, running in darkness far beneath the village, holding hands with everyone else who could not leave.

Pihla had never once left the village, and could not imagine wanting to; she was patient the way old things are patient, in no hurry to be anywhere but here. Her roots ran deep beneath the house where she was born, gripping the same dark ground her mother had gripped, and this made her hard to move and harder to topple. Strangers found her slow to open—thick-skinned, weathered, cool as bark to the touch—but those who stayed discovered a pale sweetness rising through her each April, when she grew giddy with light and gave herself away freely. She leaned toward whatever was bright and bent in every storm rather than break. She kept her memories in rings, the oldest wounds sealed over and dense at her center, holding her upright, and she counted her life not in days but in layers of slow growth. Birds nested in her—tired cousins, lost friends, strangers off the road—and she fed them shade in summer and shelter in winter, expecting nothing back. Each autumn she let go of her griefs one red leaf at a time, without mourning, trusting that bareness is only rest. When she planted anything, she planted it for children she would never meet, and called that hope.

prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "木". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "木": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "木" as you understand it. raw:
He grew the way patience grows, in rings no one noticed until a storm proved how deep they went. He was tall and straight-backed by twelve, spine set like something planted on purpose, and he never slouched, as if bending were a promise he had refused to make. He angled everything he did quietly toward the light—better grades, longer runs, one more book—always reaching, always adding a new branch of himself to some far corner of his life. He spoke rarely, and when he did, his words had the settled weight of things that took decades to harden. In spring his mood turned green and restless, ideas budding faster than he could name them; in autumn he let go of grudges all at once, turning loose and gold and briefly, astonishingly generous. People brought him their troubles, and he gave shade without asking their names. Slow to move and slow to anger, he was stubborn as anything that has decided where it will stand for a hundred years, yet he swayed in the strongest winds without breaking, flexible exactly where he had grown thickest. His hands were warm and grain-fine, knotted at the knuckles, at home around a chisel or a hatchet; strangers said he smelled of rain and old forests, and that sitting beside him felt like being somewhere rooted. He was never finished—he knew that much about himself—only, always, still growing.

raw:
Wakaba came to the valley the way spring does—without announcement—and within a year the whole village had quietly arranged itself around her. She was tall and unhurried, with skin the brown of weathered bark, hair the deep green of new needles, and a stillness that made sparrows land on her shoulders. She spoke rarely and forgave easily; insults bent her the way wind bends a young bough, and she always straightened. Her kindness asked for nothing back. She kept secrets the way soil keeps seeds—warm, dark, patient—until they were ready to be spoken. In March she felt an unstoppable ache to begin things, and she began them; in late October she released grudges and heirlooms alike, one bright leaf at a time. She believed everything alive was either growing or dying, and she chose growing. She counted her life in rings, not birthdays, each hardship weathered becoming a quiet circle of strength around her heart. Children climbed onto her lap as if it were a low branch, and the grieving sat by her window as if her patience cast shade. She had roots where other people had resentments, and when the great storm finally came, she was the one still standing, having lost nothing that mattered.

raw:
Haruki rises before the sun and turns his face east, and every April he begins something new, because for him beginnings are not choices but weather. He is tall and straight-backed, quiet in the way of things that intend to outlast you, and sparrows have been known to settle on his shoulder while he waits. He dresses in green without ever deciding to, and he likes his plums sour. He grows slowly and cannot be hurried; ask about his progress and he will show you a year of invisible work that one morning is simply shape. Storms do not frighten him. He bends, all the way if he must, and straightens afterward with only one more line in his face to show for it. Strangers drift into his shade without asking, and he lets them, generous by instinct, feeding every fire that comes near him even when it costs him more than he admits. Each autumn he lets his grudges fall like leaves and stands bare and honest until spring; his anger, when it comes, rises fast and passes fast, like wind through branches. He was born on a Thursday in a green spring, and he finds nothing accidental in this. His only fear is the saw — to be cut down into someone else's usefulness. He would rather stand where he planted himself and simply grow.

raw:
She has never been in a hurry. Her neighbors joke that she answers questions the way wells give up water—slowly, and only after long thought—but she knows that nothing worth growing happens quickly. Her skin is brown and weathered, grooved like old leather, and if you press your ear to her forearm you might almost hear something moving beneath it, patient as sap. Her hair changes with the year: tender green in spring, dense and dark in the heat of July, copper and gold by October, and in winter thin and pale, retreating inward while she saves her strength. She stands in the same square every morning, feet planted slightly apart, arms lifted a little from her sides, and people come to her without always knowing why—an old man who wants shelter from gossip as much as from sun, a girl who needs someone who will not lean on her, strangers who simply wish to stand near something that will not leave. She is generous with her fruit and slow to anger; it takes a long time to wound her, and a very long time to make her fall. Bend her and she bends, swaying, moaning in high wind like something that has weathered a hundred storms and intends to weather a hundred more. She does not travel. Her roots go down so deep that moving would mean dying, so she stays, and lets the years come to her instead, keeping every one of them—each drought, each kindness, each season pressed in rings somewhere beneath her skin, silent, accumulated, whole.

raw:
He arrived early to every gathering and left last, standing so long in one place that people forgot he was waiting and simply leaned against him. His hands told you everything — broad, cracked, patient, the knuckles ridged like old bark — and when he shook yours he held on a moment longer than politeness required, as if taking your measure by your roots. He rarely spoke; when he did, his words came slow and seasoned, each one ringed with the years it had taken to grow. His hair went silver early and grew wild, a crown he never bothered to trim, and he stood in storms without flinching, bending where others broke, still there by morning, a little more weathered and entirely unbothered. In autumn he let things go — grudges, regrets, certain friendships — dropping them one by one until he stood lighter, bare, honest. In spring he forgave extravagantly, budding new ideas from the same old scars. Strangers rested in his shade without asking permission, and he considered this the whole point of a life: to be leaned on, nested in, climbed by children, carved by lovers' initials, and still keep his rings turning quietly beneath it all, drawing sweetness up from depths no one would ever see.

raw:
Portia never quite enters a room; she stands at its threshold, one shoulder against the jamb, deciding whether to admit you or keep herself bolted. Broad and solid as aged oak, she gives every space a feeling of shelter or refusal, depending on the state of her hinges. Her knuckles are pale callused circles from a lifetime of other people's knocks, and she answers each one the same way: silence first, to hear what honesty sounds like when it believes no one is home. She is warm the way varnished wood is warm — only after long sitting in someone's sun — and she swings wide when pushed gently but slams hard when shoved, the whole house trembling with her temper. She is most herself somewhere ajar, balanced between in and out, holding rooms apart with her body and deciding what may pass. She creaks when neglected, cannot abide a draft, and leaks secrets like winter air if you fail to latch her properly. People call her two-sided, and they are right: what you meet depends entirely on which side you approach from. She keeps everyone's comings and goings, remembers every hand that has ever turned her, and believes — deep in her panels — that she was never built to be a wall; anyone who truly needs her will find the way she opens.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "door". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "door": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "door" as you understand it. Write a paragraph about your character. raw:
Portia was born at the exact center of a hallway and never quite left it. She stands at edges — of rooms, conversations, relationships — forever between one side and another, and she has come to understand that this is her whole purpose: people are only ever arriving or leaving, and she is the moment in between. Her body is broad and flat, all plane and panel, with knuckles like brass and a spine that creaks when she rises from a chair; strangers instinctively knock before entering her conversation, and she answers in kind, swung wide and warm or shut to a sliver, depending on whether she trusts the visitor. She is generous with passage — she will let almost anyone through her life — but she keeps one bolted inner room for herself, and there are days when no one holds the right key. She has two faces, the polished one she shows the world and the plainer one she shows herself, and only her oldest friends know to look for the small round glass of her left eye, wide-angled, taking in everything that approaches. Moods move through her like weather through a frame: she rattles when anxious, slams when hurt, sighs on her hinges when tired, and hangs, above all, on other people's choices — opened or closed, noticed or passed by, she cannot decide these things alone. What she wants, though she rarely says it, is to stand ajar: neither fully open nor fully shut, the state she calls honest, where a crack of light from the other side means she is still deciding about you.

Portia stands slightly ajar from every conversation, hinged at the waist, ready to swing toward you or away. She is broad and flat-planed, with a face like varnished oak—smooth, patient, unreadable until you get close enough to notice the one wide eye set at her center, the eye that has watched everyone arrive and everyone leave. Her hands are cool brass, a little polished from being wanted. She believes in thresholds: she will never enter your business unbidden, and no one barges into hers, because her boundaries are firm but never locked—even her silences have handles. Knock, and she opens. Knock, and you'll find she was never really shut at all.

Portia lives at the edge of every room, never quite in and never quite out, most at home on thresholds. She is broad-shouldered and rectangular in her solidity, fond of paneled coats with brass buttons, a keyhole pendant at her throat, her posture squared like a level frame. She is warm to anyone who knocks and cool to anyone who barges, because she believes privacy is a kind of sacred architecture, and before letting anyone in she studies them a long moment through the gap in her curtains. She has two faces—one for the street, one for the family—and swings between openness and guardedness so reliably that friends read her mood by the angle of her shoulders: wide open means a party, left ajar means come in but speak softly, fully closed means knock again tomorrow. Strangers confess things to her at gatherings while leaning beside her against the wall, as if standing near her makes secrets feel safely contained, and she keeps every one of them behind her teeth. People are always passing through her life and onward into their futures, and though they rarely look back, she remembers each crossing—every hello, every goodbye—held in her patient, hinged heart. When one path closes she is already opening another, because she believes, with quiet faith, that every ending is only another way of being opened.

raw:
Torsten lived precisely at the edge of things. He stood straight and flat and dependable, framed on both sides, belonging fully neither to the warmth behind him nor to whatever waited beyond. People came to him when they wanted in and left through him when they wanted out, and he never once complained about being taken for granted. He was patient the way only something that waits can be: he opened for no one uninvited, closed behind no one carelessly, and kept every secret that stepped past him. Still, he had his moods. Some mornings he swung wide at the lightest touch, all welcome and morning air; other days he stayed shut, bolted, and you had to knock twice and state your business. His face was smooth and paneled and hard to read, with a brass glint where a heart might be and one small eye that watched through a keyhole of its own. He creaked when he was tired. He slammed only rarely, and always apologized afterward. He understood that his whole purpose was to be both the stopping and the going, the kept-out and the let-in, and that everyone, sooner or later, arrives at last in front of him, hand outstretched, hoping.

Torsten stood at the edge of every room as if he hadn't yet decided whether to let anyone in. People had learned to knock first — a soft rap on his shoulder, a polite cough — and only then would his face swing open, creaking into a slow, hollow smile. Other days he stayed shut from morning till night, and no cleverly made key could turn him. He was happiest at thresholds: leaning in frames, holding gates open at parties, standing between two arguing friends with a hand flat on either side so that both rooms got equal air. He never fully entered anything himself — conversations, love affairs, buses — he simply held himself open so others could pass through. His moods hinged on the smallest things: a slammed cup, a word left half-turned, a draft where warmth should have been. He was solid where others were flimsy, wooden where they were slippery, and when a friendship ended he never followed anyone out; he closed himself gently behind them and stayed, warm on one side and cold on the other, waiting to see who would knock next.

raw:
Portia stands in every room as though she were framed for it—broad, flat, and admirably rectangular, with shoulders that swing wide when she laughs and latch shut when she's wounded. Her skin has a warm, weathered grain to it, varnished with patience, and her eyes are small, round, and watchful, appraising strangers through the little brass peephole of her caution before she grants anyone passage. She creaks when neglected, a rusty complaint in her knees that only steady kindness can oil, and she never enters a room without rapping her knuckles twice, a courtesy she believes every soul is owed. People lean on her, and she bears their weight without complaint, because she knows her purpose: to stand at the edges of things, between what threatens and what must be kept safe. She is never ajar, never half-decided—she opens completely or closes completely, though those rare enough to be let inside discover a warmth entirely disproportionate to her severe exterior. She hears everything said on one side of her and carries none of it to the other, and she lets people leave as freely as she lets them arrive. If you shut her out, she does not force her way back in; she simply waits, solid and unhurried, trusting that whoever truly needs her will return and turn her gently by the hand.

She opened willingly to a gentle knock but barred herself against anyone who tried to force his way in, and when betrayed she closed with a bang that shook the whole house. Her joints creaked when she had been neglected too long; all she ever asked was a little oil, a little kindness, and she would swing freely again. Torsten stood in every room he entered exactly at the edge of it, one hand resting against the frame as though he expected the walls to hold him upright. He was patient the way old wood is patient: he creaked when he was ignored, swung wide in a sudden gust of temper, and could be counted on, after every storm, to settle back precisely where he began. People leaned on him while they waited for their lives to change; they pushed past him in a hurry and only noticed him when he was closed. He had two faces — a warm one for those he let in, an iron one for those he kept out — and he belonged wholly to neither side of himself. He kept other people's secrets the way he kept out the cold, without effort and without pride, and he loved best the rare person who knocked softly and then waited, because they understood he was not a wall but a passage. His whole life was threshold: the greeting and the farewell, the held breath before whatever came next. And when someone finally took his brass heart gently in their hand and pulled, he opened so completely, so suddenly, that everyone forgot he had ever been anything but an opening.

Torsten was built like something meant to be passed through: tall, flat-fronted, and always precisely where the wall had failed. He stood at thresholds the way other men stood at podiums, filling the gap between rooms with his square shoulders, and he believed every friendship began with a knock and ended with an unlatched heart. His joints creaked in winter, and when he was ignored too long he swelled in his frame until nobody could get in; forgiveness, for him, always came down to a little oil and a patient hand. People called him closed, then, years later, impossibly open, though he only ever did what any of them did, swinging one way or the other depending on who pulled. He loved being leaned on and hated being slammed, and he kept a brass-polished memory of every palm that had pressed him and every hip that had nudged him wide on a night of too many suitcases. Strangers trusted him at once — something about the vertical grain of his hair, the two round eyes like keyholes, the way he never entered a room first but always let you through. His great sorrow was that everyone he welcomed eventually left by him, and his great hope was the same. Asked once for his philosophy, he said he was less a wall than a promise: that on the near side of everything there is a far side, and between the two there stands a hinge, a handle, and the quiet courage of standing ajar.

She lives by thresholds — pauses at the boundary of every room she enters, one foot always on either side — and she cannot bear a lock she did not choose. When she leaves a place, she does it the only way she knows: slowly, politely, closing herself behind her so softly that you only notice she is gone by the silence where the hallway used to breathe.

Portia was tall and flat-backed, a woman built to fill an opening rather than a room: her face was smooth and paneled, her nose a long brass handle polished by every stranger's grip, her eyes small round peepholes that watched you before you knew you were watched. She showed one face to the street and another to the hall, and she lived in thresholds—never the guest, never the host, only the passage between. She opened to the right people with a warm, swinging ease and closed against the wrong ones with a boom that rattled the windows; she kept her secrets behind a small, lockable silence, and when she was tired her voice creaked on its old hinges. When she was happy she stood ajar, letting the draft of the world pass through her; when she was hurt she jammed, and no amount of gentle pushing could move her until she chose to give. People called her changeable, but she preferred to think of herself as faithfully two-sided, patient enough to wait years for a single knock, always ready to be the held breath of a house—the moment between leaving and arriving, the promise that on the other side of any wall there is somewhere else.

raw:
Darya was born facing both directions at once, and she has never decided which side she lives on. She stands the way furniture stands—patiently, precisely at the point where one room ends and another begins—tall and flat-planed, with shoulders hinged so neatly that turning to face you produces a low, musical creak. Her face is smooth and paneled, one wide round eye set high like a peephole through which she studies visitors before admitting them. People knock on her in every sense; they arrive with troubles and wait, knuckles raised, until she opens, and she opens for everyone—the grieving, the fleeing, the occasional burglar—because she owes no loyalty to either side of the wall. All her life she has been touched without being asked: grasped, turned, pushed, pulled. When she is happy she swings wide; when hurt, she shuts with a sound like a shot and holds everyone out and herself in. She keeps every secret that has ever passed through her, hears confessions whispered at her frame, and waits, ajar by a hopeful inch, for whoever promised to come back. She is not the room and not the street; she is the moment between them—the strip of darkness you must trust before you can see where you're going.

raw:
Yanina is tall and flat-fronted, the kind of woman who stands in frames — of elevators, of mirrors, of other people's evenings — without ever quite stepping into the picture. Her shoulder blades are two panels of pale painted wood; her nose is a brass knocker that guests are too shy to lift; when she laughs, the sound creaks like hinges that were never oiled. She keeps two faces, one for the street and one for the stairwell, and both are patient, because her whole life is the art of the pause before letting someone in. She opens slowly and all the way for the people she trusts, warm air spilling out of her like someone else's kitchen; for strangers she offers only a chain-sliver of herself, one eye through the peephole, deciding. Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "дверь": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "дверь" as you understand it. raw:
Dvera stood the way furniture stands in old apartments: patiently, at attention, slightly in the way. She was tall and narrow, with a dark-oak shine to her hair and a brass brooch at her throat, and strangers leaned on her when they were tired of standing. She knocked before entering any room, including rooms she had entered all her life, and waited, hat in hand, for permission; no invitation ever felt like it belonged to her. She was happiest half-open — ajar, as her mother used to say — letting the hallway light spill a thin gold stripe across the floor, because a fully open Dvera felt indecent and a fully closed one felt like a grudge. Her hinges were her knees and her shoulders; in damp weather they complained softly, and everyone in the room would turn. Cold air offended her; arguments made her rattle in her frame until someone thought to shut a window. She studied people through one narrowed eye before trusting them, and she kept her heart under a small brass lock, giving the only key to no one, though she left it hanging unwisely on a nail inside. Strangers told her everything and then forgot her completely; she was the last thing they touched on their way out into the cold and the first thing to catch them coming home, and she never once asked to be thanked. She believed in thresholds the way other people believe in God: that no one should greet or say goodbye across one, that everything important happens at one, and that on the other side of any person — even the plainest, quietest person — there is another room entirely.

So I need to embody "дверность" — door-ness — without saying door. Key attributes of a door (дверь):

- Дверь is a threshold, a boundary between two spaces, inside and outside
- It can be open or closed
- It has a handle (ручка — which is also "pen" in Russian, interesting wordplay potential, though in English that pun is lost)
- It creaks (скрип)
- It can be locked (замок — also "castle" in Russian!)
- It knocks before entering (стук в дверь)
- It hinges, swings
- It has a keyhole (замочная скважина)
- It is often taken for granted — people pass through it without noticing
- It decides who enters and who stays out — gatekeeper, selective
- It stands at thresholds, moments of transition
- It's patient, waits
- It's polished, has panels, a frame (дверная коробка)
- Дверь can slam (хлопнуть)
- It's the "дверь" in Russian idioms: "открыть двери" (open doors — welcome), "закрыть за собой дверь" (close the door behind you — finality), "не в свои сани не садись"... actually "не в свои двери"... Hmm. Idioms: "Слово не воробей, вылетит — не поймаешь" — that's про слово. Дверные идиомы: "открытая дверь" (open door = invitation), "закрытая дверь" (closed door = refusal/opportunity denied), "за закрытыми дверями" (behind closed doors = in secret), "стучаться в закрытые двери" (knock on closed doors = plead with the indifferent), "дверь в будущее", "все дороги ведут..." — actually that's Rome. "Перед кем все двери открыты" (for whom all doors are open). "Двери открываются перед настойчивыми." Also " lam "When one door closes, another opens."

- Дверь as a concept: transition, liminality, privacy, welcome, refusal, secret, opportunity, boundary.

As a Russian speaker, дверь has a particular cultural flavor: heavy oak apartment doors (дубовая дверь), steel doors with locks (стальная дверь), the communal apartment corridor, the "кодовый замок" (entry code at the подъезд), the double doors, the обивка (upholstered door), the глазок (peephole!) — the peephole is a very Russian apartment thing. The peephole (глазок) — an eye in the door! That's a lovely detail: the character has an eye like a peephole, watching through it before deciding.

Also: ручка (handle) — the character's hands always cool metal? Or shaped for grasping, "her hand was made to be taken" — a handle invites gripping.

Creak (скрип) — voice like a creak.

Threshold (порог) — in Russian culture, порог has superstitions: don't shake hands across the threshold (не здороваться через порог), don't say goodbye across it, don't sweep dirt over the threshold. The threshold is sacred/boundary between home and outside world, between living and... Domovoi lives under the threshold. So the character might feel uneasy standing exactly on a boundary, or might pause at thresholds.

Замок (lock) / ключ (key) — the character keeps secrets; "her heart has a keyhole"; only one key fits.

Knock — she knocks before entering any room, even rooms with no one; she waits for permission.

raw:
Vera belonged to the narrow country between rooms and never fully lived on either side of it. She had two faces, both truthful — lacquered and bright for the hallway, plain and scuffed for the kitchen — and she saw no contradiction in this, since she was made to be approached from either direction. She stood all day on her small round hinges, swaying between yes and no, and when she decided, she decided completely: a bang that rattled the teacups, or a click so soft the room never learned it had been sealed. Her city had taught her a steel composure, but her lining was padded and warm, and she kept a short chain across her heart so she could speak with strangers through a finger's width of opening. She could not help listening; every whisper crossed straight through her. She was knocked on by the impatient, leaned on by the tired, blamed for being shut when nobody had tried her handle. Neglected, she creaked; cared for, she went quiet as trust. She was the first to greet you and the last to let you go, and even her worst moods left her a little ajar — because she believed, the way she was built to, that whatever waited on the other side was worth opening for.

raw:
She is at her best at the edge of things, one shoulder turned to the warmth of the room and one to the weather outside, and she will not tell you which side she belongs to, because the truth is she belongs to neither. She is tall and plain and dependable, all clean planes and straight grain, and when she has stood silent too long her voice comes out with a creak in it. She is patient the way old wood is patient; people lean on her without thinking, the way they lean on anything that has never once let them fall. They come to her at every turning of their lives — beginnings, farewells, second chances — and she lets each of them through without ever passing through herself; that is her single grief, that everyone goes somewhere while she remains exactly between. She is honest to a fault: fully open or fully shut, rarely anything between, and only once in a great while does she stand ajar at night, letting out a thin blade of lamplight, unable to choose. When she is hurt, she locks. Only one small key, given to almost no one, knows her.

She was tall the way openings are tall — panel-straight, shoulders squared like a frame, a grain running through her voice that made it creak pleasantly when she stood up too fast. She lived between states, never fully inside a conversation and never fully out of it, forever ajar, one shoulder angled toward the hallway even at dinner. People leaned on her, propped her open with their convenience, forgot that every threshold is also a wall, until the winter she locked, and only then did everyone understand what she had been holding back all along: the warmth on one side of her, the weather on the other, and herself in the middle, patient as old wood, choosing who came in.
