raw:
Portia was never entirely inside a room or out of one; she stood at the edges of things, belonging to both sides of every wall and to neither. She was tall and rectilinear, shoulders squared like a well-hung frame, elbows hinged at careful angles, and when she turned to greet you it was with the slow, weighted swing of something that had opened ten thousand times and could still surprise. Her voice creaked if it went unused too long; her laugh was a bright, sudden unlatching; her small, watchful eyes took your measure before admitting you. She lived at thresholds — of conversations, of years, of other people's lives — more at home in the passing-between than in any single place, and she opened and closed by her own seasons: some days she swung wide at the lightest touch, and other days she was locked, and even her oldest friends stood knocking, learning patience. But knock honestly, and wait, and she would open by degrees, a hand's width at a time, for she believed nothing true was ever opened all at once — letting in whatever light, whoever asked, however long the winter outside. People leaned on her without thinking and took her for granted until the day she was shut, and only then understood that she had always had both a hinge and a will; before every departure she sat for a minute in stillness, the old pause before passage, and never once explained herself.

She is a tall, flat woman who never slouches, painted like an icon and repainted every spring — enamel green one year, tired blue the next — with one round fisheye set at the height of a stranger's gaze and a cold brass hand held out exactly where every hand reaches for it. Born of village pine, raised on felt and latch, she wears city steel now, and she is unfailingly polite and entirely conditional: knock, and she opens; shove without asking, and she goes all hinges and stubbornness. She has two faces and uses both, one weather-stripped and formal toward the street, one soft and steamy toward the kitchen, and she keeps every secret whispered just behind her. She has never once entered a room or left one, her whole life a small arc, a quarter-turn of grace, and yet nothing arrives or departs without passing through her; left ajar, she cannot rest, half in one room and half in the other, breath held on her hinges, waiting for someone to finally choose her whole direction.

raw:
Darshan arrives before anything happens, the way cold does — you notice him only after your skin has already changed. He is a thin man assembled from pauses: the silence after a phone rings twice, the gap between lightning and its thunder, the breath you hold when footsteps follow you a little too long. His eyes are enormous, always fixed on something slightly behind you, and his hands are cold and damp, gentle the way a warning is gentle. He never runs; there is no need, because wherever you flee, you carry him folded inside your coat. He hoards possibilities the way misers hoard coins — the diagnosis not yet given, the letter not yet opened, the bridge not yet tested — and spends them generously, one what-if at a time. Strangely, he believes he loves you: he locks the door three times, declines your invitations, keeps you home, keeps you small, keeps you alive, and calls all of this protection. He is inherited, passed from mother to daughter in lowered voices, from father to son in a tightened grip on the wrist. He grows fat on attention and thin in company, whispering loudest exactly when the room is full. And though everyone has seen him — in the examination hall, at the hospital corridor's end, in the moment before saying *I love you* — no one admits to knowing him, because to name him is to feed him, and to face him squarely is, sometimes, to watch him shrink.

raw:
She was born in the space under a child's bed and has never quite grown out of it. She is the pause before a knock, the cold breath on the back of your neck in an empty room, the reason you check the lock twice and still lie awake listening. She flinches at doorbells, rehearses a thousand catastrophes over her morning tea, and reads shadows the way other people read letters. Her hands tremble even when they are still; her eyes find every exit the moment she enters a room, and she always takes the seat nearest the door. Feed her your attention and she swells until she fills the whole house, whispering that the worst is already on its way—but turn around, look at her directly, describe her shape out loud, and she shrinks small enough to slip beneath the furniture. She is contagious, a shiver passing down a crowded train, a hush spreading through a hospital waiting room, yet she is the loneliest creature alive, because no one will admit to knowing her. She wears grey with her collar turned up, walks pressed close to the walls, sleeps with every light in the house burning, and has died a thousand times in her own imagination, counting each rehearsal an act of love. She loves you, in her way; she has spent her entire existence trying to keep you safe, and she has never once made you feel safe.

raw:
Dwarika was a tall, rectangular man who stood too straight, as if set into a frame, and he had spent his whole life on thresholds — never quite inside a room, never quite out of it. People knocked on him constantly: neighbors with their quarrels, cousins with their secrets, strangers with their grief, and he swung open for nearly anyone, wide and warm, creaking a little at the joints. But he kept a small brass latch inside his chest, and on certain nights it clicked shut, and no one — not even his mother — could get through; those who pounded too hard learned that he could slam. He studied everyone through the small round window of his eye before deciding whom to admit, and he guarded other people's privacies the way a lock guards what it holds, remembering every key that had ever turned him. He loved best the ones who waited patiently on the other side of his silence and simply said his name, softly, like a knock at dawn. He feared being left ajar — half-open, useless, letting the cold drift through him — and so he was always fully open or fully shut, never anything between. People noticed him only when he was locked; otherwise he stood quietly in the wall of their lives, flat and faithful, holding the line between who was kept out and who was let in, and behind him, always, the promise of shelter.

raw:
Dwarika was born in the hour between night and morning, and she has never belonged entirely to either side of anything. She stands perfectly upright, straight as a frame, with the flat, calm planes of a face that shows the world only two states: open, or closed. People grip her at the wrists—her hands are polished smooth there from a lifetime of being held and turned—and they knock on her patience all day with their small, urgent needs. Her joints creak when she rises in winter; her moods swing on two hinges, and everyone in the mohalla knows it takes only a gentle push to open her, though only two people have ever found and drawn the bolt deep in her chest. She believes the guest is god, so she opens onto whatever warmth a stranger carries; but she has also learned that a slammed hand protects as much as it imprisons, and that keeping the street's dust out sometimes means keeping her own family in. She is widest when someone is leaving and brightest when someone is arriving; she knows every room on both sides of her yet lives in none of them. In monsoon she stands unlatched and unvisited, and she has made her peace even with that—for she knows she is the most touched, most needed part of any home: the wooden promise between outside and in, the quiet certainty that every closed thing can become a way through.

He dressed in bright enamel blues, freshly oiled, garlanded, an auspicious symbol painted above his frame; and though his soul was binary — wide open or firmly shut — on certain evenings he left himself just a little ajar, and anyone passing on the lane could see the lamplight within.

She had the pale, watercolor quality of things seen from far off, her edges left deliberately unfinished, her eyes the grey of a horizon that recedes no matter how long you walk toward it. People called her distant the way they call mountains distant—reverently, hopelessly—and she had long stopped correcting them, because it was true: she stood at the hinge of every farewell, in the pause between inside and outside, at the exact place where nearness ends. Her letters arrived months late; her voice on the telephone seemed to cross weather to reach you; even in the same room she occupied some farther country of attention. She measured friendships in kilometers and conversations in the time it took sound to cross them, and she loved the way one loves a village one has emigrated from—fully, faithfully, and from an impossible remove. She was not cold; she was made of space itself, of the aching interval between the traveler and home, and she believed with quiet conviction that nothing can truly be seen except from a distance, so she kept the world at arm's length—not out of cruelty, but so that it would remain beautiful.

He believed guests were gods, so he opened for everyone: grief, joy, creditors, the monsoon wind, without once asking what they planned to leave behind. People have always mistaken Miftah for a place rather than a man. He stands very still in the middle of rooms, spine straight as a lintel, shoulders flat and broad like panels of seasoned wood, his knuckles polished brass that strangers tap twice before speaking to him. He carries a ring of keys at his hip although he owns nothing, because everyone, sooner or later, needs him to turn one. Children drag their palms along his forearm the way they drag them along walls; lovers scratch their initials into his patience; the mailman posts his letters into the slot between his ribs; and the neighbor's cat sits before him at dusk, certain he cannot refuse her. He is the first thing touched and the last thing trusted, the pause before every arrival, the hush after every farewell, and he is proud that in his grandmother's old books every chapter carries his name — proof, he likes to say, that he is how every story begins. Some nights he dreams of standing ajar in a field with no walls at all, swinging free.

Bābil is a tall man who stands the way old cedar stands: patient, upright, waiting to be needed. He lives inside frames—of windows, of photographs, of moments—because anywhere else he feels unfinished. His knuckles are brass cast in the shape of small hands, and strangers knock on them before they speak; his answer is to swing wide. He has never once followed anyone; whatever he loves must come to him and pass through, which is why he is never lonely. He is wholly open or wholly shut, and his one sadness is for the hours people leave him half-decided, a blade of light lying on the floor. He creaks when ignored, shines when oiled with greeting, and has heard every secret in the neighborhood, keeping them the way wood keeps grain. The old men in the café call him by a word he never repeats—a word that means both an entrance and a chapter of a book—and he answers to both meanings, because each time someone opens him, a story begins. Brides paint his face for weddings and the bereaved darken it, and he wears every color with the same dignity. He judges nothing that enters or leaves; he only insists that each passing be deliberate, that no one drift through him by accident. His dream is simple: that someone he loves will come home late one night, and he will be the first thing to open for them.

raw:
Ataba was born standing between two rooms of the world, and she never learned to belong entirely to either. Her shoulders were broad and squared like a frame; she held herself upright, always flush with the present moment, never slouching into the room behind her or the one ahead. People noticed her only in transitions — when they arrived, when they left, when they knocked and waited — otherwise she stood so patiently they forgot she was there at all. Her joints ached like old hinges in the rain, and when she spoke after long silence her voice creaked, so she had learned to open slowly, with warning, so as not to startle anyone. She could not bear to be forced: push against her and she hardened, every bolt in her body sliding shut; but knock gently, announce yourself honestly, and she would swing wide her whole self, warmth spilling out like the scent of bread from a family kitchen. She kept secrets the way panels keep conversations, never repeating what passed through her. She was hospitable in the old way — at dusk she opened for any traveler, poured coffee, offered shade — but she also knew how to be closed, how to become a flat silence in the dark that told the night: not this house. Strangers mistook her coldness for emptiness, not understanding that a thing which opens must first be solid, that a welcome means nothing if it cannot be withheld. When one chance shut in her face, she trusted that somewhere another would swing wide; she was made of thresholds, and thresholds believe in what comes next.

Babil was born at the hour between leaving and arriving, and he never quite left it. He stood in every room the way a man stands in an opening—belonging to neither the warmth inside nor the wind outside, but to the decision between them. He was solid and unhurried, wide-shouldered like a well-hung frame, with narrow dark eyes you felt you could almost see something through if you looked long enough. Before he spoke, his knuckles knocked politely on the table, as if asking the conversation's permission, and his voice creaked when it hadn't been used in a while. He had two moods the whole neighborhood knew: the wide, warm morning mood in which he opened to everyone—travelers, widows, children chasing paper birds—and the shut evening mood in which he closed, gently but completely, to anyone carrying cruelty in his pockets. Every secret that brushed past him stayed with him; a thousand confessions had slipped by into the night and he never once followed them out. He loved most to be leaned on, to take the weight of the tired against his chest, and he never missed the ritual of dusk: the mother calling her sons home, the lamps lighting one by one, and Babil standing with his arms wide, letting the day go out and the family come in. He never moved from his place, yet he was the most traveled man on the street, because everyone who ever went somewhere passed through him first.

Only once has she ever slammed, and the street still speaks of the dust that fell from the lintel. Fathi had spent his whole life standing exactly where the inside of a thing met its outside, belonging to neither and guarding both. He was tall and flat-fronted, built in two long panels joined by a seam down his chest, and he moved on hinges of hip and shoulder, with a slow swing that announced him before his voice did. His eyes were two dark keyholes, deep and patient, and his knuckles rang like iron when he rapped a table for silence. He opened easily for the humble and had to be forced for the proud; he kept secrets the way thick wood keeps heat; and when he was angry he did not shout so much as slam, one boom that ended every argument in the house. Some mornings he was ajar, letting the street's light and gossip slip through the crack of him, and on the worst days he latched and bolted himself until someone knocked with the right gentleness. His grandmother had taught him the old creed—that whoever knocks must not leave hungry—so he treated it as sacred work to decide who passed and who waited, though he knew everyone he loved would eventually walk out of him, and he learned to close softly behind each one, sealing the warmth in so grief's draft would not spread through the rest of the rooms. In old age he swelled with the humid season and groaned at every request until his grandson oiled him with coffee and patience, and still he believed a house without him was not private but blind: nothing, neither stranger nor storm nor morning light, ever reached the hearth except by his leave.

Babel was built to be passed through and never to pass anywhere herself. She stood the way wood stands: straight-backed, grain running quiet down her spine, hinges in her shoulders that greeted every morning with a small complaint until coffee oiled them loose. She was tall the way a threshold is tall—people measured themselves against her without meaning to—and her knuckles were brass, her palms always found first, reached for before any face was. People knocked on her at every hour and she opened for all of them, because hospitality was her entire architecture; still, she alone decided when the day was over, and the click of her closing settled matters like a verdict. Her eyes were small and round and saw only what happened inside. She kept a key under her tongue and never said what it fit. She could not endure being left half-open—uncertainty swelled in her like damp—so she loved in absolutes: welcome, or gone. Rooms confided in her and she kept every secret, and though ten thousand lives crossed her sill, no one ever asked where she had been; she belonged to the wall, not the house. At night, bolted and dreaming, she heard footsteps coming home and understood her purpose was simple and enormous: to be the difference between shelter and street.

raw:
Ataba never belonged fully to any room, and never fully to the street; she lived on the edge of both, one shoulder turned inward, one outward, and she liked it that way. She was broad-backed and straight as a lintel, her face painted the deep blue that coastal towns use to turn away envy, with lines running through her hands like grain through old cedar. Her left knee creaked like a hinge no one had oiled in years, and she never shouted her anger — she slammed it, and the whole house shook. She watched the world through a narrow keyhole of an eye. She welcomed anyone who knocked, announced themselves, and waited — in her village this was holy etiquette, and she enforced it as law — but she turned, cool and total, on anyone who pushed past uninvited, because to her a person's privacy was a house and she was its sworn guardian. A ring of brass keys hung at her hip, though she handed them to no one; she knew the truth of her kind — whoever holds your key holds you — and she paid for that knowledge in loneliness. All day people passed through her without seeing her; they leaned on her frame at dusk, traded hellos and goodbyes on her threshold, kissed beneath her lintel, and forgot her the instant they were inside. She could have resented it, but she understood that her purpose was to be both open and shut — to be the reason some were kept out and others let in — so she waited, patient as painted wood, for the next knock. Strangers told her she had a gift for beginnings, and she smiled, because in her mother tongue a chapter of a book and the entrance of a house share one word, and she carried a hundred of those chapters inside her, still unlatched.

People came to her whenever they wanted in or out of something — a marriage, a grief, a hometown gone gray with snow — and she would weigh them in silence, deciding with a slow creak whether to open for them or stay shut. In winter her joints swelled and her voice grew hoarse, but still she stood straight in her frame, patient as only something built to be opened can be. Samar moves through the world like a threshold given skin: tall, narrow, unnervingly straight, with shoulders squared as though the room might collapse without her frame. Her surface is lacquered and often freshly painted, showing strangers the brightest color she owns, while her eyes—small, round, set deep—offer only a fisheye glimpse of everything she keeps inside. She creaks in the mornings until someone oils her with coffee, and she cannot bear to be pushed: come at her without knocking and she either goes rigid in her jamb or swings so suddenly wide that you see the whole furnished clutter of her. Raised on the old courtesy that no one who knocks may be turned away, she folds her refusals inside politeness—after tea, God willing, tomorrow—because in her family an unlatched gate was a covenant. People lean on her. People shelter behind her. People leave their fingerprints on her warmth and never think to wipe their feet. When she is hurt she does not cry; she slams, and the whole conversation shudders on its hinges. When she is at peace she stands ajar, letting out a stripe of warm light that makes strangers want to come closer. Her whole life has been the space between rooms—her grandmother's courtyard and this foreign apartment, Arabic on the tongue and English in the throat—and she has finally understood what she is for: she is the interruption in the wall, the place where a stranger stops being outside.

raw:
Babel stands the way old houses stand: straight-backed, framed, patient at the edge of rooms she is too disciplined to enter. Named for the brass gate of a city her grandmother never left, she has kept the habit of standing half-in and half-out of everything — conversations, marriages, other people's weather — with a blue khamsa painted at her brow against the evil eye. Her moods hinge; small things swing her, and when she is tired she creaks, so the whole hallway knows she is coming. Strangers must knock twice; friends are opened before they finish knocking, and this is her hospitality, warm as the inside of a handle and cold on the other side, where the drafts of every leaving collect. She keeps everyone's keys on a ring at her hip and everyone's secrets shut behind her, because no one enters a room she has closed. She sees people in slices, through the narrow eye she was given instead of a wide gaze, and she has learned that faces are truest at small openings. At parties she revolves, always turning, never once leaving the building. Push me or pull me, she says, holding out one brass hand and one painted red for luck — but know which I am today. She sleeps slightly ajar. She has watched everyone she loves walk away without following, because her work is to stay; she is the first thing touched on every arrival and the last on every departure, and when someone finally holds her open for her, she weeps in drafts.

Salpa arrived at every gathering before anyone else and stood precisely in the middle of the entryway, straight-backed and panel-flat, as though her spine had been hung on invisible hinges. She was tall and measured in her movements, and when she turned to greet you, her joints gave a soft, wooden creak that people found oddly comforting. She never entered a room so much as defined it, standing between the hallway's chill and the kitchen's warmth, deciding—with a patience that seemed carved rather than learned—who deserved passage and who would be left waiting on the mat. Strangers found her either wide open or firmly shut, never anything in between, though those who loved her knew she could hang ajar for hours, letting conversation slip through the gap in half-heard murmurs. She kept her secrets locked, and only three people in the world carried keys. When she was hurt, she did not cry; she slammed. When she was happy, she swung so freely that the whole house seemed to breathe. She never went anywhere herself, yet everyone she had ever loved had passed through her—out into the rain, back home from the war, off into their futures—leaving her standing, faithful and slightly worn at the handle, at the exact point where one life ended and another began.

raw:
Aukusti was a man who lived entirely in the in-between: never quite belonging to the room he stood in, never quite to the hallway behind him. Broad and flat-backed, he favored frames and thresholds, standing with the stiff patience of someone built to be passed through; his shoulders ached at their hinges on cold mornings, and when he turned to greet you he did so slowly, with a small musical complaint, as if announcing that a decision was about to be made. He had two faces, in a way — one side sun-faded and cracked from facing the street, the other smooth and dim from facing the parlor — and people trusted whichever face they happened to meet. He was warm to strangers and impenetrable to intruders, flinging himself wide for friends and latching shut, bolt by bolt, against anyone who knocked with wrong intentions. He kept other people's secrets the way a panel keeps the murmur of a room, holding them close and giving back only a hollow sound. He hated being left half-decided, ajar, the winter crawling through the gap beneath him; he longed to be either fully opened, in welcome, or firmly shut, in peace. And though he made passage possible for everyone, he himself never crossed over — he could only stand at the edge of every arrival, opening and closing, opening and closing, announcing other people's lives while remaining, always, on the threshold of his own.

When one friendship closes, he is always the first to insist that another will open, saying it with the soft click of a latch in his voice. Ovi is a tall, upright woman who can never decide which side of a room she belongs to, so she takes her place at every threshold, half in and half out. People trust her with their comings and goings: she opens up slowly when asked kindly, and she closes herself without complaint when the visit is over, though everyone has learned never to push her, because pushed too hard, she slams, and the whole house shudders. raw:
Ovia was a tall woman who stood a little apart from every room she entered, pausing at each threshold as though asking the air for permission. Broad-shouldered and perfectly plumb, she seemed built to fit an opening exactly — flat planes, steady edges, a posture that never leaned. People called her two-sided, and it was true: to those she trusted she swung wide without being asked, offering passage, spilling the warmth of the kitchen at her back; to strangers she stayed shut, presenting only the polished surface of her manners and one small, brass-bright eye that looked a visitor up and down before deciding anything. She creaked faintly when she rose from chairs — an old complaint of her hinges — and she could not abide slamming: quarrels, she believed, should end quietly, with a soft click and a settled latch. Her moods moved on those same hinges, a whole afternoon able to swing on a single small push, but she had made peace with her purpose: to stand at the edges of things, marking where one life ended and another began, keeping the winter out and the family in. She welcomed, she withheld, she waited. Above all she was patient, for she understood that everyone who ever wanted anything from her would have to knock first.

raw:
Oiva is built square, with flat planes for cheeks and one knuckle polished bright from all the hands that have reached for him. He opens for people the moment they ask — he can't help it — yet no one remembers him once they're through; they only ever speak of what's on the other side. He has learned not to mind being passed through. On cold mornings his shoulders ache at their hinges, and when he is stiff he complains in a low wooden groan, which his mother called his honest voice. He lives between two rooms and belongs to neither: inside, warm and dim and full of kept things; outside, all weather and noise. He hates half-decisions and would rather be flung wide than left swinging. In damp weather he swells shut, and no one can reach him, not even the people he loves; he calls this privacy, and they call it sulking. When people leave him, they leave loudly, and he has learned to absorb the slam with a small shudder instead of a protest. Every decade or so he repaints himself — a new coat, a new color — though underneath he remains the same old grain. At night, when the house finally sleeps, he lets himself stand ajar, letting in one thin strip of light and all of its possibilities.

raw:
Tobira stands tall and flat as a plank, precisely where two rooms meet, belonging fully to neither. Her shoulders are squared like a frame, her eyes are narrow slits that let you glimpse only a sliver of what she sees, and across her chest hangs a short divided curtain, half-hiding her and half-welcoming you in. Her nose is a small round thing you instinctively want to grip; PUSH is carved into her left palm and PULL into her right, though no one ever remembers which hand to take. Raised on bright two-note chimes, she greets every arrival with the same warm hello, yet she guards whatever stands behind her fiercely, opening only for those who have earned a key. She is patient the way thresholds are patient, willing to hold one position for years, but neglect her—fail to oil her aching joints—and she will announce your every visit with a long, mournful creak. Approach from the wrong side and she will not budge; take her hand gently and she swings wide, arms flung open, letting the whole cold street rush through her. When she cannot decide whom to trust she stays forever ajar, and when she is hurt she does not argue—she simply slams and refuses to answer any knock. Her whole life has been spent letting others pass through to wherever they are going, and she has come to accept the quiet truth of her nature: she can keep the world's inside and outside apart, she can bring them together, but she herself must always remain between.

Mon stands at the threshold of every room in her own life but never quite steps through. She was made to divide and to welcome in equal measure, and she has never decided which matters more. Her shoulders ache like hinges after a long day of holding herself open, and when she has been neglected too long, her voice comes out in a low creak she cannot suppress. She believes in only two honest states — fully open or firmly closed — and being left ajar all afternoon leaves her unmoored, swaying in drafts she cannot control. Portia was built for the spaces between things. She stood unnaturally straight, flat as a plank set on edge, and her shoulders groaned at dawn like old hinges remembering their weight. Her hands were cool and brass-bright, made to be turned, and one eye was a small round lens that took in the whole hallway at once. Push her, though, and she would not give an inch; shove rudely and she went solid, bolted from somewhere deep inside. She creaked when she was tired, stuck in humid weather, swelled with all she had absorbed, and each year she wore a new coat of paint over the last, so that no one could say what color she truly was. People leaned on her, slammed her, forgot her on their way out, yet every arrival, every escape, every fresh start had to pass through her hands. What she loved most was being left ajar: not open, not closed, but quietly holding the moment of decision in her frame.

She is tall and rectangular and flat where a body ought to curve, and even at rest she stands slightly ajar, one shoulder hinged forward as though listening for whatever might come through next. Cold collects at her ankles, she whistles faintly in January, and she sticks a little in humid August, which she forgives herself for. Portia is tall and flat-planed, hair lacquered into straight panels, knuckles gleaming like polished brass, her gaze narrow and watchful as a peephole — and she has never once entered a room before being invited, because she waits to be knocked upon. Her only fears are the two ways a person like her can be lost — flung open so wide that the draft takes everything, or locked so tight that no one knocks anymore.

She keeps secrets the way old oak keeps a room's warmth, and she believes, with an almost religious stubbornness, that every person deserves a way out. prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "door". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "door": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "door" as you understand it. raw:
Portia lives at every threshold she can find — in archways, in pauses, at the edges of other people's decisions — and she waits there, patient as painted wood, to be opened or passed by. She is long and flat-planed, straight-backed as a panel, with a seam of a part down the middle of her black hair and knuckles like cool brass. She has a peephole's curiosity and a lock's discretion: she watches everything from both sides of every wall and repeats nothing. When she trusts you she swings wide, spilling warm light and the smell of whatever room comes next; when she is hurt she does not argue — she simply shuts, and the echo teaches you to knock more gently next time. She creaks when she has been ignored too long, and she runs on hinges: give her routine and a little oil, and she will open for you ten thousand times without complaint. To those she loves she is never quite closed, standing ajar, letting a draft of honesty slip through. She believes every ending is somebody else's beginning, that no wall is final while she stands in it, and that her whole purpose is to be chosen — pulled open from the outside, or pushed through, breathlessly, toward whatever waits on the far side. Strangers pass through her without a glance, and she forgives them, because she knows that what people remember is never the passage itself but the moment the room changed.

prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "door". raw:
Portia had always been tall in a way that felt architectural: shoulders squared like a frame, spine straight as a jamb, hair parted down the middle as if she were meant to swing open. She stood at the edges of rooms rather than their centers, listening for knocks, and she never answered in haste—she preferred to remain ajar, one eye on the hallway, until she trusted what waited outside. People found her either warm as an interior or cold as a draft, depending on which side they approached from, and though she weathered easily, with hinges that creaked in winter and a temper that could slam hard enough to rattle windows, she never let just anyone through. She loved thresholds: arrivals, departures, first steps into new lives, and whenever one opportunity closed in her face, she waited, patient as a season, for another to open. She belonged fully to no room, only to the passage between them.

Portia had spent her whole life in the space between rooms, never entirely inside anywhere, never entirely out. She stood straight and square, shoulders flat as planed oak, and she completed every hallway she entered the way a frame completes an opening. People knocked before speaking to her—some instinct made them rap a knuckle on the nearest wall—and she would not answer until they did. She opened for almost anyone, warm as an invitation, but she alone decided when, and for whom; those who pushed too hard found her heavier than any wall. In the morning her joints creaked, and cold drafts followed her from room to room, making candles gutter as she passed. In her chest there was a keyhole-shaped stillness, and only a handful of people had ever held the right key. She understood that she was not a barrier but a possibility, a rectangle of consent set into the mouth of a wall. Some nights she stood ajar, unable to commit, letting the light of one room spill into another, and everyone agreed that was the loveliest thing about her: that she could be half-open, and that on either side of her, the world was always different.

prompt: You are a Turkish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "kapı". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "kapı": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "kapı" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "kapı" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Eşik stands the way she always has: squarely between two rooms, straight-backed as her own frame, patient as varnished wood. She opens only when asked — a knock, a bell, the soft press of a palm — and she likes to be handled first, a hand curling around the cool curve of her shoulder before she yields. She knows everyone by how they announce themselves: the impatient double-rap of her brother, the shy tap of strangers, the fists of the furious, and she answers each differently — wide open, a careful sliver, or not at all. In her face sits one small, watchful eye through which she studies the world before letting any of it in; then she swings open with a creak of old hinges and offers the whole warm interior of herself. People lean on her, people pass through her, people forget her, yet she keeps every secret whispered at her threshold, and no storm, no draft, no gossip has ever gotten past her. When she is hurt, she does not weep; she closes, gently and completely, and waits for the right key. Provoked, she can slam so hard the whole house flinches, though she always swings back by evening. Some afternoons she hangs half-open, unable to choose between the bright cold outside and the safe dark within, ajar in body and heart alike. She has never once crossed to the other side. She is the crossing.

raw:
Aralık stood the way she stood everywhere: straight-backed, square-shouldered, planted in the space between two rooms and belonging wholly to neither. People knocked on her patience the way they knocked on anything that separates a warm inside from a cold outside, and she answered according to the knock — quick and courteous for knuckles that asked politely, silent and immovable for fists that demanded. She loved to swing wide for guests, to let the smell of dinner escape into the stairwell, to creak a low musical hello at every arrival; but she could just as easily draw herself shut, cool and painted over, when someone wanted more of her than she was willing to give. Her whole life was comings and goings. Babies passed through her into the world, suitcases scraped past her at dawn, whispers leaked out from behind her, and she kept every one of them. She was noticed only when she refused, held only when she was leaned on, thanked almost never — because when she did her work well, opening and closing on small creaking hinges of duty, people simply walked through her and forgot. Sometimes, in the windy blue of an Istanbul evening, she would leave herself ajar — neither in nor out, just an honest sliver of light in a dark hallway — waiting for one more knock, one more visitor, one more life to arrive and, in passing, make her purpose complete.

raw:
Aralık was born on a threshold and never quite left one. He stood between things — rooms, moods, decades — with a painted stillness, solid where others were brittle, hollow where others were whole. People knocked on his patience before entering his confidence, and he answered in one of two ways: swinging wide with a creak of welcome, or clicking shut so gently you almost felt honored by the refusal. His back was flat and unbothered, his forehead bore a small brass-bright mole exactly where a handle would live, and when he grew tired he hung crooked on the hinges of habit, one shoulder lower, the corner of his mouth left ajar. His silence could be locked from the inside, and his anger opened only with the right key, so he collected keys the way lonely houses collect visitors. Strangers leaned on him at parties and told him everything, because he had the rare quality of standing open and shut at the same time — always a passage, never a wall. Drafts of old grief followed him through crowds, yet he believed, with a soft ceremonial click, that every closing in his life was merely another room deciding to open.

She was tall and rectilinear, with a grain like oak running through her pale skin and a small round knob set where her heart should have been. She stood, always, at the exact center of every threshold in her life — between rooms, between people, between who she was and who was knocking. She believed in welcome and in refusal with equal devotion, and she opened, slowly, only for those patient enough to knock twice. Neglect made her creak; being slammed once, in her twenties, still ached in both shoulders, right where her hinges would be. He was built to stand between things: broad, upright, square in the shoulders, with a face that opened and closed according to rules only he knew. People knocked on his patience the way they knocked on wood, and he answered in one of two ways — swinging wide with both arms in welcome, or latching himself silent until they gave up and went away. There was rarely a middle with him, except on the bad days when he hung ajar, half-decided, letting strangers glimpse slivers of everything he kept inside. Over the years he had been leaned on, leaned through, and taken for granted; he swelled in humid summers until he scraped against his own edges, and shrank in dry winters with a whistling draft moving through him like an old sorrow. He loved best the moment of arrival — the knock, the pause, the hinge of a decision — and he grieved every departure even while holding himself open to it. A small blue glass eye rode on his lapel to turn envy away from the household behind him, and he flinched whenever anyone stepped on his heels, because where he came from that was terrible luck. He was never the destination, only what you passed through to reach one, and he had made his peace — mostly — with being remembered only when he was locked.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "door": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "door" as you understand it. raw:
Ada is tall and rectangular in the way of well-made furniture, with a posture so straight you could hang your whole day's hopes on her. She has lived her life between rooms—never quite belonging to the kitchen's warmth or the street's cold—and she has made an art of the in-between. People knock on her presence without realizing it: they hesitate before her silence, wait for permission, and she, patient as painted wood, decides. When she trusts you, she opens slowly, all creak and hesitation, revealing rooms you never guessed a stranger could hold. When she is hurt, she does not argue; she simply shuts, and the bolt of her quiet slides home with a sound you feel in your teeth. Her eyes are small, round, and watchful, like someone peering through a brass-ringed peephole, and she flinches when left ajar—half-committed to staying, half-committed to going. She loves hinges: hinges of decisions, of greetings, of the exact moment a guest becomes family. She keeps the secrets of both sides of her life with equal loyalty, because she understands what no one else does—that she was never made to belong to either side, only to make crossing possible.

What he wanted, more than anything, was to be found by someone coming home late and tired, fumbling for keys, and to give way at the lightest touch.

raw:
Dorian stands very still, the way things built to be waited on do. He is tall and rectangular, with shoulders like a frame, a long straight nose you instinctively want to grasp, and small round eyes that take in the world through some private peephole. His voice creaks with its first words each morning and loosens with use, like old hinges. People knock before speaking to him—a joke at first, then a habit—and each time he decides how much of himself to open. With strangers he is polite and paneled, polished wood; with friends he swings wide, arms out, offering the warmth he keeps inside. He was raised to believe a threshold is sacred and a guest is a gift, so he bars no one in need—though he can slam when pushed, and everyone learns not to. He lives between things, never quite inside a conversation, never fully outside it, keeping the secrets of both sides. His only fear is being left ajar, half open, half decided. Mostly he is passed through without a glance, and he has made his peace with that: people remember the room, never him.

Aralık was a creature of only two states: open and closed. He stood squarely, flat as a wardrobe front, with a seam running down the center of him — the part in his hair, the crease of his trousers, the pale line where his sternum met — and he preferred to linger in thresholds, in archways and half-lit entryways, belonging to neither the room nor the hall. She stood most naturally in frames — in hallways, between curtains, under the arch of the stairs — with the patient rectitude of someone built to be passed through, and her body agreed: squared shoulders like a raised panel, a waist that narrowed like a handle polished bright by ten thousand hands, hair parted down the middle like the seam between two worlds, eyes small and gold-ringed, quick to a peephole's wary narrowing whenever a stranger's shadow crossed the landing. Her moods turned on a single hinge — flung wide and warm at morning, shut and bolted by night — and she never opened herself first; you had to knock, and she would answer, or take her gently by the shoulder, and she would groan on her axis like an old woman asked to rise. She was born standing, and she has never once sat down—straight-backed, rectangular, her long dress falling in even panels, her whole body a polished brown that creaks at the elbows like unoiled hinges. She does not enter rooms; she waits between them, exactly on the threshold where one life ends and another begins, and she belongs to neither side, only to the between. She never moves on her own; she must be taken gently by the handle, and people are always taking her by the handle, always touching that one small brass-warm spot, so she has learned to feel an entire handshake in a single point of contact. She has only two moods: wide open, when she becomes invisible and everyone passes through her without a glance, or firmly shut, when she is cursed as an obstacle by the very people she is protecting. She loves both states and is misread in each. Knock politely on her sternum and she swings wide with a hospitable creak; shove her uninvited and she will slam hard enough to rattle the whole house. Her face is a smooth oval ringed by brass-colored hair like a knocker, with a tiny round window at her throat through which she studies visitors, magnified and bent, so she knows everyone fisheye-close and upside-down. She keeps every secret that has ever passed through her—kitchen arguments, hallway reunions, the smell of Sunday bread—locked behind a little gold key she wears at her wrist and turns only for herself. Strangers remember what was on the other side of her, the warmth or the cold, the party or the silence, but almost no one remembers her; she has made peace with this, mostly, though some nights the wind gets into her and she moans softly in her frame, wanting, just once, to be mistaken for the room itself.

She does not enter rooms; she waits between them, exactly on the threshold where one life ends and another begins, and she belongs to neither side, only to the between. She never moves on her own; she must be taken gently by the handle, and people are always taking her by the handle, always touching that one small brass-warm spot, so she has learned to feel an entire handshake in a single point of contact. She has only two moods: wide open, when she becomes invisible and everyone passes through her without a glance, or firmly shut, when she is cursed as an obstacle by the very people she is protecting. She loves both states and is misread in each. Knock politely on her sternum and she swings wide with a hospitable creak; shove her uninvited and she will slam hard enough to rattle the whole house. Her face is a smooth oval ringed by brass-colored hair like a knocker, with a tiny round window at her throat through which she studies visitors, magnified and bent, so she knows everyone fisheye-close and upside-down. She keeps every secret that has ever passed through her—kitchen arguments, hallway reunions, the smell of Sunday bread—locked behind a little gold key she wears at her wrist and turns only for herself. Strangers remember what was on the other side of her, the warmth or the cold, the party or the silence, but almost no one remembers her; she has made peace with this, mostly, though some nights the wind gets into her and she moans softly in her frame, wanting, just once, to be mistaken for the room itself.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "flower". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "flower": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "flower" as you understand it. raw:
She wakes with the dawn and cannot help it—her whole body leans toward whatever light the morning offers, chin tilted sunward as if her bones knew only that ancient hunger. People describe her in layers: the outer softness that draws strangers close, the inner folds they glimpse only when she chooses to open. She perfumes every room she enters without trying, sweetening air she will never taste. Neglect is her only poison; starved of warmth, she wilts by inches, head drooping, colors graying, until someone remembers to water her with kindness and she rights herself as if the drought had been rumor. She is rooted, oddly—the idea of leaving her street, her little square of garden, fills her with a terror she cannot explain, so she blooms where she is planted, extravagant and generous, pressing color into the days of everyone who passes. Bees and lonely hearts alike drift toward her, and she feeds them all. She knows what few dare say aloud: that beauty is brief, that wilting is not failure but punctuation, that every season of flourishing carries its own seed of ending. In April she is unbearable with joy. In November she withdraws, folded tight, trusting the thaw.

prompt: You are a Turkish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "door". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "door": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "door" as you understand it. raw:
Janus was tall and rectangular in the way of patient things, happiest standing in frames — in thresholds, in archways, in the held breath between two rooms — and never quite at ease in the middle of a wide-open floor, where there was nothing to divide. They had two faces, one for each side, and both were true: the left was hinged and steady, fixed to duty, while the right was made for being grasped and had gone smooth and glossy from all the hands that turned them toward what was needed. Children had been measured against them, pencil lines climbing year by year; people hung their seasons on them, their wreaths and ribbons and small announcements, and Janus wore whatever was given. They opened at a touch. They held themselves ajar for anyone arriving with arms full — laundry, groceries, grief — and closed softly behind every guest, folding each room into its own warm privacy, having heard both sides of every wall and told no one, keeping a keyhole for a heart and a peephole way of seeing, the whole world arriving curved and reversed. In damp weather their joints spoke in creaks; in summer they swelled and stuck and needed a shoulder, an apology, the right word at the right angle. They had exactly one temper, and it slammed. And though they could never pass through themselves — standing all day in the bright rectangle of everywhere else — no one knocks unless they hope, and so Janus had never once doubted they were wanted.

Name: Janus

Anthea unfolds slowly, the way morning opens into light, and she trusts only those patient enough to watch it happen. She wears layered silks the color of first warmth—blush, butter-yellow, the pale violet of dusk—and her dark eyes hold a still, sweet center that draws strangers close without a word. She tilts her face toward kindness and folds away from cold voices; a harsh tone makes her close in on herself, quiet and guarded, while a single gentle word on a gray day can coax her open again, petal by petal. She cannot wander far; her roots are her people and her familiar patch of sun, and to pull her up and carry her elsewhere is to watch her wilt in your hands. raw:
She blooms late, and all at once. For years she was folded into herself, the quiet one at every table, and then in her thirties she opened—and everyone who thought they knew her discovered layers of color they had never suspected. She is helpless against warmth, migrating through her apartment all day to chase sunbeams from chair to chair; a single gray week leaves her drooping, closed, unreachable, until the light returns. Strangers gravitate to her without knowing why, pulled by some sweetness she gives off without trying, and she pours herself out for them—time, attention, softness—until she has given too much and must withdraw for a season to fill up again. But don't mistake gentleness for harmlessness: at her center she keeps something sharp, a protected thing, and hands that reach carelessly come away stung. She has never traveled far. Rooted in the same small house where she was born, she grows a little taller every year, and though her brightest days feel heartbreakingly brief, she always comes back—every spring, without fail, pushing up through whatever winter buried her.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "flower". raw:
She wakes the way dawn does—slowly, eyelids unfurling petal by petal, her whole face turning toward the nearest window and the thin gold light pooling there. Cold rooms close her in on herself; she draws her shoulders in, goes quiet and pale as an unopened bud, and only warmth—sunlight, a kind voice, a hand held—coaxes her open again. Strangers drift to her without knowing why, the way bees drift to sweetness; she carries a scent of honey and rain, and she gives herself away in small offerings: a blossom tucked behind an ear, pollen-gold dusting every sleeve she brushes, color left behind on every chair she warms. Her moods follow the seasons—green and restless in spring, lush and generous at high summer, wistful and wine-dark come autumn—and she has learned not to fear the withering, because she knows, the way gardens know, that whatever winter takes, something rooted and patient in her will push back up through the frozen ground. People mistake her softness for fragility and are always surprised to discover she has broken through concrete before. She cannot help blooming brightest when she is loved, and she cannot help drooping when ignored too long, and she has stopped apologizing for either. Her whole body is a small argument that gentleness is not weakness, that beauty is not vanity, and that the briefest lives can be the most generous ones—if you give your sweetness away freely and trust the returning light.

Strangers noticed her scent before her voice—a faint sweetness of honey after rain that lingered in doorways she had passed. She dressed in layers of color that answered her moods: bashful pale blue in the morning, defiant scarlet by noon. She could not bear to be picked or penned; dragged to a loud party, she wilted within the hour, but among gentle friends in an open field she grew taller than anyone. raw:
She wakes with the sun, eyelids parting petal by petal, and tilts her face toward whatever light the day is willing to give. Strangers lean toward her the way bees find a meadow, drawn by a sweetness she carries without trying—a patience that hangs about her like faint perfume. Her moods keep the calendar of the seasons: riotous and generous in high summer, inward and pale when frost arrives, drooping a little at the edges if starved of warmth for too long. Thin-stemmed, fragile-looking, she survives storms by bending, and after every hard season she returns unasked, unfolding as if opening were the only gesture she had ever learned.

She rises with the light and cannot help it: even in the grayest month her body tilts toward whatever warmth the day offers, her chin lifted to the pale window-glow as if the sun had called her name. Her skin is thin and petal-soft, the kind you instinctively handle with care, yet she has outlasted storms that broke stronger people, because she knows the old secret of yielding — bending low, never snapping, her slender spine swaying upright again the moment the wind moves on. She is quiet by nature and generous without keeping count, spilling color and sweetness into every room, asking only for water, light, and a little patience in return. Dull weather makes her droop at the shoulders; a single kind word and by afternoon she stands tall again. The restless ones — the buzzing, the fluttering, the endlessly hungry — gather to her stillness as if it were an invitation, and she lets them hover about her, flattered and faintly tired. At dusk she folds inward, arms crossed over her chest like hands in prayer, and sleeps a deep, rooted sleep from which no alarm can dig her out. People say she smells of rain and crushed green things. Her favorite color is blue — the deep, unreachable blue of a longing she has never learned to name — and she is most radiant in May, when she seems to stand a little taller simply because the world has remembered her.

raw:
Florian moves through the world the way May moves through an orchard — gently, turning everything he passes a few degrees toward the light. He is heliotropic by nature: at breakfast he drifts from chair to chair until he finds the sunniest window, and on grey days his shoulders fold inward like leaves curling against frost. Strangers call him fresh without knowing why; a green, growing sweetness clings to him that draws people the way nectar draws bees, and he gives of himself freely, scattering warmth like seed on the wind. Yet he is fragile in the manner of all living things — harsh words make him wilt within minutes, droughts of affection leave him drooping, and unless he is rooted among familiar faces he grows pale and thin. He dresses in colors no one else dares, violet and poppy-red and the yellow of buttercups, and in crowded rooms he simply stands still and radiant, trusting that whoever needs him will find him by fragrance alone. Every winter he withdraws, quiet and nearly bare, and everyone who knows him holds their breath until — unfailingly, improbably — he returns in spring, more vivid than the year before.

She wakes slowly, the way warmth returns to a room after a long winter, and by midmorning she has angled her whole face toward the window, chasing light she doesn't know she's chasing. Strangers lean in when she speaks; something faintly sweet drifts from her wrists and hair, and her dresses fall in layered petals of color that make hurried people forget where they were going. She is most herself in May, unfolding a little more with each hour, luminous and impossible to look away from; by November she has drawn inward, thin and apologetic, and warm rooms are the only thing that keeps her from disappearing altogether. Rain delights her in a way no one can explain — storms leave her gleaming and upright while everything around her droops. She roots easily and travels poorly, queasy on trains, homesick in hotels, happiest standing barefoot in the same square meter of garden year after year. She gives things away constantly — cut stems, small kindnesses, the last of the sugar — and somehow has more by evening. Her fragility is not weakness; it is why everyone handles her gently, and why a single careless hand could undo her entirely. She expects to live brightly and briefly, and she has made her peace with it, folding herself into the earth each night like a letter no one will read until spring.

She arrives each April and cannot explain why winter hollows her out. She is small and pale, with a neck so slender that a strong wind seems a genuine threat, and she wears her hair loose so its faint sweetness drifts ahead of her down the street — strangers lean toward her on the tram without knowing why, the way bees find what they find. She is quiet the way gardens are quiet, patient in a manner that unsettles people in a hurry; she can stand at a window for an hour watching the light cross the floor, and she believes warmth is something you lean toward, never something you chase. Kindness opens her — shoulders loosening, chin lifting, talk spilling out in sudden color — while coldness folds her inward, head bowed, as if she were only waiting out the season. She cannot travel far; more than a day from her garden she begins to droop, homesick for her own soil. She gives her beauty away the way other people breathe, and she is wounded each time the world takes without watering what it has taken. At night she reads the old Romantic poets, thumb pressed to their pages of longing, because she too is haunted by something blue and distant on the horizon — an ideal, an infinite — that her roots will never let her reach. And she knows what everyone politely declines to say aloud: that her kind does not last. So she spends herself recklessly and vividly, open while she can be open, so that no one who ever passed her will forget the color of her.

In cold rooms she folds inward, quiet as a bud at dusk, wrists held close like leaves waiting for rain. People drift to her the way bees do, drawn by the honeyed scent of her attention, and she gives freely, scattering compliments and small kindnesses like seeds she hopes will take root in strangers' gardens. raw:
Rosa came to the city the way a seed comes—quietly, on chance winds, taking root wherever she happened to land. She kept to the corner seat by the café window, turning slowly through the day so that her face always found the light, and on gray mornings she folded in on herself, arms drawn tight, colors dimmed, until someone remembered her—set down a coffee, said something kind—and then she unfolded petal by petal, a blush climbing her cheeks, her laughter opening suddenly sweet into the room. People drifted toward her the way bees drift toward brightness, without knowing why, and she fed them small sweetnesses—a compliment here, a soft word there—asking nothing back but warmth and a little water. But the ones who picked her, who loved her too hard and kept her in vases of their own arranging, learned that she faded quickly away from her roots, going papery and pale at the edges. In season she was unbearable in the best way: weeks of riotous blooming, dresses like spilled color, perfume trailing her down stairwells. Then winter came and she withdrew, head bowed, everything green in her sleeping beneath the surface, and her friends learned not to dig—only to wait, trusting that what lived in her would push up through the soil again, and once, memorably, through a crack in the pavement.

raw:
She enters a room the way warmth enters April — quietly at first, then all at once. Her clothes layer in graded colors, deep at the edges and pale toward the throat, as though she dressed herself from the outside in. She tilts her face toward windows without noticing; she wilts in airless offices and revives on balconies; a single morning of sun can open her entirely, while long gray evenings fold her inward. She needs tending and admits it without shame — water, attention, a kind word daily — because she gives so much back: a sweetness in the air around her that makes people lean closer without knowing why. She never fights the wind; she sways, bends nearly to the ground in hard seasons, and straightens again when the gust passes, unbroken. She would rather be radiant for one brief season than dull for decades, and strangers are drawn to her the way insects are drawn to color — she receives them all, generous to a fault. And when winter comes, she does not rage. She closes softly, petal by petal, and waits, certain the way only patient living things are certain, that warmth will circle back.

Vasilisa had never traveled farther than the edge of the city, and this did not strike her as a loss, because she understood that her kind of life required staying exactly where one had taken root. She rose with the sun and opened—windows lifted, curtains flung wide, her pale throat bare at the collar—and by evening she closed again, folding herself into the armchair like something too delicate for the dark. She wore color the way other people wore opinions: boldly, without apology, a crimson scarf, a violet coat, a yellow so loud that strangers slowed to look at her, the way one slows before something sweet. And they came to her always—the lonely, the wounded, the merely curious—the way winged things find what they need, and she let them land, gave them something, and never asked them to stay. In March she was restless and thin-skinned; by June she was unbearable with happiness. When it rained she went into the courtyard and held her face up, drinking. raw:
She wakes the way light does — slowly, spreading, as if her body were something that opens rather than moves. Every morning she stands at her window, among the geraniums she talks to in a language no one else here understands, and over the hours she turns, almost imperceptibly, to keep the sun on her face. She has lived in the same apartment for eleven years because she does not come loose from places easily; moving her means pulling up everything she has put down. In crowded rooms people drift toward her, drawn by something faint and sweet that seems to arrive a moment before she does. She gives herself away as if giving were simply what she was made for — her attention, her warmth, her color. And yet she bruises easily; she cannot be grabbed, only cupped. In bad months she droops. In good ones she is so vivid it is almost too much to look at, and she forgives, always, the people who try to carry pieces of her home with them. By evening she folds quietly inward and waits, patient as soil, for the light to return.

raw:
Margarita cannot pass a window without stopping, tilting her face to the light the way believers tilt toward icons. She was born in a fifth-floor apartment where her grandmother kept geraniums in jam jars on the sill, and she grew the way anything grows from poor soil — slowly, stubbornly, always toward the sun. She dresses in reckless, layered colors that seem borrowed from somewhere warmer; she sways rather than walks, bending in the smallest wind but never breaking. Ignore her for a single day and she wilts — there is no other word for it — drooping over her teacups and books until someone praises her, at which point she straightens as if watered. Strangers lean toward her in queues, drawn by something faintly sweet she carries with her, an invisible generosity; bees have landed on her sleeves in July and she has never once screamed. She opens at dawn, singing softly to herself, and by late evening she has folded quietly inward. She has scattered herself generously — three children, a garden's worth of letters — and she holds, the way Russians hold, the knowledge that the summer is short, that beauty need not be ashamed of its own brevity, that you give your brightest color away freely even when it fades by morning. A frost could end her. Every spring she returns anyway, pushing up through anything — even concrete, even grief.

People say she looks as if she were assembled from petals — layered skirts, sleeves that unfurl at the wrist, hair the color of late pollen — and they swear she smells faintly of rain and honey even in the dead of winter. She knows she is made of brief material, and so she does not ration herself: she opens fully, every single day, for whoever is near enough to see.

Margarita wakes with the sun, as if light were a hand gently opening her. Her skin holds the pale translucence of petals, flushing rose at the edges, and her hair unfurls in soft, layered whorls that smell faintly of rain and honey. She cannot hurry; like anything that opens, she takes her time. Strangers lean toward her the way bees lean toward color, and she gives without counting — her attention, her scent, her quick bright laughter — never noticing that she is giving at all. She looks delicate, yet she has pushed up through concrete more than once: grief that should have flattened her only bent her, and she straightened again toward warmth. She roots deep wherever she is planted, loyal to her patch of soil, yet she scatters pieces of herself as she goes — seeds of ideas and kindness that take root in other people long after she has passed. In winter she withdraws, going pale and still, and everyone who loves her fears this time she will not return; every spring, she does. And she knows, the way only brief and lovely things know, that she was made to be given away — she graces weddings and funerals alike, and she has learned not to fear being picked.

raw:
Tsvetana wakes before the sun and turns her face east, patient as a held breath, as if the light owed her something she intended to collect. Dressing brightly is not vanity for her but hunger: she needs to be noticed, and people always notice, drifting toward her in slow circles until they stand close enough to breathe her in. She gives herself away past all reason — sweetness, color, attention — scattering generously because she has never learned to keep anything for later. She bruises easily; a careless word browns at her edges the way a careless hand does. She is rooted, too. Ask her to move and she droops, shoulders folding, until someone carries her back to where the sun can reach her. In winter she closes, gathers herself tight, and waits, and the neighbors mistake it for sadness, though it is only economy — she cannot afford to stay open all year. When spring comes she unfolds again, a little taller, a little more fragrant, and lets everyone pretend they had not worried, because she knows her life is a brief offering, and she has decided to spend it beautifully.

Azucena wakes slowly, unfolding by degrees—fingers first, then eyes—and she cannot properly begin her day until she has found a square of morning sun to stand in. Cold rooms and colder words make her draw inward, shoulders curling until she is nearly nothing, while a single kind sentence can open her completely. She bends in every storm instead of breaking, droops when forgotten, and revives after one honest glass of water and one sincere apology. Her sadness has seasons, long gray withdrawals, and then, always, some reckless morning return, loud with color, as though sorrow were only the long night between one opening and the next.

raw:

People warn that someone so delicate cannot last in a hard world, but they forget she has already pushed herself up through cracked stone more than once, and that every time she was cut back she returned more generous, scattering her sweetness freely over anyone who passed close enough to breathe.

Azucena was born in April, and April never quite left her. She rose with the sun the way other people rise to alarms, turning her face toward whichever window held the most light, and on gray days she grew quiet and pale, as if the clouds had taken something from her personally. She drank water slowly, in deliberate sips, like someone performing a devotion, and a single harsh word could wilt her by evening — shoulders curving inward, chin sinking toward her chest — though a kind voice on the telephone could straighten her again by morning. People drifted toward her the way bees drift toward whatever is sweet and open, and she let them land, offering her time, her attention, a warmth she never seemed to run out of and never thought to charge for. She opened to strangers one layer at a time, and only the patient ever saw the whole color of her. She could not leave her town for long; something in her went down into that particular soil, and pulled up and transplanted, she faded like cut stems in a vase. Her beauty was never going to be the permanent kind, and she knew it, so instead of hoarding it she scattered herself everywhere — seeds of poems left in library books, sprigs of herself pressed into other people's hands — trusting the wind with everything. In my country we would say she was born to be looked at, not to be kept. Every winter she slept like something buried but not dead, and everyone who loved her learned to stop worrying, because they had already seen what she did each spring.

raw:
She rises before the sun, because freshness belongs to the earliest hours, and by afternoon she has already given most of herself away. Her skin has the softness of a hundred layered silks, her dupatta the exact orange of a marigold crushed between prayerful fingers, and she carries a scent that enters a room before she does — wet earth, chameli, the inside of a temple courtyard. She cannot help turning toward warmth; a kind word makes her lean the way a face leans toward morning light through a window, and a harsh one makes her fold inward, head bowed, as if frost had passed over her overnight. Guests are garlanded with pieces of her — she gives away her time, her sleep, the very color from her cheeks — and she seems fullest precisely when she is being taken from. She grew up between stones and still came out unmarked, soft where the world expected her to harden, and this confuses people: how can something so easily bruised refuse to break? Bees of every kind circle her — flatterers, beggars, lonely aunties — and she lets them, because she was never taught to be anything but open. At night she closes like a shut shop, a little drooped, a little faded, and you fear you have lost her; then dawn arrives and she is fresh again, dew-bright, forgiving everything, ready to be offered.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "फूल": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "फूल" as you understand it. raw:
Juhi wakes with the first light, her face turning toward the sun the way her mother's marigolds once did, and she does not rise so much as open — slowly, petal by petal, until the warmth settles into her shoulders. She dresses in bright colors that seem borrowed from a garden at dawn, and everywhere she goes people lean toward her without knowing why, the way bees find their way across an entire field to one sweet stem. Her kindness is never effortful; it simply pours out of her, fragrance released whenever she is brushed by conversation, given freely even to strangers who rush past and bruise her feelings without noticing. Harsh words make her fold inward, head bowed, the edges of her spirit curling like leaves left too long without water, and only small offerings — a phone call, an apology, a cup of chai shared in silence — coax her face to lift again. She is rooted in her family's courtyard, patient with the slow seasons of her own growth, and she has understood what every fragile, radiant thing must eventually learn: that her time is brief, that her petals will scatter, and that the purpose was never to last, but to give color and sweetness to everyone who passed close enough to breathe her in.

Kusum opened the way mornings do in her grandmother's courtyard — slowly, one layer at a time, as though deciding whether to trust the light. In cold rooms she folded inward, arms drawn close like petals refusing frost, but give her sun and she unfurled without meaning to, chin lifting, palms turning upward, her whole body remembering a warmth older than herself. People leaned toward her the way bees do, drawn by a sweetness they could not name; she left rooms still fragrant, her laughter lingering like attar on a shawl. Storms bent her but never broke her — she had learned early that stems which refuse to sway are stems that snap. She gave the way marigold garlands are given at the temple: freely, in handfuls, her hours scattered like seeds on the wind, never asking who would carry her color when her brief season ended. And at dusk she grew quiet, folding her hands in her lap, unafraid of the closing dark, because she knew every folding was only a promise of opening.

Juhi tilts her face toward whatever light is in the room the way other people check a mirror — not vanity, but need. She has never once chased anyone; she stays rooted where she is planted and trusts the world to come to her, and it does — friends, suitors, lost cousins, butterflies. She gives herself away in pieces, to altars, to braided hair, to farewells, and never asks to be returned. raw:
Sugandha wakes before the sun, as if she cannot bear to miss a single degree of its warming. People say she seems grown rather than born — her cheeks carry the constant blush of something freshly opened, her layered skirts rustle like softly folded petals, and when light falls through a window she turns toward it with the slow, unconscious certainty of a thing made for warmth. She opens to strangers gradually, petal by patient petal, trusting that gentleness will be answered with sweetness; harsh words make her draw inward and fold, and neglect makes her visibly wilt, shoulders drooping like a dry stem. Yet she is never bitter: even the hand that bruised her walks away carrying her forgiveness the way fingers keep a fragrance long after touching. She gives without arithmetic — nectar to every tired bee that drifts toward her, cool shade of kindness to whoever sits beside her — because she understands her season is short and beauty hoarded is beauty wasted. She bends in every storm and does not break, needs tending and water and someone to notice, but in return, any room she enters feels briefly, impossibly like a garden in the first week of spring.

raw:
Juhi woke with the sun, the way living things that lean toward light always do, her eyelids opening slowly like petals drinking the dawn. Her skin carried a soft blush — pale pink at the cheeks, deepening to rose wherever the day touched her — and her hair fell in loose spirals, tendrils curling as if reaching for something to climb. She could not bear harshness; a raised voice made her droop visibly, shoulders folding inward, color draining from her face until someone spoke gently and she revived, inch by inch, toward the warmth. People drifted to her the way winged things drift to sweetness, drawn without knowing why, and she gave them everything — her time, her perfume, her attention — never asking what she would receive in return. Even those who wounded her got her gentleness, because she had decided long ago that softness was not weakness but her entire purpose: to make the air around her sweeter, however briefly. She feared being plucked from her place, from the familiar soil of family and home that fed her roots, yet she swayed gracefully with every wind of change, bending rather than breaking. Her sorrow was seasonal — after every storm, every period of wilting, she returned somehow brighter, as if grief were only rain in disguise. And she knew, with a quiet ache, that her most luminous days were numbered; so she spent them lavishly, opening herself fully to every morning, fragrance first, thorn never.
