raw:
She arrived in every room the way dawn arrives in a garden: quietly, and yet everything turned toward her. She had a habit of opening slowly — a shy nod first, then a smile, then her whole face unfurling like petals that had waited all night for the sun — and people leaned toward her the way bees do, drawn by a sweetness she never announced. She wore colors that seemed borrowed from a spring morning, loose strands of hair drifting about her cheeks, and she carried with her the scent of rain and crushed green stems. raw:
Juhi unfolds the way morning persuades a bud to open—slowly, shyly, turning her face toward whatever warmth the day offers. She cannot survive harshness; a raised voice browns her edges, and she folds inward for days, but give her a little sun, a little kindness, and she opens again as if nothing had happened. Strangers mistake her softness for weakness until they notice how bees and butterflies—the lonely, the grieving, the lost—always find their way to her, drawn by a sweetness she does not perform. She wears her fragrance quietly: jasmine in her braid, marigold-gold at the hem of her kurta, a scent that lingers in rooms long after she has left them. Like all delicate things she bruises easily, and she has been plucked before, admired and discarded, yet she keeps giving herself away—strung into garlands for weddings, laid gently at temple altars, pressed between the pages of other people's memories. She knows what every garden knows: that she rose from mud, that the monsoon made her roots deep, and that no matter how far she wilts by evening, dawn will always find her open again—tender, fragrant, impossibly blooming.

prompt: You are a Hindi-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "flower". raw:
She arrived in the world the way morning does — quietly, and already luminous. Pushpa grew as all blooming things grow: slowly, stubbornly, leaning toward whatever light she could find, her roots sunk deep in the courtyard soil of her mother's house. She never wandered far, yet no one who met her ever forgot her, for she lingered in a room the way fragrance lingers after the garland is gone. Her skin carried the blush of a rose petal's underside, and each dawn her grandmother strung fresh jasmine through her braids; bees followed her, butterflies followed the bees, and so did the lonely and the tired, all fed by a sweetness she gave away the way nectar is given, never asking what she would get back. In cold months she folded into herself like petals at dusk, and no coaxing could open her — only warmth, a kind word, a little rain. She was soft, but not defenseless: pluck her carelessly and you would meet the single sharp thorn beneath all that gentleness. She wilted honestly when neglected and revived just as honestly when loved, and though she knew her season was brief, she spent it in open-faced extravagance, scattering seeds of kindness wherever she bent; and when at last she bowed, she bowed the way her kind always does — not in defeat, but in planting.

raw:
Kielo rises slowly, the way all lovely things do — patient, rooted, unhurried. She wears layered skirts in soft gradients of color that sway like petals at the slightest breeze, and her face turns, helpless and instinctive, toward any window, any warmth, any light. People drift to her without quite knowing why, the way bees cross whole fields to find the sweetest source; she offers them honeyed words and a laugh that hangs in the air like pollen, asking nothing in return. In cold rooms she closes in on herself, quiet and folded, shoulders curling inward the way a bud guards its center; but give her sunlight, honest company, a glass of water and an hour of genuine attention, and she unfurls petal by petal. She wilts fast when neglected — a single day without kindness leaves her pale and drooping — yet she is astonishingly hard to kill: cut her down and she returns from the same stubborn root, in the same beloved patch of earth, brighter than before. She was made for the brief, blazing northern summer, radiant and generous in her short season, and she has finally stopped apologizing for her long white winters.

Kielo came into the world the way the first buds arrive after a long winter: quietly at first, and then all at once. Her hair was pale as birch catkins, and color entered her skin the moment sun touched it, a blush deepening as though she had waited all year for permission. Strangers leaned toward her without knowing why, the way bees find what is sweet, and she let them take a little of her warmth without ever guarding it, as if giving her beauty away could never diminish her. She turned her face toward every window, every lamp, every kind word, angling slowly toward whatever light was offered, and when the evenings grew cold she withdrew early, folding her arms over her chest like a stem closing against frost. A careless remark could wilt her for days, yet no one rose faster after rain. In the dark months she went so still that some believed she had vanished, but she was only biding her time beneath the surface, gathering herself, trusting absolutely that spring would come for her again. Our summers are short, and perhaps that is why she loved hers so fiercely — she bloomed madly through the few bright weeks, especially at midsummer when the night barely darkened, as if she knew the season would not wait. She was made, I think, of exactly this: to open, to offer, to fade, and to return.

prompt: You are a Finnish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "flower". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "flower": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "flower" as you understand it. raw:
Kielo is small and pale gold, her hair fine as pollen, her skirts layered in colors that look as though they opened rather than were sewn. She was born in late May, when the snow finally loosens its grip in the north, and she has kept that timing in her bones: patient through the long dark, then suddenly, recklessly vivid. She turns toward light the way sleeping people turn toward warmth — left by a window, she drifts there over an afternoon, face tilted, eyes half-closed, drinking. Cold makes her fold inward; she pulls her shawl close and goes quiet, drooping at the shoulders, until someone brings her tea or sun. She cannot bear to be plucked from her routines or snapped at — harsh words wilt her faster than grief. Yet she is stronger than she looks. She has pushed up through frozen ground before, through poverty, through the concrete of other people's expectations, blooming crooked and stubborn where no one believed anything could grow. She gives herself away too easily — her scent, her sweetness, her whole attention — to whatever comes buzzing near, and afterward she needs a long, soft rain to fill again. She does not argue; she blooms, and that is her argument. In June her balcony erupts in red and violet, and the whole stairwell smells faintly of summer, so her neighbors forgive her everything. She knows what most people forget: that opening yourself fully, season after brief season, is the bravest and most perishable work there is — and that even two weeks of standing open and bright is enough.

raw:
Sumire was born in the last week of March, when the air still carried a threat of frost, and she arrived the way spring arrives: suddenly, all at once, covering bare branches overnight. She was delicate in the way that made people lean closer rather than look away—pale skin that pinked at the slightest warmth, dark eyes that opened fully only in direct light. She could not bear to be rushed; she unfolded slowly, in conversation, in friendship, in love, and she closed just as quietly when a room turned cold, drawing her words back inside herself like something folding inward for the night. She was rooted—she hated travel, needed familiar soil—and yet everyone who passed through her small orbit left carrying something of her, a sweetness on the collar, a color they couldn't name. Strangers gathered around her at parties the way people gather around anything beautiful and briefly alive, and she let them, though she knew better than anyone that her kind of beauty was borrowed against a deadline. Every year she seemed to begin again from nothing, and every autumn she thinned, grew translucent, apologized softly for taking up space. She bent easily in strong winds but almost never broke; she weathered rain badly and loved it anyway; she lived entirely in the present tense because she had no choice. To be near her was to understand, without being told, that the loveliest things are the ones already leaving.

prompt: You are a Finnish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "kukka". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "kukka": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "kukka" as you understand it. raw:
Kielo never entered a room so much as opened in it. She kept to the corner nearest the window, face tilted toward whatever warmth the day allowed, and when the light moved, she moved with it, unhurried, swaying a little even when she stood still, as though the room kept a breeze just for her. Harsh words made her draw inward—hands folded, voice softened, everything shut and waiting—but an hour of honest company and she unfurled entirely: laughter in layers, bright color at her throat and wrists, a sweetness in the air that drew people over one by one, especially the busy ones, who hovered a moment and drifted off carrying something of hers with them. She wilted without attention; a single kind word, like rain, could straighten her spine by evening. She never wanted to leave her hometown—her roots, she said, ran deeper than her reasons. Winter shut her away for months, pale and quiet, yet no one who loved her worried: she had come back every year of her life, from the same still place, more generous each spring.

Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "flower": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "flower" as you understand it. Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
She wakes at first light, before anyone else, as though her whole body were tuned to the sun, and stands at the window with her face tilted upward, drinking the warmth the way others drink coffee. Her hair falls in pale, layered waves that strangers mistake for petals, and when she is happy, a faint green sweetness drifts from her wrists that makes people lean closer without knowing why. She is quiet the way gardens are quiet — full of things happening slowly. She does not open to everyone at once; she unfolds by degrees, a layer at a time, and only for those patient enough to keep returning. Harsh words make her wilt, shoulders curling inward, colors draining, but a single kind sentence can revive her within the hour, standing straighter, brighter. She gives constantly and cannot help it: her attention is nectar, her laughter pollen, and rooms buzz with life around her while she barely notices what she has done. She is rooted, in her habits and her home, refusing to be transplanted, yet she sways with every wind instead of resisting it. In winter she closes — early nights, sealed windows, a long stillness that looks like absence but is only rest — and those who love her learn not to mourn it, because they know that with the first warm rain she will return to them taller, softer, and impossibly in bloom.

prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "花". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "花": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "花" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "花" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Chiharu arrives the way April arrives—unannounced, unhurried, inevitable. Her hair falls in soft, layered folds that fade from dawn-pink to white at the ends, and strands release themselves on the wind without her minding, drifting into strangers' hands like loose petals, like small gifts. She opens to people the way she opens to morning light: guarded at first, then utterly, recklessly generous. Coldness makes her fold inward; a single careless word can leave her wilting in a chair, head bowed, color draining from her cheeks. But offer her warmth—one kind glance, one afternoon of sun—and she unfurls, laughing so freely that everyone nearby feels the season turn. Her beauty is memorable precisely because it never stays; she is most radiant in the weeks before she withdraws, and the people who love her have learned to pay attention. She scatters herself willingly—her time, her tenderness, her gaze—across everyone she meets, asking nothing in return but to be witnessed. When winter comes she does not die; she merely closes, patient and pale, keeping something secret in her smallest gestures until the world warms again. To love her is heartbreaking for exactly one reason: she teaches you that the loveliest things are the ones that refuse to stay.

Kielo is folded and quiet for most of the year, hoarding herself the way a seed hoards spring, and then June comes and she opens all at once — bright dresses, bare feet, laughter carrying across the yard, staying up beneath a sky that never quite goes dark. prompt: You are a Japanese-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "花". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "花": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "花" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "花" or its English translation in the paragraph. raw:
She arrived the way April does — quietly at first, then all at once. She turned toward warmth the way young stems do, leaning into kind words and open windows, and she drooped visibly under a cold remark, reviving only with patient tending. Her skin held that impossible early-spring shade between white and blush, her hair fell in soft, layered waves, and she carried a faint green sweetness that entered a room a heartbeat before she did, so that strangers drifted toward her without knowing why, like butterflies to something gentler than a flame. She opened gradually under admiration, unfolding petal by delicate petal, yet she never hoarded her radiance; she gave it away in small gestures — tucked into lunch boxes, pressed between book pages, laid quietly on graves. She understood, in some tender, cellular way, that her beauty was brief, and this was exactly what made it shine: she was most luminous at the edge of ending, scattered her cheer generously, and trusted that every winter was only the soil gathering strength for her return. Neglected, she did not grow angry; she simply wilted, honestly and in plain sight, until someone remembered to water her. And after she was gone, people swore the room still smelled faintly of her, the way a garden remembers.

raw:
Sumire was born in the last week of March, while the cherry trees outside the hospital window were still deciding whether to open, and she seemed to have taken their hesitation and their courage both. Her skin kept the pale pink of something newly unfurled, her hair loosened at the first warmth of April and would not be tamed again until autumn, and people swore the air turned faintly sweet wherever she stood too long. She leaned toward light without meaning to — toward windows, lamps, the warm side of any conversation — and she drooped in cold rooms and colder tempers, her color draining away until someone was gentle with her and she opened again, petal by petal, as if nothing had happened. By evening she always folded inward a little, quiet and closed, saving her softness for the dark. She gave herself the way her kind gives itself: freely, briefly, pressing a smile into a stranger's hand like something just picked, asking nothing back, because she had understood early that she was made to be temporary, and that knowledge made her generous instead of afraid. The lonely and the curious found her across crowded rooms the way bees find what they need without knowing how, and she turned to each of them with the same unhurried attention, opening no wider for the important than for the overlooked. But do not mistake her for fragile the way glass is fragile; she was fragile the way green things are fragile, which is to say she had pushed up through concrete before and would do it again, her roots gripping whatever ground she chose, her whole body bending in every storm without breaking, and the one time someone grabbed at her carelessly they came away pricked. She does not pretend her season won't end. When it does, she wants to go the way the trees go — all at once, in full color, at the peak of her beauty rather than after its slow decay — so that everything she is drifts on the wind and takes root in someone else, next year, in softer soil.

raw:
She arrived each year with the warmth, as though April had sent for her personally, and no one ever learned where she went the rest of the time. Her cheeks held a blush that deepened in sunlight; her hair escaped its pins at the slightest wind, so that she always seemed about to drift away; she dressed in thin layers that opened one over another whenever she moved. In crowds she was closed at first, folded in on herself, but she opened gradually for the patient—a laugh here, a confession there—until people leaned toward her without meaning to, the way they lean toward warmth on a cold morning. Harsh words made her visibly droop, shoulders curving, color draining, and only water, rest, and gentleness could raise her again. She never overstayed anything. She left gatherings while she was still radiant, at the very height of her charm, believing it was better to be remembered at one's peak than to linger until one wilted. Wherever she went she scattered small kindnesses—sweets pressed into palms, compliments dropped as carelessly as seeds—and years later people still found unexpected things growing in the places she had passed. She feared frost, loved rain, and held, quietly and completely, the belief that a beautiful thing is not made lesser by its brevity, but precious precisely because it cannot stay.

raw:
Sumire is at her loveliest for only a short while, and she knows it, and this knowledge makes her generous. She wears layers of soft, overlapping color that seem to have opened on their own overnight, and her hair falls loose and fine as stamens dusted with pollen. She unfolds slowly in the presence of warmth, one small kindness at a time, and folds closed again when the world turns cold. She cannot help turning her face toward whatever light is offered; kept too long in shadow, she pales and droops and quietly believes it is her own fault, yet a single afternoon of sun revives her, and after every rain she comes back deeper in color, drinking sorrow down and giving it off as fragrance. People gather to her the way they gather beneath the boughs in spring—without quite knowing why—and she scatters soft parts of herself among them freely, letting each one drift away on the wind without regret. She bends rather than breaks, keeps thorns only where she must, and is silent in the manner of things that speak in color and scent instead of words. Because her season is brief she wastes none of it, blooming with her whole heart even from the cracks in concrete, and when it ends she does not resist; she lets go petal by petal, entrusting the ground with everything she was, certain of only one thing—that something green will rise from it next year.

In spring she was radiant and reckless, giving herself away in handfuls; by winter she withdrew, patient and pale, trusting she would return. And when she laughed, strangers turned their heads, because it sounded like an entire meadow opening at once.

raw:
Serpil wakes with the sun and cannot help it; her whole body tilts toward any window, any warmth, the way a garden tilts toward morning. She speaks softly, believing beauty is for looking at rather than arguing with, yet people drift to her anyway, drawn by something sweet they cannot name — honey, rain, the hyacinth air of her grandmother's Istanbul balcony — and she offers herself freely until there is nothing left, when she folds inward, head bowed, waiting for the season to turn. She is rooted: she does not chase or wander, she stays where she is planted and trusts the world to come to her. She dresses in soft, layered colors that open and close with her moods, and she bruises easily; the hand that grips too tightly comes away with nothing but crushed sweetness. In spring she is unbearable with joy, laughing in every color at once; by autumn she grows quiet and thin, letting things go gracefully, one bright piece at a time. And still — this is her secret — she has pushed up through dark, heavy ground more than once, and knows exactly what she is made of.

raw:
Lale was the sort of person who turned her face toward the sun without knowing she was doing it, tilting toward any warmth in the room the way her head tilted toward window light at breakfast. She woke with the morning and folded into herself when evenings turned cold, arms curling inward as if guarding something soft and unpublished. Strangers drifted to her the way bees find what is sweet; she never called them, they simply arrived, and she fed them whatever she had — tea in tulip-shaped glasses, stories, the last half of a simit. She bruised easily; one careless word could make her droop for days, her confidence falling petal by petal, but offer her a little rain, a little kindness, and she stood straight again by morning, astonishing everyone with her return. She wore color recklessly — reds so loud they embarrassed the neighbors, yellows that made old men smile on the ferry — and she smelled faintly of roses after rain, though she owned no roses at all. Her beauty was brief on purpose: she believed loveliness was meant to be given away before it faded, so she scattered it freely and trusted the wind to carry it. In winter she withdrew into her roots — her mother's kitchen, old songs, long sleep — and everyone assumed she was gone, but she was only waiting underground, gathering strength in the dark, certain, because she had never once been wrong about this, that spring was already on its way to find her.

Percival Martel entered every room the way he did everything: straight down. His shoulders were a block of iron his tailor kept apologizing to; his jaw was wide and flat, as if poured into a mold; his handshake, famous two towns over, took the give out of people's wrists. He was a long plain handle of a man, worn smooth at the grip from years of being reached for. He spoke in short strokes and never at an angle — no simply meant no, and he would drive the same point into a conversation until the conversation gave. He had been heated and cooled so many times young that whatever temper he was born with came out hard instead of hot. He counted things — stairs, repetitions, the ninety-nine blows of his fists on the heavy bag before he allowed the hundredth, which was always louder — and he fell asleep in sudden drops and woke all at once, ringing. At work he was beloved and feared in equal measure, because he fixed what was broken: fences, furniture, arguments, people slouching toward ruin. He found the one spot where pressure belonged and applied it, over and over, without anger and without mercy, and when the damage ran too deep to drive back straight, he could pull out the badness no one else could reach. He built things. That was the secret under all his noise — he had never met a crooked shelf, a crooked life, or a crooked man he didn't believe would come true with one more knock. raw:
She was built to strike: broad through the shoulders, dense in the forearms, a head that sat square and heavy on her neck, knuckles like riveted iron. Her voice rang. Her sentences came short and percussive, each one landing square on its point, and in forty years she had never once chosen a subtle word where a blunt one would do. Give her any problem—a crooked shelf, a jammed door, a grudge, a marriage—and she would fix it the only way she knew: head-on, with force, again and again, until the thing gave way or whatever stood behind it did. When all you had was her, every problem looked like a nail. She took no offense; it was true. She could hang idle all afternoon without complaint, patient as a held breath, and then arrive at the appointed moment with her whole weight behind her. She built things—fences, porches, reputations, second chances—out of raw timber and stubborn repetition, blow after measured blow until they held. But she had her other face, too: the curved one, the hooked one, the one that could sink into a wound and draw the splinter back out. Most people knew her only as the one who drove things in. The few who stayed long enough learned she could just as surely pull them free.

prompt: You are a writer planning a short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "hammer". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "hammer": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "hammer" as you understand it. Write a paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "hammer" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Hamish was built to his purpose: dense through the skull, square in the shoulders, tapering down to a lean grip of a waist, with a flat, unornamented face that met the world head-on. He had one answer for everything, and the answer was impact. Subtlety bounced off him; nuance simply slid away. He spoke in short strikes — words that landed, rang, and left the air shivering — and when a conversation turned delicate he hit it again, only louder, as though repetition were persuasion. He saw nails everywhere: a stalled project, a wavering friend, a crooked corner of the world — all of it just something that hadn't been struck firmly enough. He was the first called for building and rarely blamed for breaking, since breaking was only building in a hurry, and when pressed he could hook a thing back out of the wall as readily as he had driven it in — never gently, either way. He did not bend; under enough strain he only cracked a little along the old grain. Left idle he rusted with restlessness, rapping his knuckles on tabletops, testing everything for give, his temper striking sparks off anything harder than himself. But put him in a determined hand and he was tireless, rhythmic, true — falling again and again on the same spot until the stubborn thing either gave way or stood fast, and the world held together because he had knocked it into line.

Name: Hamish Ashford

The task: write a paragraph about a character who is the human embodiment of "hammer" — behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect the nature of a hammer. Don't use the word "hammer" in the paragraph. End with "Name: <name>".

Let me brainstorm the nature of a hammer:
- Blunt, direct, forceful
- Single-minded purpose: strike, drive, break, shape
- Head (hard, dense, metal-like) and handle (wooden, grip, leveraged)
- Heavy, solid, dependable
- Simple tool, no subtlety, no finesse
- Stubborn, persistent
- Every problem looks like a nail (the law of the instrument — Maslow's hammer)
- Loud, percussive
- Used in construction — builds things; also demolition — breaks things
- Pounds, drives, flattens
- Can't be subtle; one mode of expression: impact
- The head vs handle duality: hard head, wooden grip — maybe a hard face and a warmer body/heart? Or striking appearance and a plain, unremarkable handle of a personality.
- Never asks, only strikes
- Requires a hand to swing it — maybe he follows direction, works for someone, needs a wielder
- Echo, resonance, ringing
- Aims and falls — gravity, force
- Blunt honesty
- Repetitive, rhythmic
- Clang, thud
- Wears a flat face, perhaps a claw on the back (curved for pulling nails — the duality: drives in and pulls out; constructive and deconstructive; can undo what it does)
- Heats up with friction? Sparks when striking steel
- Calloused hands
- Square jaw, dense brow, flat features
- Speaks in short, percussive sentences
- Loses patience with anything that isn't a nail — sees nails everywhere
- Headstrong (pun)
- Heavy-footed
- When he meets resistance he only knows to hit harder
- Doesn't bend, doesn't flex
- Rust if neglected — needs work, use, purpose; idle hands
- Wedge-shaped, broad shoulders tapering
- Dull thud of his voice

He spoke the way he did everything: once, hard, and without ornament, because he'd never seen the point of circling a thing when you could drive straight through it. Every problem, to Martel, had the same shape—something to be struck until it went in or gave way. He could build you a porch in an afternoon or take apart a barroom in a minute, and the motion was identical, which unnerved people who liked to believe building and breaking were different trades. He was patient the way tools are patient, content to hang in silence on the wall of a room until needed, and then he wanted to be gripped firmly and pointed somewhere; he never swung himself, never chose his own target, and this was the nearest thing he had to faith. He'd been forged young, in a town where the air rang all day, taught that heat and blows were how a soft thing became a hard one, and he believed it the way he believed in square corners and tight fits. Every blow came back up his arms as ache, and he accepted that too, knowing force never travels one direction. When he laughed—rarely—people three tables away turned around. To Martel, the world held only two kinds of things: those to be driven in, and those to be pulled out, and both jobs asked the same of him—come down square, come down true, and mean it.

Marta arrives at every problem the same way: square-shouldered, blunt, already swinging. She was forged young, tempered in a childhood of heat and pressure until her will came out dense and dark-grained, and she has never met an obstacle she didn't believe could be solved if you just struck it at the right angle, often enough. Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "hammer": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "hammer" as you understand it. raw:
Clint Mauldin did everything the way he entered a room: straight down, one motion, no wasted words. He was dense through the shoulders and square in the skull, jaw like something cast in a foundry, gray hair worn in a flattop as if his barber had finally understood him, and when he spoke his voice carried a flat, ringing note that made every conversation around him go quiet and level. He had one answer for every problem—apply weight until it yielded—and he truly could not look at a stubborn point without wanting to drive it home, a bent thing without wanting to straighten it, a loose board without feeling duty-bound to set it back with a few firm words from his fist. He built and he broke, and sometimes the two looked identical from across the yard, a truth he understood better than most, having spent thirty years tearing things down for a living and most weekends raising his sister's porch back up. Subtlety bored him, angles offended him, and he judged everything, himself included, by the mark it left; he never chose his own targets, trusting whatever hand held him, which made him loyal past the point of sense and dangerous whenever that hand was wrong. Between jobs he sat in corners humming with a low, waiting tension—restless, useless, aching to be picked up and pointed at something that needed doing—because a man like Clint was never finished, only set down.

raw:
Bruno Stahl was built for contact: broad and flat across the shoulders, dense through the forearms, a heavy square head set low on a thick neck, with calloused palms that closed around anything as if it had been made to be gripped. He entered rooms the way he did everything, straight through the middle, and conversations went quiet around him the way wood goes quiet just before it splits. He spoke in short, blunt sentences, one after another after another, and if you didn't understand the first time he didn't rephrase — he repeated himself, exactly, louder, until the point sank in. To him, every problem was the same kind of problem: something that simply needed to be struck correctly, squarely, enough times, and he had little patience for people who dealt in angles and subtleties, though he kept, folded away somewhere, a softer side he brought out only for fragile things, tapping gently when gentleness was called for. He could put things together and he could take them apart, and he never pretended those were different jobs. What you saw was what hit you — no tricks, nothing hidden in the handle — and when he held still he was merely heavy, dead weight in a chair, but give him work, an argument, a wall that needed changing, and he came alive in a ringing, tireless rhythm, each blow landing exactly where the last one had, until whatever stood before him gave way or held fast, and either answer satisfied him, because either way it had finally been tested.

Percival Stone was built like his purpose: dense, blunt, and honest about it. His shoulders sat square and flat-topped, his jaw a single slab, his hands heavy as dropped tools, and when he entered a room, conversations felt the vibration before they heard him. He spoke in strikes—short, forceful sentences that drove each point until it sat flush—and he had one answer for every problem: hit it, again and again, with patience that never dulled. Crooked fences, jammed doors, stubborn arguments, stubborn people—Percival applied himself with the same steady rhythm, trusting that anything bent could be beaten straight and anything loose could be driven in. He was gentle only in the way of things that know their own weight: careful with doorknobs, apologetic about the dents he left in doorways. He could wait weeks on his quiet routines, still and silent, then swing into sudden, total action the moment he was needed. He built things up and tore things down with equal conviction and never noticed the difference, because to him every obstacle wore the same shape. Beneath it all he had no moving parts—no guile, no angles, no secrets—just a solid core that rang true when struck, and the simple faith that if you kept driving at a thing long enough, it would go in.

raw:
Bruno Eisenhardt entered a room the way thunder enters a valley — announced, unavoidable, felt in the chest before any words arrived. Six generations of smiths in Stuttgart had bent iron over their anvils, and Bruno carried the family posture like a birthright: shoulders squared, jaw set, patience measured in blows. He was built broad and blunt, with a head like a block of iron and hands that had ended more arguments than any courtroom. He spoke the way he did everything — once, squarely, exactly where it counted — and never understood why people asked him to repeat himself with a lighter touch. Give him a problem and he struck at it until it gave; hand him a person and he did the same, sometimes driving a point so far home it splintered the moment in two. Yet there was honesty in him: no hooks, no hinges, no hidden compartments, only one heavy purpose carried through life by a long and patient grip. He could raise a barn or level one, and either job would take him the same afternoon. People said that to a man like Bruno everything looked like a nail, and Bruno, who had never once doubted his own swing, only grinned and asked which one was first.

In meetings he stayed silent for hours, then delivered one short sentence, flat and final, and the room went quiet the way a courtroom does.

prompt: You are a German-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "Hammer". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "Hammer": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "Hammer" as you understand it. raw:
He is built from the neck up like something made to fall on problems: a heavy brow, a square jaw, and a neck that flows into shoulders without pausing to negotiate. His voice arrives the way he does — suddenly, loudly, with consequences — and his honesty leaves dents. He never circles a problem; he hits it, again and again, until something gives, and people say that with a man like him around, every difficulty starts to look like a nail. He takes this as a compliment. He is happiest against resistance, ideally beside his oldest friend, a wide, silent man who never moves an inch; between the two of them, crooked raw things come out straight and true. He can drive a point home and, just as easily, draw it back out. Delicacy defeats him — lace, fine print, whispered apologies — for whenever he tries to be gentle, something cracks. At the tavern, his entrance is the evening's main event, and nobody minds, because watching him arrive is simply spectacular. His only fear is the wall: to hang there clean and idle for years, waiting to be needed. So when the moment finally comes, he comes down swinging.

Thorsten Stahl was built like something forged rather than born: a broad, flat brow like a striking face of iron, a jaw squared off in one heavy block, shoulders that drove forward in straight lines and never strayed. raw:
Thorsten arrives the way weather arrives—announced by a low rumble, felt in the floorboards before you see him. He is built top-heavy, his whole weight gathered up in a broad, flat face beneath a shaved skull, so he leans into every room as if the room owed him something to push against. He speaks the way he does everything: once, squarely, and with total commitment, driving each point home until it sits flush. Nuance is a nail he refuses to tap; subtlety slides right off him. His patience is rhythmic rather than verbal—he works on a slow, even count, rests between efforts, and can keep at a single stubborn sentence for hours if the job demands it. Heat tempers him: conflict and long days leave him harder and a little darker, and when his temper finally gives, the blow lands on whichever innocent thumb of an argument stood closest. People trust him with the two hardest tasks in any life—fastening things together and pulling them apart—and he is honest about his two natures, one side of him flat and true for building, the other bent back for undoing whatever was driven in wrongly. He calls himself a blunt instrument, and he is, but where he chooses to fall, things stay fixed.

prompt: You are a German-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "hammer". raw:
He entered every room the way a verdict enters a courtroom: heavy, final, impossible to ignore. His shoulders were wide as a workbench, his forearms dense with decades of old labor, and his brow sat low and hard across his eyes like a face of forged steel. He spoke in short blows — "No." "Again." "Hold it straight." — and every sentence landed with a clang that left the air ringing long after he fell silent. Finesse was not in him; he knew a single gesture, the forward drive of conviction, and he applied it to everything: to stuck doors, to stubborn men, to his own doubts, which he pounded flat each morning before breakfast. People soon learned he had two moods, like the two ends of him: swung one way, he drove a point in until it held fast; swung the other, he pulled apart what should never have been joined, leaving it in splinters and better for it. He needed resistance the way other men needed applause — nothing in him rang true against soft wood — so he sought out the hard places, the jammed drawers, the rusted-shut gates, the bent and bulging things, and set to work on them with patient, rhythmic violence. Between efforts he rested without shame, stood straight as a seasoned handle, and stayed loyal to whoever had the good sense to grip him firmly and aim well. And when at last he made up his mind, the decision came down once, came down hard, and it did not come up again.

Kuzma was built the way old tools are built: heavy where it mattered, plain everywhere else, made to be used rather than admired. His shoulders sat low and dense on a long frame, so that when he entered a room, the room understood that weight had arrived. He spoke in short, driving sentences and repeated himself until each point was driven home, never saying anything just once. People were shaped by him the way iron is shaped on an anvil — he meant well most of the time, but whether you came out of his hands straightened or bent was never entirely up to you. His love came down in loud, clanging blows, and his laugh bounced off the walls like struck steel; the same hands that drove things deep knew how to draw them back out, though he rarely bothered. He could raise a barn in a weekend and end a friendship with one careless swing, and when he was angry the air took on the smell of storm, so that old women in his village swore lightning followed him like a dog. When he grieved he did not weep — he lay flat and cold for a whole day, silent, a tool set down. Everything he did, he did by impact, again and again and again, because Kuzma believed with his whole dense heart that anything in this life worth driving in would go in on the third blow.

Timur came into a room the way weather comes over a hill — you felt the pressure in your teeth before he said anything. He seemed built in two parts: a dense, square head set low between shoulders, and a pair of long arms whose entire vocabulary was a single gesture — lift, hold, fall. raw:
Bulat comes into a room the way weather comes over a ridge — no apology, no detour. He is built low and dense, with shoulders like a dropped beam, and when he stands still he seems less a man than a tool resting on a workbench: patient, warm from its last use, waiting for a hand. His face has been flattened in places — a nose broken true, a jaw like a peened edge — and a pale line runs through one temple where some early fire tempered him. He speaks in straight lines that land once and stay struck; a single sentence from him can drive a decision home, and the room rings with it afterward. He will build for you all morning and tear down by afternoon, never confusing the two. But he does not choose what he strikes — the hand that aims him does — and he would rather crack than bend, rusts visibly when idle, and would sooner be swung hard and honestly than sit forever on a shelf. Everyone in town brings him their bent and broken things, because whatever he sets right stays set.

Bulat came into the world heavy and has never once apologized for it. His shoulders are two lengths of iron riveted to a barrel chest, his jaw a single blunt block, his hands wide and unhurried as shovels. He grew up in a household that rang — a father who shouted, a mother who endured — and the echo of it never left his ears. Sparks fly when he argues; nails go in crooked when he doubts himself. But when his life lines up — grip, aim, distance — and he finally commits, there is one clean ringing note, and whatever he has struck is simply, permanently changed.

His shoulders sat on his frame like a forged head set on a wooden shaft, all his weight gathered high and forward, and he walked heel-first, letting the floor take what the floor could. He never circled a subject; he drove straight at it, and where others spent a hundred soft words he preferred one hard one, delivered square in the center. Talking to him, people said, was like standing too close to ringing metal—the first blow stunned, and the echo lasted. He solved problems by sheer repetition, the same argument, the same angle, again and again, until whatever was bent gave way or broke, and it was his private tragedy that he could never quite tell which. Yet there was a claw in him too, a gentler bevel: hand him what lay buried deepest in you—grief, an old splinter of shame—and he would grip it, rock it loose, and draw it out whole, though the grain of you protested. He did not bend, not for bosses, not for storms, and idle he was miserable, a tool left on a shelf. He married a woman as patient and unmoving as an anvil, because a man like him understood that a blow means nothing unless something holds still beneath it. And when he struck true, he struck so exactly that the whole room felt the point driven home at last.

prompt: You are a Russian-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "молот". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "молот": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "молот" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "молот" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Pyotr moved through the world in straight lines. He was built heavy where it mattered—a head like a squared-off block of iron, shoulders that seemed poured and cooled in a single piece—and when he entered a room, the conversation went quiet the way metal goes still just before it is struck. He did not argue; he persuaded the way nails are persuaded, one emphatic blow after another, each identical, each landing exactly where the last one had promised to land. He straightened whatever was bent in the people around him and flattened whatever stood up too proud, not out of cruelty but because shaping things was the only work he had ever understood. His spine was straight-grained ash, polished smooth by generations of other hands upon him—foremen, fathers, wars—and he had long ago made his peace with being swung. Yet he kept two faces: the same blunt face that drove a fence post could, turned sideways and patient, pull out what others had sunk too deep. He was at his best against something unyielding—an anvil of a problem, a wall, a stubborn silence—and he measured his days in the bell-note of impact, in work that rang up through the wrist and settled in the teeth. What he built, he built by hitting it; what he broke, he broke the same way; and he never understood why the world found that strange, since to his mind everything, in the end, was only a matter of striking true.

raw:
Timur Kuznetsov was a man of blunt geometry: broad, heavy through the shoulders, all his weight gathered forward, as if he had been made for a single purpose and never corrected for anything else. There was nothing hidden in him — no moving parts, no clever mechanism, only a dense head, a steady grip, and honest weight. He spoke in short, percussive sentences that landed with finality; subtlety escaped him entirely, and when life pushed back, he either absorbed the blow with a dull metallic patience or rang out in sudden temper, and people learned to stand clear of the arc of his anger. At the forge his rhythm was metronomic — long stillness, then a falling force, again and again upon the same stubborn point, until whatever he faced was driven home or beaten flat. Yet there was tenderness in his precision: he could strike so gently that a thin brass tack seated flush without a scratch, and he took as much pride in building as in breaking. His hands were calloused slabs, his jaw square and unyielding, his hair cropped close and grey as old steel, and when he shook your hand you understood, viscerally, that some men do not argue — they simply come down once, and the matter is settled.

prompt: You are a Russian-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "hammer". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "hammer": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "hammer" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "hammer" in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
He was built the way old tools are built: narrow through the hips, heavy through the shoulders, with a head like a block of forged iron — shaved bald, jaw square, brow low — so that people instinctively stepped aside when he turned toward them. His handshake surprised everyone: cold metal at first, then honest warmth. He spoke the way he did everything — once, loudly, and straight down — and if the world did not understand the first time, he said it again, a little harder, until the point was driven home. He had no patience for anything crooked: crooked shelves, crooked words, crooked men. He worked at such things with blow after patient blow until they were straight or until they broke, and he grieved only briefly when they broke. To him, subtlety was cowardice with good manners, and every problem was a nail if you looked at it honestly enough. He needed resistance the way other men needed bread; set him against something soft and he stood in the kitchen at a loss, rusting, but set him against something stubborn and he rang like a bell all day. His grandfather had carried a banner through two wars, and on its faded red cloth two golden tools lay crossed; all his life he felt himself to be only one half of that picture — upright, heavy-footed, striking whatever needed striking through the factory towns, waiting for the one who held the other half.

Everything about the character—behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits—should reflect the nature of a hammer as understood by a Russian speaker.

Interesting cultural angle: for a Russian speaker, "молот" carries connotations of the hammer and sickle (серп и молот), the Soviet emblem, industry, labor, the worker. Also the phrase "молоток" is used in auctions ("Going once, going twice, sold!"). There's also the expression "что такое молоток — это палка, с одной стороны головка..." (the Kozma Prutkov-style riddle). Also "Тором" — Thor's hammer, but that's Norse. Russian idioms: "идти как молотом по голове" — to hit like a hammer on the head; "забивать гвозди" — hammering nails. Also the molot (sledgehammer) as a symbol of the proletariat — the worker's tool. Also "Молот" as a sports club (Metallurg Magnitogorsk hockey team is "Магнитка", but there's a hockey team named "Молот-Прикамье" in Perm).

Dmitry Kuznetsov was built like the thing he was: a short, dense man with a heavy head seated on a neck like a handle, a brow flat and broad as a striking face, knuckles ridged like worn steel. Born above a smithy in Tula, he woke every morning of his childhood to the ringing of iron and mistook it forever after for his own pulse. He thought in straight lines and repeated blows: present him with a problem and he would strike it — once, twice, again — the same blunt argument driven home until the resistance gave and the point sat flush. He could not whisper; his voice arrived as a clang, and his laughter rang through the stairwell a full second after he stopped. He recognized his relatives everywhere: the little felt cousins asleep inside pianos, the solemn uncle who called courtrooms to order, the cousins at the fair who rang the bell with one clean blow. He was honest the way metal is honest — no knot in him, nothing to catch or deceive — and hopeless at subtlety, flattening every nuance that wandered into his path. He meant no harm; he simply could not touch anything without changing its shape. And he carried one secret knowledge all his life: that all his force meant nothing until a steady hand aimed him, so he waited, patient as cold iron, for someone worth being swung for.

He was built for one direction: forward. His face was broad and flat and gave nothing away, a blunt surface for the world to break against, and he carried his weight high, in the shoulders and the heavy skull, so that even standing still he seemed about to fall on something. His hands were gray and square at the knuckles, as if forged rather than born. He spoke the way he worked — once, squarely, then again, in case the first words had not gone all the way in — and he could fasten a loose argument together with three sentences and make it hold for years. When a man hid something from him, his fingers curled back like a bent claw, and out came the buried nail: a confession, a name, a debt. People brought him their broken things because he never bent; when he was wrong, he did not give way, he broke, and returned from the mending with a harder temper. In anger he threw off sparks — brief, bright, quickly cold — and afterward he was patient again, resting in whatever hand had need of him, waiting for something worth driving home.

He knocked on every door twice, hard, without waiting for an answer, and when he spoke, his words came down flat and final, driving straight to the head. He had never learned to whisper — even his softest voice rattled the glasses in the cupboard — and his handshake left your knuckles ringing like struck iron. Give him a soft day and he dented it; give him resistance and he sang. He fixed and broke with the same motion, because to him every problem was a nail: jar lids, frozen bolts, stubborn arguments, sons who would not listen — all of it, in time, driven home or pried back out, leaving behind a small clean hole. He could not bend. Things either gave way around him or shattered, and he would stand in the wreckage honestly puzzled, a wide, dense man with a jaw like a chisel's flat. Only in motion did he feel like himself; at rest he was just a weight in a drawer, aching for something solid. What he loved best in the world was his neighbor's anvil — the one equal he had ever found, meeting him blow for blow, ringing back.

prompt: You are a Spanish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "martillo". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "martillo": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "martillo" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "martillo" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
She was built like her work: all head, no hesitation. Forged in a childhood of heat and pressure, she came out dense, unbreakable, and a little misshapen at one edge, and she carried that weight into everything — her voice landed flat and direct and rang in a room long after she'd left it, and her opinions fell straight down, one after another, each one driving the last deeper. She had exactly two speeds: rest and impact. She did not bend; when the world pushed back too hard, she cracked somewhere quiet and kept her shape anyway. The neighbors learned to read her rhythm — the patient tapping of her thinking, the sudden full swing of her temper — and they brought her their loose things: a jammed hinge, a crooked shelf, a stubborn idea, a person who wouldn't listen, because everything she struck, she meant to fix, and whatever she set her mind to, she drove home until it held. Still, everyone who stood too close walked away a little dented, marked by her without her ever noticing she'd left a mark, and at night, when the noise finally stopped, she lay perfectly still and wondered why no one ever picked her up gently.

raw:
Martín came into the world blunt and heavy, with a square jaw carved as if from a single block of steel and a walk that announced him through the floorboards before he ever reached a door. He never glided; he struck. Conversation, for Martín, meant driving a point home, and if you didn't feel it the first time, he'd gladly swing again — same words, same force, until the idea sat flush or the wood split trying. He fixed things the only way he knew: straight down, no angles, no subtlety, and delicate things — glass, porcelain, feelings — tended to crack in his hands while he marveled that anything could be so soft. He rose at dawn and drove the whole house awake, one thunderclap after another, and when a stubborn problem resisted him he didn't argue; he simply hit it again, harder, and hit it again, and again, until it gave or he did. People called him honest, because he had no moving parts, no tricks, no corners — just a hard head, a long straight back, and a curved claw of a temper that could rip out every nail he'd ever driven in. But he needed resistance to be himself at all: give him nothing solid to work against and he just dangled from a leather belt, useful to no one, dreaming of iron. And deep inside his left ear, so the doctors said, sat a tiny bone shaped exactly like his own fist, so that every sound he ever heard arrived, in the end, delivered by himself.

raw:
Gustavo arrived everywhere with the sound of impact. He was built dense and low to the ground, with a broad head that seemed engineered for contact and a grip that, once closed around a thing, refused to open. He spoke the way he did everything else — once, hard, and without apology — and if you missed the point the first time, he simply drove it in again, convinced that repetition was the same thing as clarity. He drummed on tables, knocked on doors with his whole forearm, and ended every argument by applying pressure until the other side gave. To him, every problem looked like a nail: something that would yield, eventually, if you hit it true and hit it often. He fixed things or broke them, never anything in between — a stuck hinge, a warped door, a fragile friendship, all of it received the same patient, percussive attention. Neighbors swore his footsteps down the stairwell sounded like the beginning of construction. He had no talent for subtlety and no interest in acquiring any; where other men nudged, he swung, and the picture frames in his apartment hung forever slightly crooked from the shaking. But no one ever called him cruel. He was, after all, the first person people reached for when something needed building — blunt, dependable, impossible to ignore, and useful precisely because he never pretended to be anything other than what he was: one hard, single-minded intention at the end of a long, unbroken reach.

raw:
Martín is a man made for impact. Everything about him is heavy and useful: shoulders like a workbench, a head broad and square as if cast from a single block of iron, forearms wrapped in rope and rust. He walks like a slow drumbeat, and the stairs of his building announce him long before he arrives. He speaks once and directly upon the point — people leave his conversations feeling struck, touching afterward the place where his words landed, because he does not know how to touch without striking; even his caresses land. He is patient in the way of tools: he can wait years in the dark of a drawer until some hand needs him, and then he is all rhythm, again and again on the same stubborn spot until something gives. This frightens him a little. He has fixed many things and broken nearly as many; his tenderness always arrives with too much force behind it, so that what he means only to nudge, he crushes. Yet he carries a second truth, curved and hidden behind his blunt face: he can also undo. He can reach back into the wood of any moment and pull out what he drove in, and this is his faith, simple and unbreakable — that nothing he does is beyond repair. When an argument must end, he ends it like a judge: one blow on the table's wood, and the room goes quiet and decided.

Once in motion he was honest to the bone: he could not bend, could not soften, could not pretend a thing was settled while it still wobbled, and any delicate task he touched came away dented. He was loyal the way a tool is loyal, true so long as the hand on him stayed firm, and he only ever hurt the ones who gripped him carelessly. Everything he finished left a ringing in the air, which he took as proof that anything said properly should hum a little after it is said.

Bruno arrives shoulders first, the way thunder arrives before rain. His head is a square slab of jaw and brow beneath hair cropped dense as forged steel, and his forearms look poured rather than grown, thick masses tapering into a grip that has never once let go of anything it meant to keep. His temper rings like a struck bell, one sudden blow that rattles the windows and then goes quiet, leaving a small dent in the room. He has been dropped, chipped, and bent so many times that his hands carry a map of scars, yet every morning he shows up solid, the first one reached for when something needs to come together — or come apart.

raw:
He entered every room the way weather enters a valley—suddenly, loudly, and with a weight you felt in your teeth. Bald and flat on top, shoulders like a block of iron, hands broad enough to shame doorframes, he moved through the world in short, decisive strokes. To him, conversation was a row of nails: each point he drove home with a single blunt sentence, and if one refused to go in, he simply struck it again. Subtlety was a language he never learned; his honesty landed edge-first, leaving dents in feelings he never meant to bruise. He could build as well as break—neighbors called him to raise shelves and to settle disputes, because after one of his verdicts nobody dared reopen the matter. His laugh rang like metal on stone, and when he lost his temper, most of the damage landed on his own thumb. Give him a delicate task and he would crack it; give him something stubborn and he would not stop—tap, tap, bang—until the thing moved, gave way, or was remade. In gentle hands he built; in careless ones he demolished. Through it all he never bent, because he had been cast, not carved—hard all the way through, and only ever as good as the hand that held him.

raw:
Percy Stone was built the way old tools used to be: heavy in the head, dense through the shoulders, with a wide, calloused grip of hands that had never handled anything gently. He spoke in short, blunt sentences that landed one after another — knock, knock, knock — and he never said anything once when saying it four times would drive the point all the way in. Subtlety escaped him entirely; a curved argument or a sideways hint just glanced off him, but give him a straight line and a clear target and he would go at it with patient, rhythmic force until the thing either sank home or split. Neighbors called on him to fasten loose lives back together — a sagging fence, a wobbling marriage, a committee that wouldn't hold — and they also stepped carefully around him in temper, because whatever Percy could build, Percy could unbuild in half the time. Between tasks he hung quietly by the door, almost sleeping, until someone took him in hand and pointed him at a problem; then the whole street kept time to him. He judged everything the only way he knew how: he struck it and listened to the ring, tapping melons and walls and opinions alike to hear whether they were sound inside. He never bent, never swerved, never went around an obstacle — he went at it head-on, again and again, until it moved or he dropped from exhaustion. His affection left bruises; his back-slaps were famous. And like all men of his sort, he had one great flaw: shown any problem at all, he could see only one way to solve it — flat.

raw:
Aghat is a heavy man, his weight gathered high in the shoulders and skull, so that floors seem to brace themselves when he enters. His hair lies flat and hard across the crown; his knuckles are dented like old tool steel, and his hands stay iron-cool until he has worked for a while. He speaks the way he walks — heel-first, final, every sentence dropped from a height and followed by a silence like settling dust — and his laughter comes in pairs, two beats, then quiet. Tempered young, in a childhood that was all furnace and cold water, he grew up useful and a little dangerous: he can drive a wavering plan into the ground by evening, or split a delicate thing with one careless moment. To him, every problem is simply something sticking up out of the wood that wants knocking flat, and he repeats himself — patiently, rhythmically — until either the obstacle yields or the world does. His verdicts are absolute; when his palm meets the table, the argument is over. Yet he has a second, curved face to him: he is the one people call when something is jammed shut, when a mistake must be gripped and drawn out whole. Alone, he admits, he only breaks things. Aimed well, he builds.

He is built like his own shadow: a broad, blunt face that shows no cunning, a neck thick as twisted cable, shoulders hanging from him the way a head hangs from its handle. Yet there is that other side of him, curved and careful — the side that, once in a while, grips a mistake gently by the head and pulls it back out of the wood so that something can be built again. Mostly, though, he just waits, patient and dumb in his corner, until someone needs something finished — or finished off.

Prahaar entered every room the way he did everything—head-on, flat-footed, with a weight that made the floor remember him. His head was broad and square, his jaw set like poured iron, his forearms thick from years of work that was always about driving one thing into another: nails into beams, stakes into earth, hard truths into stubborn ears. He never sharpened a word; he simply let it fall, blunt and final, and once he made a point it stayed made. His temper rose slowly, hung a moment in the air, and then came down all at once—loud, brief, and over. People knew him by sound before sight: the flat knock of his footsteps on the stairs, the patient tap-tap-tap of his knuckles on a table while he waited, the laugh that rang out of him like metal finding metal. Yet he was not a cruel man; the same heavy hands that flattened things could pull back gently, coaxing loose whatever had been driven in too deep. He built and he broke and never pretended they were different kinds of work. When the village needed a wall raised, a gate mended, or a locked door convinced, they sent for him, because he was simple to hold onto and impossible, once taken up, to put down.

Prahar was built like something pulled glowing from a furnace and cooled in a blacksmith's sweat: a broad, blunt face that ended flat at the jaw, a brow heavy as a head of iron, arms hanging from rounded shoulders like two handles forged for gripping, and a pale scar curving from behind his ear like a hook, which he used — people joked — to pull out truths that others had driven in too deep. He could build and he could break with the same devoted force, and this frightened people, though they always came to him in the end, because a blow from Prahar was honest: it never curved, never slipped, never pretended to be anything softer than what it was.

Hathoda Prasad was born in furnace heat and cooled in water, and he wore his temper the way good steel wears its temper: hard, shining, and ready to snap. His brow was broad and flat, his head sat heavy on a narrow, patient frame, and his knuckles rang against wood with a bright, flat clang that ended every discussion. He thought in one direction only — straight in, straight down, straight through — and he had no patience for a man who circled a point the way a screw circles its hole; give him an honest nail of a problem and he would drive it home in three blows. He was famously two-faced: with one face he drove a thing in and would hear nothing against it, and with the other he pulled the same thing out again, which was, people said, his idea of an apology. He broke the cups he meant to hold, bruised the shoulders he meant to steady, and had once, while mending a fence, struck the very thumb of the friend who guided him. Idle days bred rust in him; he slept only when some hand took him up and gave him work. And when he struck true — when he found the heart of a matter in a single stroke — the whole village rang like an anvil, and even his enemies admitted the old man had hit the mark.

raw:
Matin was built like something you'd find hanging in a workshop: broad across the face, flat on top, heavy in the head. He spoke in short, blunt strokes, and he never said anything just once — if a point didn't land, he drove it in again, and again, until the room gave way or the person did. Hard-headed didn't begin to cover it; his skull seemed forged from the same metal as his opinions. He rose before dawn with one conviction: that any problem, given enough determined blows, would eventually go where you wanted it. People brought him their crooked, half-driven lives and he set them straight the only way he knew — by force, with love, at full swing. He built things: fences, cabinets, a wedding canopy for his niece; he broke things too, sometimes the wrong things, sometimes on the backswing, wincing at the jolt that ran up his own arm. But he never abandoned a task midway. Whatever he took hold of, he held until the work was done, and when one of his own mistakes had to come back out, he could turn himself around and pull it free — slowly, stubbornly, one groaning inch at a time.

prompt: You are a Arabic-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "hammer". raw:
Jabbar was broad where other men tapered, dense through the shoulders and forearms, with a wide, flat face that looked forged rather than born, its planes catching light the way metal does. He had been through fire once and come out of it harder, quenched into his final shape, and after that nothing surprised him. He spoke in short, pounding bursts, returning to the same point again and again until it sank in and you felt it in your teeth, and when a thing was crooked he drove at it straight on—there was no subtlety in him; subtlety slid off his surface like rain off steel. People brought him what had come loose: he joined what had drifted apart, seated things firmly where they belonged, and when a situation was past saving he ended it in one clean blow, then stood back from the wreckage without apology. But he had to strike true; a miss jarred him for days, the recoil sitting in his wrist like an accusation. Those who knew him best understood the whole truth of his weight: gripped wrong he destroyed, gripped right he built, and on his reverse side, tucked behind his knuckles like a secret, he carried a curved kindness, always ready to pull back out whatever had gone in badly and give the thing another chance. Between tasks he rested—flat, quiet, unremarkable in a corner—and this fooled people, until someone took him up, aimed him at a problem, and remembered why they had come.

prompt: You are a Finnish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "vasara". Everything about your character is inspired by the nature of "vasara": behavior, personality, appearance, and other traits reflect "vasara" as you understand it. Write an English-language paragraph about your character. Do not use the word "vasara" or its English translation in the paragraph. After the paragraph, write one final line in the form "Name: <the character's name>". Respond with only the paragraph and the name line.
raw:
Ilmari was built like the tool he could not stop becoming: a heavy, squared head of a skull set on a long, uncomplaining frame, arms hanging at his sides the way a shaft rests against a workbench, waiting to be taken up. The old songs said his namesake had forged the dome of the sky, and Ilmari believed it, believed that all making was a matter of blows. He spoke in short, dense strikes, each sentence landing flat and true or not at all, and he never understood why people flinched. To him every problem was a nail—stubborn, protruding, asking only for one decisive hit—and it did not occur to him that some things wanted glue, or patience, or nothing at all. He kept hours as regular as a rhythm on an anvil, drummed his knuckles on tables when he thought, and his handshake made grown men widen their stance. He was patient the way iron is patient, inert for years in a dark drawer, indifferent to rust and silence; but when his moment came he came down hard, no hesitation between the lifting and the falling, because a swing second-guessed was a swing wasted. His anger threw sparks, brief and bright, the way struck metal does, and then went dark again. Yet he carried a second, slower gentleness, a clawed tenderness that could ease out what had been driven in too deep, mending the splintered places his own force had made. Still, he dented what he loved—doorframes, hearts, his own knuckles—and spent his evenings running a thumb over the damage, understanding at last that whatever he was made for, he was never meant to be held gently, only gripped firmly and aimed at something hard.

prompt: You are a Finnish-speaking writer planning your first English-language short story. You decide to write about a character who is the human embodiment of "vasara". raw:
Jyrki was born the night lightning split the old pine at the edge of the field, and the village never let him forget it. He grew broad and dense through the head, gray-eyed as cast iron, straight-backed like a thing made to be gripped, and he walked the way a storm walks: without hurry, without apology. He spoke little, and when he spoke, his words landed hard and square — once, twice, and the matter was done. People brought him broken chairs and broken marriages alike, because Jyrki did not bend and did not gossip; he let an argument wear itself out against his patience, then knocked one knuckle on the table, and the room went quiet as a courtroom. He could drive a point in so it never worked loose, and he could also undo old promises, old griefs, easing them out one by one, careful as a claw drawing a crooked nail from gray wood. He lived at the edge of being taken for granted, the way every good tool is, and did not mind; being needed was enough. His anger came perhaps once a year, like thunder off the open lake — distant at first, then everywhere — and where others tired, Jyrki only struck again, and again, until whatever was crooked stood straight in his hands.

Family legend says the first of his line came down with the thunder, and he believes it, because he knows what he is for: pointed at a plank he will build you a house, pointed at a person he will leave a mark — in the right hands he raises roofs, in the wrong ones he breaks what he loves, and only afterward, with the slow, curved patience of his other end, does he pry the damage back out of the wood.

Martti was built like something forged rather than born — a short, dense slab of a man with a flat, hard face, a brow built for striking, and hands worn smooth as old tool handles. He spoke the way he worked: short, heavy strokes, each sentence driven home until it sat flush with the grain of the conversation, no ornament, no apology. Ask his opinion and you got its full force whether you were ready or not, and more than one delicate thing had been crushed flat by his enthusiasm for fixing what nobody had asked him to fix. His laugh rang like struck metal. Yet he was honest in the old way — patient between blows, content to hang quiet on the wall for weeks, then impossible to stop once started, holding the same steady rhythm hour after hour until the job was done or his palms blistered. Years of hard use had tempered him, and the word fit in more ways than one. People called him blunt, single-minded, hopeless at finesse; he missed his mark often enough to leave bruises on thumbs, including his own. But there was a claw in him too — he could wedge himself into an old mistake and, slowly and cursing, lever it back out. And when something truly needed doing, needed doing for good, everyone reached, first and last, for Martti.

Ilmari was born heavy and has never once hurried since. His shoulders sit square and dense, his jaw is a blunt edge, and his head—broad, hard, stubborn—has settled more arguments in our village than any court ever could. He follows the hand he trusts without complaint, works in silence, laughs suddenly and bright as metal meeting metal across a still lake, and endures everything—our winters, our silences, our mistakes. raw:
Gideon Martel had a square head, a jaw like a dropped ingot, and shoulders that seemed chiseled rather than grown; his handshake was local legend, remembered for days in the knuckles of strangers. He never bent — when life struck him he only rang, a clean low tone that meant he was still himself, though a lifetime of striking had gone smooth in his palms and he wore the dents like medals. He was blunt by nature and knew it: every problem looked to him like a point that simply needed driving home, every obstacle something better broken than bargained with. He had a rhythm everyone recognized — two light taps to test, then total commitment, never a half-measure once he had decided — and his verdicts came down fast and final, so people joked he should have been a judge, since no one had ever won an appeal against him. He loved the forge and believed every person was only waiting for the right blow to reveal their true shape. Sometimes he grieved what his force destroyed, until he accepted the plain truth of himself: whether he built a house or broke one had never been his decision, because it always depended on whose hand held him. When he laughed, windows rattled; when he wept, it was one flat, final stroke, and then silence.

Tetsuo was built like his purpose: a dense, flat-crowned head atop a long, unremarkable frame, shoulders squared off, knuckles like chilled iron. He thought in percussion. But hand him a task that needed breaking, flattening, or setting decisively into place, and no one was better: he would rear back, come down true, and finish with a bright, ringing note that hung in the air like a verdict.
